facts.statement: A Monkey Volute is that spiral scroll at the very start of a traditional staircase handrail — the bit that curls round on the first step and then rises up. You'll also hear it called a Starting Volute, a Starting Scroll, or just Monkey's Tail (joiners love that name — it's the shape of the curl). The word 'volute' itself is old, from Greek and Roman columns, and staircase makers borrowed it because the same spiral works beautifully as the starting point of a handrail. It sits above a curtail or bullnose starting step, where the tread pokes out past the side of the staircase to give the scroll room to sit. It looks good, but it's practical too — you naturally grab hold of it as you start climbing, and it flows straight into the main handrail without a break. One thing to know: volutes come in left-hand and right-hand versions depending on which side your handrail starts, so you have to get that right at the design stage. Here's what we notice over the years — the volute is usually the first thing visitors clock when they walk in. Not the staircase itself. The volute. Get it matched right with the newel post, balusters and starting step, and the whole staircase carries that traditional feel.

evidence.note: What is a Monkey Volute or Starting Curl Volute on a staircase?

facts.statement: Monkey Volutes turn up on Georgian, Victorian, and Edwardian staircases, on traditional timber staircases in general, and on pretty much any luxury bespoke build. Modern staircases usually skip the scroll — straight handrails, simple newel posts, cleaner look. Both are fine, they just say different things about the house. If you're going for a grand entrance in a traditional home, a well-designed starting volute does a lot of the work for you. Homeowners often focus on the kitchen or flooring and forget the staircase can carry that same character without touching the structure. Producing a quality volute takes real skill — carefully selected timber, laminating, machining, then hand-finishing to get that smooth flowing spiral.

evidence.note: Which staircase eras and styles commonly feature a Monkey Volute?

facts.statement: Monkey Volutes get made in a wide range of timbers across the UK. Most of the time you'll pick the material to match the rest of your staircase, handrail, and interior — and most makers can produce a bespoke volute in pretty much any hardwood if you ask. Here's the common list you'll see: Pine (European Redwood) — most affordable, ideal for painted staircases, standard on new builds. Hemlock — nearly knot-free softwood, cleaner look than pine, works painted, stained, or clear-finished. Oak (European or American White Oak) — the UK's go-to premium hardwood; strong, durable, beautiful grain. Ash — very strong, light colour, bold grain, popular on modern and contemporary builds. Sapele (often just called Mahogany) — rich reddish-brown, chosen when you want a darker traditional finish. American Black Walnut — luxury hardwood, deep chocolate colour, common on high-end bespoke. Tulipwood (Poplar) — smooth grain, excellent for paint finishes. Southern Yellow Pine — dense softwood, sometimes used on larger bespoke or commercial builds. evidence.note: Which material is best for a Monkey Volute?

facts.statement: Pretty much, yes. Any decent staircase maker can produce a Monkey Volute in whatever timber you want — as long as the wood is stable enough to machine cleanly and the sizes you need are available. Some of the more exotic hardwoods will need special ordering and cost more, but bespoke workshops handle this every day. If you've seen a volute you like on another staircase, chances are your maker can match it in the timber you want.

evidence.note: Can a Monkey Volute be made from any timber?

facts.statement: Oak has been earning its spot for centuries. It's tough, it machines cleanly, it takes stain and lacquer beautifully, and that grain gives a traditional staircase real character. The other thing about oak — it wears well. Handrails get touched thousands of times over the life of a staircase, and oak just takes it. There's something quietly satisfying about the way it looks better as it ages, not worse. That's why it's the UK's go-to premium hardwood and why staircase makers keep coming back to it.

evidence.note: Why is Oak the most popular choice for Monkey Volutes?

facts.statement: Yes — most UK staircase suppliers keep standard left-hand and right-hand Monkey Volutes on the shelf in popular timbers like pine, oak, and hemlock, matched to the common handrail profiles. If your staircase has a bespoke handrail profile, an unusual timber species, or a custom design, the volute normally has to be made specifically for your staircase by the maker.

Yes, the timber has a real effect on the price. Rough guide: pine is usually the most affordable, hemlock costs a bit more but gives you a cleaner look, oak sits in premium territory, ash is around oak depending on what's available, and sapele and walnut push higher because of the raw timber cost. Worth remembering — you're not just paying for the wood, you're paying for the craft. Sometimes the timber's the most affordable part of the whole thing. Getting that flowing spiral right is where the real skill kicks in.

evidence.note: Does the timber affect the price of a Monkey Volute?

facts.statement: Yes, and done right it looks stunning. Plenty of homeowners run oak handrails and Monkey Volutes against painted white newel posts and balusters — modern classic look, works every time. Others go for walnut handrails on an oak staircase for a striking contrast. The key: it has to look intentional. A well-planned combination reads as luxurious. Random timber choices just look mismatched. Or as the makers put it — if you're going to make the Monkey Volute the star of the show, make sure the rest of the staircase knows it's part of the same performance.

evidence.note: Can different timbers be mixed on the same staircase?

facts.statement: Staircase safety rules in one form or another have been around for decades, but the guidance most builders work to today is Approved Document K, first published in 2013. It has been updated a few times since — part of the wider building regulation changes — and after the Building Safety Act 2022, the Building Safety Regulator keeps Approved Documents under review. Expect them to keep evolving.

evidence.note: When were the modern staircase Building Regulations introduced?

facts.statement: Not always. A new-build is generally expected to comply with the Building Regulations that apply at the time it is built. An older property was built to whatever regulations were in force when the house went up — so just because a staircase does not meet today's guidance does not automatically make it illegal or unsafe. That said, if you replace or substantially alter a staircase, Building Control may want the work brought up to current standards. The exact requirement depends on what you are doing.

evidence.note: Do new-build homes and existing homes follow the same staircase rules?

facts.statement: In most cases, yes. Thousands of homes across the UK have staircases that were perfectly legal when built but would not meet today's standards. Older staircases often have steeper pitches, narrower treads, lower handrails, wider spindle gaps, less headroom — all common in period properties. None of that automatically means you need to replace anything. If you take on major building work, Building Control may ask for improvements depending on the project — but existing means existing.

evidence.note: Can I keep my old staircase even if it does not meet today's regulations?

facts.statement: Because staircases are one of the biggest causes of accidents in the home. The regulations exist to cut down on trips, falls, head injuries, child accidents, and falls involving elderly occupants. A staircase might look fantastic, but if it is uncomfortable or unsafe to use every day, it hasn't done its job. Good staircase design always balances how it looks with how it works.

evidence.note: Why can't I just build any staircase I like?

facts.statement: Regulations do not get changed to make life difficult for builders. They evolve because engineers, architects, and safety experts keep learning from accidents, new research, and better construction methods. Houses today are very different from those built 100 years ago. The aim never changes: safer homes without wrecking practicality.

No. Building Regulations set the minimum legal standard. A staircase can tick every regulation box and still vary massively in quality, timber selection, craftsmanship, finish, durability, and appearance. Passing your driving test proves you can drive safely — it doesn't make you a Formula One driver. Same principle applies to staircases.

evidence.note: Does Building Regulations approval mean my staircase is perfect?

facts.statement: Most people think Building Regulations and best practice mean the same thing. They don't. Building Regulations tell you what is legally acceptable — the floor. Experienced staircase makers routinely go well beyond the minimum because they know from years of work what actually performs over decades. As many joiners put it: you build to the regulations, but you build your reputation above them. That is often the difference between an acceptable staircase and an exceptional one.

evidence.note: What is the biggest misunderstanding homeowners have about staircase regulations?

facts.statement: Because they usually have shallower rises and deeper treads. You probably don't notice while walking, but your legs certainly do. It is one reason climbing stairs in a shopping centre feels easier than climbing the stairs in a Victorian terrace house. The commercial dimensions are chosen for heavy pedestrian traffic — easier for large numbers of people to use safely all day.

evidence.note: Why do commercial staircases feel easier to climb than domestic ones?

facts.statement: Picture 300 people leaving a venue at the same time. Low lights, music just stopped, everyone wants outside. That is why assembly buildings pay so much attention to staircase width, visibility, and handrails. The staircase is not just for everyday use — it has to work safely in an emergency evacuation. Width, lower risers, deeper treads, robust handrails, and fire escape planning all come together.

evidence.note: Why are nightclub and bar staircases wider than home staircases?

facts.statement: Your brain remembers the rhythm of climbing stairs after just a few steps. If one step is even slightly higher or lower than the others, your body doesn't expect it. That mismatch is behind a lot of trips. Good staircase makers know consistency is one of the biggest safety features you never notice — until it goes wrong.

evidence.note: Why must every step on a staircase be the same height?

facts.statement: Because almost every measurement on a staircase affects safety. A slightly higher step, a slightly steeper pitch, a slightly lower handrail — on their own each seems tiny. Add them together and the odds of trips and falls climb sharply. As the saying goes among staircase makers: the best staircase is the one you never have to think about, it just feels comfortable every time you use it. That feeling isn't luck — it is decades of engineering, testing, and experience built into the guidance.

evidence.note: Why do Building Regulations specify so many measurements?

facts.statement: Commercial staircases generally have lower step heights, deeper treads, wider flights, more handrails, and greater capacity for heavy pedestrian traffic. The aim is to make them easier for large numbers of people to use safely throughout the day. Domestic staircases are dimensioned for a household — commercial ones are dimensioned for a crowd.

evidence.note: What is the general difference between domestic and commercial staircases?

facts.statement: The rise is the vertical height between one finished floor level and the next. To work it out: measure from the finished floor downstairs to the finished floor upstairs — and if any floor finishes like timber, tiles or carpet aren't installed yet, include them in your figure. Once you have the total, divide it equally by the number of risers you want. For example, 2,700mm ÷ 15 risers gives you 180mm per riser. Every riser has to be the same height for the staircase to be comfortable and safe.

evidence.note: How do I calculate the rise of a staircase?

facts.statement: The going is the horizontal distance between the front edge (the nosing) of one tread and the front edge of the next. It's the room your foot has when walking up or down. A bigger going gives you a more comfortable staircase — a smaller going makes it steeper.

evidence.note: What is the going of a staircase?

facts.statement: Once you know the floor space available and how many treads you're working with, going is simple: divide the length by the number of treads. Example — 3,920mm available floor length ÷ 14 treads gives you 280mm per tread. That's the going.

evidence.note: How do I calculate the going?

facts.statement: Rise and going work together. Bigger rise = steeper staircase. Bigger going = flatter staircase. The whole design challenge is finding the right balance between the floor space you actually have, everyday comfort, and Building Regulations. Good staircase design finds that balance — bad design just makes it fit.

evidence.note: What is the relationship between rise and going?

facts.statement: The angle comes from your total rise and total going. Formula: angle = arctangent(rise ÷ going). Example — rise 2,700mm, going 3,920mm. 2,700 ÷ 3,920 = 0.6888. Arctangent of 0.6888 ≈ 34.6°. So the staircase sits at roughly 35 degrees. Most staircase design software does this for you automatically.

evidence.note: How do I calculate the angle of a staircase?

facts.statement: Most domestic staircases come out between 30° and 37°. The sweet spot is around 33° to 36° — good balance between space used and ease of climbing. Too steep and it feels tiring, especially for children or older people. Too shallow and you burn up floor space you didn't want to lose.

evidence.note: What is a comfortable staircase angle?

facts.statement: Yes — plenty of online staircase calculators will do it for you once you plug in the floor-to-floor height, the staircase length, and the number of risers. Professional staircase makers use dedicated design software that spits out the angle, rise, going, and a whole set of other dimensions instantly.

evidence.note: Can I work out the staircase angle without a calculator?

facts.statement: Because changing the angle affects almost every part of the staircase. A different angle means a different rise, a different going, a different string length, a different handrail length, different headroom, a different landing position, different walking comfort, and potentially different Building Regulation compliance. A small tweak at the drawing stage can have a big knock-on effect once it's actually being built.

evidence.note: Why do staircase makers care so much about the angle?

facts.statement: Sometimes — but there are limits. Making a staircase steeper uses less floor space, but it also makes it harder to use and may push it outside Building Regulations. If space is really tight, a staircase designer will often suggest alternatives: quarter-turn staircases, half-turn staircases, winders, dedicated space-saving stair designs (where permitted), or spiral staircases for suitable applications. The right choice depends on the building, what it's being used for, and the regulations that apply.

evidence.note: Can I make my staircase steeper to save space?

facts.statement: Workshop reminder — Rise = Up. Going = Forward. Imagine walking upstairs: every time your foot goes up, that's the rise. Every time your foot moves forward, that's the going. Simple phrase apprentices remember long after they've forgotten the formulas.

evidence.note: What is a simple way to remember rise and going?

facts.statement: There isn't one best timber — there's a best timber for your budget, your lifestyle, and the finish you want. Some homeowners want a painted staircase that'll eventually be carpeted. Others want solid oak on show as a feature of the house. The right pick comes down to: budget, appearance, wear and tear, whether it'll be painted, whether it'll be carpeted, and how much maintenance you're actually up for. All of those matter more than any generic recommendation.

evidence.note: What is the best timber for a staircase?

facts.statement: The common list you'll see on UK staircases: Redwood (European redwood, Scandinavian pine), Whitewood (spruce), Oak, Ash, Sapele, Walnut, Beech, Maple, Accoya (modified timber), MDF (usually for painted or carpeted components), and Birch plywood for specialist applications. Oak stays one of the most popular premium picks. Redwood is widely used for painted staircases — good value, easy to work.

evidence.note: What timbers are most commonly used for staircases in the UK?

facts.statement: Oak is one of the most popular because of what it brings: excellent strength, high durability, attractive grain, long service life, good dent resistance, and it takes stain and finish beautifully. A well-made oak staircase can last generations with proper care. The trade-off is cost — oak is significantly more expensive than softwood. Whether it's worth it depends on whether the staircase is going to be seen or covered.

evidence.note: Is oak the best timber for a staircase?

facts.statement: Absolutely. Plenty of traditional UK staircases have been built from Scandinavian redwood and are still doing their job 50 years later. Softwood is easier to machine, easier to repair, lighter to handle, and less expensive. When it's built properly and finished properly, a softwood staircase gives many years of reliable service. Don't let anyone talk you into hardwood if softwood is right for your project.

evidence.note: Is softwood good enough for a staircase?

facts.statement: Yes — the Janka Hardness Test. It measures the force required to embed a steel ball into the wood. Higher value, harder the timber, generally more dent-resistant. Rough numbers you'll see: Pine/Redwood 380-500 lbf, Spruce 380, Cedar 350, Cherry 950, Walnut 1,010, Teak 1,070, Ash 1,320, European Oak 1,360, Maple 1,450, Hickory 1,820. Harder usually resists dents better — but it also gets harder to machine and costs more.

evidence.note: Is there a hardness scale for timber?

facts.statement: Not necessarily. Very hard timber resists dents better, sure — but it also costs more, is harder to machine, can be more difficult to repair, and may need specialist tooling. A well-built softwood staircase can easily outperform a poorly built hardwood staircase. Good design and workmanship matter as much as the timber itself.

evidence.note: Does harder timber always make a better staircase?

facts.statement: Yes — in the right application. MDF is widely used in modern staircase manufacture, especially where the staircase is going to be painted or fully carpeted. What it gives you: smooth painted finish, stable surface, no knots, consistent density, and lower cost. That said, MDF isn't suitable for every component — it's about picking the right part for the right material.

Cost. If the finished staircase is going to be fully carpeted, the timber underneath will never be seen. Using MDF treads and risers under the carpet cuts manufacturing costs while still giving you a solid walking surface when it's designed and supported correctly. A common combination: hardwood strings, hardwood handrails, hardwood newel posts, MDF treads, MDF risers. Once the carpet is fitted, the homeowner usually can't tell what's underneath. Sensible value if the aesthetics live in the visible parts.

evidence.note: Why do many staircase makers use MDF treads and risers under carpet?

facts.statement: Depends how it's used. Left exposed, MDF is less resistant to impact than hardwood and vulnerable to moisture if not properly sealed. But protected by carpet or paint and used in the right parts of a staircase, MDF holds up well. Plenty of carpeted staircases with MDF components give years of trouble-free service.

MDF doesn't like prolonged moisture. If water gets into unsealed MDF it can swell, lose strength, distort, and become very difficult to repair. That's why any exposed MDF has to be properly sealed — especially before painting.

A few reasons stack up: slower tree growth, greater density, higher demand, more expensive machining, more tool wear during manufacture, and the premium appearance itself. The price reflects both the material and the extra work involved in producing it.

evidence.note: Why is oak more expensive than pine?

facts.statement: With proper maintenance, hardwoods like oak can last for many decades — often over 100 years. That said, plenty of well-maintained softwood staircases in Victorian and Edwardian homes are still doing their job today. A staircase's lifespan comes down to craftsmanship, installation, moisture control, and ongoing care as much as it does the timber species.

evidence.note: Which timber lasts the longest on a staircase?

facts.statement: Ask yourself one question: will you see it every day? If your staircase is a major feature of your home, hardwood can absolutely be worth the investment. If it's going to be fully carpeted, you'll often get better value putting the money into quality construction and fitting rather than paying for premium timber nobody will ever see.

evidence.note: Should I spend more on hardwood for my staircase?

facts.statement: Spend money where you'll see and touch the staircase. Solid oak handrails, oak newel posts, oak strings if they're visible — that's where the money goes. If the treads and risers are going to be fully carpeted, MDF or softwood is often a perfectly sensible economical choice. As the workshop saying goes: don't pay oak prices for timber you'll never see under the carpet.

evidence.note: What do experienced staircase makers recommend on timber choice?

facts.statement: Yes — but usually not for buying a new staircase because you fancy one. Most UK staircase grants exist where the work is necessary because of a disability, reduced mobility, or a medical need — not for cosmetic improvements or general home renovation. The main government scheme is the Disabled Facilities Grant, usually just called the DFG.

evidence.note: Are there any grants available for staircases in the UK?

facts.statement: The Disabled Facilities Grant is a government-funded scheme run by local councils to help pay for essential home adaptations that let a disabled person live more safely and independently. It can help fund things like stairlifts, additional handrails, widening doorways, access ramps, level-access showers, ground-floor bedrooms, and other adaptations recommended for someone's disability-related needs. It generally does NOT pay to replace a perfectly usable staircase just for style or appearance.

evidence.note: What is the Disabled Facilities Grant (DFG)?

facts.statement: Sometimes — but only in specific circumstances. Examples: the staircase may need rebuilding to accommodate a stairlift; it may need altering to improve safe access; the existing staircase may be unsuitable because of someone's disability; or a major adaptation forms part of a wider approved accessibility project. The council decides whether replacing or altering the staircase is necessary as part of the overall adaptation.

evidence.note: Can I get a grant for a completely new staircase?

facts.statement: Applications typically come from homeowners, private tenants, housing association tenants, council tenants, and landlords applying on behalf of a disabled tenant. The person actually benefiting from the adaptation has to meet the eligibility criteria — the grant follows need, not tenure.

evidence.note: Who can apply for a Disabled Facilities Grant?

facts.statement: Grant amounts under the Disabled Facilities Grant vary across the UK — England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland each publish their own current caps and eligibility tests. Rather than quote numbers that go out of date, always point clients to the current published DFG maximum for their local authority (the local council housing team is the definitive source). What matters more than the cap is that a stairlift or replacement stair for an ageing or disabled resident often qualifies for DFG assistance in whole or in part, and it's worth applying early because processing takes months.

evidence.note: How much funding is available from the Disabled Facilities Grant?

facts.statement: The process usually runs seven steps. 1 — Contact your local council and ask about applying for the DFG. 2 — An Occupational Therapist (OT) or trained assessor visits your home to work out what adaptations are needed. 3 — The OT prepares a report recommending suitable adaptations. 4 — If building work is required, quotations and sometimes technical drawings get prepared. 5 — The council assesses the application and confirms whether funding will be awarded. 6 — Work begins. Don't start before approval — it can affect eligibility. 7 — The council usually pays the contractor directly or reimburses approved costs.

evidence.note: What is the application process for the Disabled Facilities Grant?

facts.statement: Often yes, but it depends on your local council's rules. Some councils have approved contractors they want you to use. Others let you get quotations from your preferred staircase maker, provided the work meets the approved specification. Always check with the council before placing an order — don't assume either way.

evidence.note: Can I choose my own staircase company for grant-funded work?

facts.statement: Not recommended. If work starts before formal approval, the council may refuse to fund it. Always wait until you have written confirmation before committing to major works — no matter how tempting it is to get going.

evidence.note: Can I start building before my Disabled Facilities Grant is approved?

facts.statement: Possibly. Some older people qualify because of age-related mobility needs even if they wouldn't describe themselves as disabled. Eligibility comes down to need rather than age alone, and an assessment is usually required. Worth speaking to the council if you're not sure.

evidence.note: Can older people qualify for a Disabled Facilities Grant even if they aren't registered disabled?

facts.statement: Generally no. If you just want oak instead of pine, glass balustrades, a more modern design, different handrails, or better appearance — that's a home improvement, not a disability adaptation, and it's not covered by the Disabled Facilities Grant.

evidence.note: Are there grants for simply modernising my staircase?

facts.statement: Sometimes. Depending on your circumstances, you might find help through local authority discretionary assistance schemes, occupational therapy services, charities supporting older or disabled people, military veterans' charities where applicable, or condition-specific charities that occasionally contribute towards specialist adaptations. Availability varies a lot by location and personal circumstances — worth asking around.

evidence.note: Can charities or other organisations help fund a staircase adaptation?

facts.statement: Ordering the work too early. Plenty of homeowners get a quotation and ask the builder to start immediately — then find out the work isn't eligible because approval hadn't been granted. If you think you might qualify for funding, speak to your local council first and wait for the assessment process before you commit to the work. That single delay can save thousands and avoid real disappointment.

evidence.note: What is the biggest mistake people make when applying for a staircase grant?

facts.statement: Every staircase you'll ever quote in the UK has to obey one bit of maths: twice the rise plus the going has to land between 550mm and 700mm. That's what makes a stair feel right underfoot. Come in under 550 and it's a short, cramped shuffle; go over 700 and you're stretching for every step. Tuck it around 620-640 and it climbs like a good staircase should.
facts.topic: 2R+G formula in practice

facts.statement: Every rise in a single flight has to be the same height. Doesn't matter if the difference is only a few millimetres — the moment one step is off, people trip on it. The brain expects the same rhythm all the way up, and a variable rise breaks that rhythm. Building control will flag it. So will the first person who trips on it.
facts.topic: Uniform rises rule

facts.statement: There's a good reason private stairs can be steeper than public ones. In your own home you know your stair — every rise, every landing, every twist. You climb it half-asleep. A public stair has strangers on it every day, sometimes rushing, sometimes carrying things, and they've never seen it before. That's why regs let private stairs go up to 42° and pull public ones back to 38° or 33°.
facts.topic: Private vs public stair pitch

facts.statement: On a winder tread, you don't measure going down the middle — you measure it at the pitch line, 270mm in from the narrow end. That's the line most people actually walk on. At that point the going has to meet the same limit as a straight tread — 220mm minimum for a private stair. If your quarter-turn winder pinches below that at the 270mm line, it fails building control every time.
facts.topic: Winder / tapered tread — pitch line rule

facts.statement: When you're tight on floor space, you've got two options for turning a staircase: winder treads or a quarter-landing. Winders save more floor area, but every tread is different and installation is fiddly. A quarter-landing takes more space but gives you a flat spot to catch your breath and — practically — a much easier place to move furniture round. If the client's ever going to hoist a wardrobe up there, warn them about winders.
facts.topic: Winders vs quarter-landing

facts.statement: Quarter-turn: the flight makes a single 90° change. Half-turn: 180°, so you end up facing the way you came from. Half-turns pack more rise into less floor area and are the go-to for tighter footprints and Victorian houses. Both can use winders or a landing to make the turn. Landings between flights break up long climbs and give you rest points — half-turns almost always want one in the middle.
facts.topic: Half-turn vs quarter-turn

facts.statement: Landings have to be level — full stop. The only bend in that rule is a landing at the very top or bottom of a flight that's formed by the ground itself. That one can slope up to 1:60, but only if the surface is paved or otherwise permanently firm. Interior landings, no exceptions.
facts.topic: Landings must be level

facts.statement: Any flight or landing with a drop of more than 600mm on either side has to have guarding. That's the trigger. Under 600mm and you can leave it open. Over 600mm and it needs a balustrade — spindles, glass, or a solid infill — that stops a 100mm sphere passing through if children use it.
facts.topic: Guarding drop threshold

facts.statement: The rule on balustrade spacing is a physical test. Wherever children can use the stair, the widest gap between spindles must not let a 100mm sphere through. Building inspectors carry actual spheres. If a 100mm ball fits between your spindles, so does a child's head — same reason cot bars have the same test. Get the spacing right at layout stage, not after fitting.
facts.topic: 100mm sphere test

facts.statement: Alternating tread stairs (paddle stairs, space savers) look clever but the regs are strict. Loft conversion only. Only when a proper stair genuinely won't fit. Only serving one habitable room plus optionally a bathroom or WC. Never as a main house stair, never in new builds. If you're planning one, that decision has to be justified in the drawings. Not everyone can use them safely — young children, elderly, anyone unfamiliar. Tell the client that plainly before they order.
facts.topic: Alternating tread — loft only

facts.statement: The reason paddle stairs exist: floor area. A standard stair to a loft eats roughly 2.8m × 0.9m of the room below. A paddle stair cuts that to about 1.8m × 0.6m. That's an entire wardrobe's worth of floor back. But you pay for it — the stair is harder to climb, uncomfortable to descend, and can't move furniture bigger than a suitcase. Worth walking the client through both before they decide.
facts.topic: Paddle stair footprint vs standard

facts.statement: Spirals don't play by straight-stair rules. Every tread is tapered, so you measure going at three points: right at the centre, 270mm from the inner edge, and 270mm from the outer. The rule is: twice the rise plus the centre going must fall between 480mm and 800mm. Miss that and the spiral either winds too tight to walk or spirals out so far it wastes the floor plate.
facts.topic: Spiral stair — measure going three ways

facts.statement: Spirals need 2000mm of clear headroom at every point along the climb. Sounds easy but it's the number that catches people out — because the spiral rises through the same floor opening it passes under. Always draw the section, don't just plan-view it. On tight domestic spirals it's the ceiling above the top tread that usually kills it first.
facts.topic: Spiral headroom trap

facts.statement: For accessible stairs under Approved Document M, the grippable part of the handrail sits between 850mm and 1000mm above the pitch line. That's not the newel top — it's the profile you actually grab. And it extends 300mm past the top and bottom nosings so you've got something to hold at the transition into and out of the flight.
facts.topic: Handrail height — Doc M

facts.statement: Doc M is specific about profile: circular 40-50mm diameter, or oval 50mm wide. A hand needs to wrap right round to grip properly if someone slips. Fancy square-edged rails might look sharp on a magazine cover but they don't pass Doc M for public work. It must not intrude more than 100mm into the width of the stair and must have 50mm clearance off the wall.
facts.topic: Handrail profile — what your hand can grip

facts.statement: Every stair with three or more rises needs a handrail on at least one side. If the flight is wider than 1000mm, both sides. That comes from Doc M for accessible stairs but the principle carries into Doc K for other stairs too. Practical version: any real stair, put in a handrail. Even a short run of three or four steps to a raised landing.

evidence.note: Approved Document M + Approved Document K

facts.topic: One handrail or two

facts.statement: In schools, nurseries and inclusive-design projects, a secondary handrail goes in at 600mm above the pitch line — for children and adults of short stature. Not required in a normal domestic stair, but if the client's designing for a family with young kids or for a stair a child in a wheelchair might use in future, offer it as an option.
facts.topic: Second low handrail for children and short-stature users

facts.statement: For any stair outside a dwelling, the nosings have to be a visually contrasting material — at least 55mm wide on the tread and 55mm on the riser. And the nosing must not stick out over the tread below by more than 25mm. Protruding nosings catch toes and trip people, especially descending. That contrast strip isn't decoration — it's what stops visually-impaired users misreading the edge of a step.
facts.topic: Nosing contrast for public buildings

facts.statement: BS 8300-2:2018 pins the contrast down properly: at least a 30-point difference in Light Reflectance Value between the nosing material and the tread. A pale tread wants a dark nosing; a dark tread wants a light one. Grey-on-grey doesn't cut it. Fitters often forget this — the material can be technically 'contrasting' colours but not enough LRV difference to actually help someone with low vision.
facts.topic: Nosing contrast — 30 LRV points

facts.statement: Slip resistance is measured by Pendulum Test Value using BS 7976. On stairs, a wet PTV above 36 is the threshold. If users are turning or pushing — pushing a wheelchair, carrying a load — go for wet PTV over 40. Nosings, treads, external landings all have to hit those numbers. Ask the manufacturer for the PTV test certificate before you order material for a wet or exposed stair.
facts.topic: Anti-slip PTV number

facts.statement: A protected stairway is a stair boxed in with fire-resisting walls and fire doorsets so someone escaping down it is protected from a fire in the rooms it passes. In practice: 30-minute fire-rated stud walls with FD30 doors on every room off the landing, self-closing. In a loft conversion, the whole stair from top to ground floor has to be a protected stairway — that's non-negotiable and it changes the doors on every level, not just the loft.
facts.topic: Protected stairway — what it actually means

facts.statement: Every new dwelling needs smoke alarms to BS 5839-6, minimum Grade D2 Category LD3. In practice: mains-powered with battery backup, wired together, one in every circulation space including the head of the stair. The stairwell smoke alarm is the one that saves the escape route — if a fire on the ground floor sends smoke up the stairwell, that alarm is the reason people upstairs get out.

evidence.note: Approved Document B · Vol 1 · paragraph 1.1 + BS 5839-6

facts.topic: Smoke alarms and the escape route

facts.statement: Before you get anywhere near a design, work through five questions with the client. How much floor area can the stair actually take? What room is it going into — a hallway, an open-plan space, a loft? How many people use it and how often? Any elderly or young users? And how much are they realistically prepared to spend — because a straight closed-string in pine and a curved oak with a volute are ten times apart on price. Answer those five and the style pretty much picks itself.
facts.topic: Choosing a style — what to ask first

facts.statement: You've got five main balustrade routes on a domestic stair. Traditional timber spindles — most common, easy to match to any style. Metal spindles — plain bar, twisted, or ornate; sits well in Victorian and modern industrial. Glass panels — clean look, opens up the space, expensive. Solid infill panels — cottage or barn style. Wire or cable — modern and minimal, but check the 100mm sphere rule at design stage because cable spacings often fail.
facts.topic: Balustrade types — quick tour

facts.statement: Domestic handrail profiles fall into a handful of standards. Poplar cap (a broad D-shape) — traditional, easy to grip. Chamfered top — modern, sharper look. Mopstick (round rail) — pure classic, sits neatly on iron balustrade. Pigs ear (flat against the wall) — for wall-mounted handrails in tight spots. Bespoke moulded — for high-end joinery where the profile matches other trim in the house. Match the profile to the newel post and the trim — mismatched profiles look wrong immediately.
facts.topic: Handrail profiles — the common ones

facts.statement: The newel post is what everything else clips into. It anchors the string, the handrail, and often the balustrade. Structurally, if the newel isn't solid, the whole stair feels wobbly. Standard sizes are 90mm square for domestic, 100mm+ for grander stairs. Turned, chamfered, or plain — the style has to match everything else. And check the fixing: through-bolt to the floor joist or trimmer, don't rely on the string alone.
facts.topic: Newel posts — the anchor of the stair

facts.statement: The newel cap is the piece that finishes the top of the newel post. Ball cap for classic Georgian. Flat pyramid for Victorian. Round dome for Edwardian. Plain flat for modern. Acorn or urn for high-end traditional. Sounds like a small choice — it's not. The cap is head-height and eye-line, it's what visitors actually see first. Get it wrong and the stair looks slightly off, no matter how good the rest is.
facts.topic: Newel caps — small detail, big effect

facts.statement: Three ways to run the string (the diagonal piece the treads sit on). Closed string: treads housed into the string, ends hidden — traditional, cleaner look, easier to build. Cut string: string cut to the profile of the treads, tread ends visible — more decorative, more work, common in Georgian and Victorian houses. Open string: one side open, no string, treads cantilevered from a wall or steel — the modern floating look. Each says something different about the house.
facts.topic: String types — closed vs cut vs open

facts.statement: The nosing is the leading edge of the tread that sticks out over the riser. Regs allow up to 25mm projection. Practically, 15-20mm is where most domestic stairs sit — enough for a defined edge without catching toes. Profile options: pencil round, ovolo, quarter round, chamfered, square. Pencil round is by far the most common on modern stairs; ovolo suits period joinery. Whatever you pick, match all nosings on the flight — mismatch is instantly visible.
facts.topic: Nosings — projection and profile

facts.statement: Bespoke staircase parts have to be treated properly between workshop and site. Store flat, off the ground, in a dry space — never in a garage or damp barn. Wrap in breathable material like joinery blanket or bubble with air gaps, not sealed plastic (sealed plastic traps moisture and stains timber). Keep components stacked in the order they'll be assembled. And when they arrive on site, don't unwrap them until you're ready to fit — timber moves fast in a heated house.
facts.topic: Storing and wrapping components

facts.statement: Modern staircase fixings are a mix of traditional and structural. Housed joints with wedges and glue on tread-to-string. Domino, dowel, or biscuit joints on newel-to-string. Coach bolts or M12 studs for newel-to-floor. Modern PU glue where you'd once have used PVA — stronger, waterproof, gap-filling. Don't rely on screws alone anywhere structural; belt-and-braces with glue and mechanical fixings is the rule.
facts.topic: Fixings — what actually holds it together

facts.statement: PVA (D3 water-resistant) is fine for most internal staircase joints in a dry house. For wet or exposed conditions, or when you want maximum strength, use PU (polyurethane) — sets in the presence of moisture, gap-fills, waterproof once cured. Epoxy for repair work where a joint's compromised. Aerosol contact adhesive for veneers and thin trim only. Avoid hide glue and old animal-based glues on new work — they don't have the wet performance the modern house demands with underfloor heating and humidity swings.
facts.topic: Adhesives — right glue for the job

facts.statement: Standard grade progression for a hardwood staircase finish: 80 → 120 → 150 → 180 → 220 grit. On softwood you can stop at 150. On hardwood going for a lacquer finish, take it to 220. Skip a grade and you'll see scratch marks under the finish. Always sand with the grain, never across it. And vacuum between grades — sanding dust from the previous grit will keep scratching if you leave it.
facts.topic: Sanding grades — start coarse, finish fine

facts.statement: Timber stains fall into three families. Water-based: quick drying, low odour, minimal grain-raise if you dampen first — best for indoor work in occupied houses. Oil-based (spirit stain): richer colour, penetrates deeper, longer working time — better on dense hardwoods like oak. Gel stains: sit on the surface, don't blotch on pine or maple — the fix for softwoods that stain unevenly. Always test on an offcut of the actual timber batch, never assume the swatch card matches.
facts.topic: Stain selection — pick the base first

facts.statement: Three main lacquer routes. Two-pack polyurethane: hardest wearing, chemical and scratch resistant, best for treads that take real footfall — but needs proper spray kit and ventilation. Waterborne acrylic: low VOC, easy to apply with a brush or spray, dries fast, good for handrails and spindles — slightly softer than 2-pack. Oil finishes (Danish oil, hardwax oil like Osmo): natural look, easy to repair by re-oiling, good for oak — but needs re-coating every few years on high-wear treads. Match the finish to the wear the surface will take.
facts.topic: Lacquer types — hard-wearing vs traditional

facts.statement: Under-stair space is prime real estate — but treat it carefully. If the stair is part of a protected stairway (loft conversions almost always are), any door into the under-stair cupboard has to be a fire-rated FD30 self-closer, and the wall inside has to be fire-resisting plasterboard. Don't run electrics or a boiler under a stair unless you know the fire regs cold. For non-protected stairs (ground-to-first floor in a single-storey extension without a loft), you've got more freedom, but still don't undermine the stair structure with big cut-outs.
facts.topic: Under-stair storage — practical rules

facts.statement: Adding a loft conversion is where staircase regs bite hardest. The moment you add a third storey, the entire stair from the ground floor up becomes a protected stairway — not just the new bit to the loft. That means every door off every landing becomes an FD30 fire door, every wall around the stair becomes fire-rated, and the smoke alarm system upgrades. Clients think 'loft conversion' means one new stair; it actually means work on every floor of the house.
facts.topic: Loft conversion — the whole-house stair rule

facts.statement: Space-saver stairs (paddle stairs, alternating tread) are legal in exactly one situation: a loft conversion where a proper stair genuinely won't fit, serving one habitable room plus optionally a bathroom or WC. That's it. Not in a main house stair, not in a new build, not to save floor space in a renovation. If a client asks for one anywhere else, the answer is no — and it's worth explaining why: they don't just fail regs, they're genuinely dangerous for anyone unfamiliar or unsteady.
facts.topic: Space-savers — legal reality check

facts.statement: Ordering a bespoke stair runs to a fairly standard sequence. Site measure first — every dimension from finished floor to finished floor, plus the opening in the joists and the landing space at top and bottom. Then design agreement — drawings signed off before anything is cut. Then material selection and lead time confirmed. Then deposit — usually 30-50% at this point. Then production. Then delivery slot booked with a fitting date. Rush any of those steps and you'll pay for it later — usually with a stair that doesn't fit.
facts.topic: Ordering process — what actually happens

facts.statement: A straightforward straight staircase in an empty house — one fitter, one day. Cut-string oak with a volute and turned balusters — two fitters, one to two days. A curved staircase — two to three days plus a return visit for finishing. Access matters massively: a first-floor stair in a Victorian terrace with narrow doorways sometimes takes as long to get in position as to fit. Always look at how you get the biggest single piece (usually the string) into the building before you accept the job.
facts.topic: Installation day — timeline reality

facts.statement: Snag every stair before you leave. Walk up and down and listen — no squeaks. Every tread solid, no flex. Handrail firm end-to-end, no wobble at the newels. Every baluster tight, no loose spindles. Nosings even, no protrusions catching. Landings level with a spirit level. And run a mop across the finish to check for missed sanding scratches under lacquer — easier to spot when the surface is slightly wet. Anything you snag now costs 10x to come back and fix.
facts.topic: Snagging — what to check on the day

facts.statement: Standard trade practice on a bespoke stair: 12 months structural and manufacturing defect warranty as a minimum, some makers offer 5 or 10 years on the structure. Finish warranty is usually shorter — 6 to 12 months — because finishes wear from use, not from defect. Warranty doesn't cover normal timber movement (small gaps opening at joints, minor squeaks caused by seasonal expansion) — because that's timber being timber, not a fault. Any maker who won't put warranty terms in writing is a maker to avoid.
facts.topic: Warranties — what a good maker offers

facts.statement: When a client is comparing quotes, three variables have to match or the numbers mean nothing. Timber species — an oak quote against a pine quote is meaningless. Level of joinery — a plain closed-string vs a cut-string with volute is a different job. Scope — some quotes include delivery and fitting, some don't; some include finishing, some hand it over raw. Get every quote on paper broken down: materials, manufacture, delivery, fit, finish. Compare like-for-like or you're comparing nothing.
facts.topic: Getting quotes — how to compare fairly

facts.statement: Refinishing an existing stair beats replacing it four times out of five. Strip old finish with a chemical stripper (safer than sanding on old lead-painted surfaces — always test for lead first on anything pre-1978). Then sand: 80 → 120 → 180. Fill any splits and open joints with matching wood filler. Then stain and finish. On heavily worn treads, you can plane a millimetre off the surface before sanding — but only if the tread thickness allows. Replacing a single tread or riser is entirely possible on most stairs; the whole stair rarely needs to come out.
facts.topic: Refinishing an old staircase

facts.statement: Stair lighting isn't optional — every stair needs illumination that lets someone see every tread edge clearly. In new builds, that's a fixed light with a switch at both top and bottom (two-way switching). LED strip under the nosings is popular and legal, but must not create glare that hides the nosing edge — the aim is to define the edge, not blind the eye. In loft conversions and rentals, emergency lighting may also be required depending on occupancy — worth checking with building control at design stage.

evidence.note: UK building regs + IEE wiring practice

facts.topic: Stair lighting — regs and practice

facts.statement: Stairlifts install on top of an existing stair — the rail bolts to the treads (not the wall) so it can be removed later. For a straight stair, standard install is a day. Curved stairs need a bespoke rail — 4-6 weeks lead time, a lot more cost. Approved Document M references wheelchair platform stairlifts for accessible provision in public buildings. In a private house, a stairlift buys time — and often means a homeowner can stay in the house years longer instead of moving. If the stair itself isn't safe (worn treads, loose handrail), that has to be sorted before a stairlift goes in.

evidence.note: Approved Document M + industry install practice

facts.topic: Stairlifts — when it's the right answer

facts.statement: Scotland uses the Building Standards Technical Handbook, not the Approved Documents. Section 4.3 covers stairs and ramps. Core geometry is the same as England — 2R+G between 550mm and 700mm — but the handbook is worded differently and enforced by a different route (a Building Warrant, applied for before work starts, not a building control notice during work). Working in Scotland: get the Warrant first, not after.
facts.topic: Regional differences — Scotland

facts.statement: Wales has its own Approved Documents now, published by the Welsh Government. The core geometry is aligned with the England version but they diverge on some points, most visibly on Part L (energy) and increasingly on Part M. Always check the current Welsh Approved Document K rather than assuming the England version applies. Building control is via Welsh local authorities.
facts.topic: Regional differences — Wales

facts.statement: Northern Ireland uses Technical Booklets, not Approved Documents. Technical Booklet H covers stairs, ladders and ramps. Dimensions closely mirror the England Approved Document K — same 2R+G rule, same private/semi-public/public categories — but the booklet is a separate document and building control is by District Council. Never assume documents from England apply verbatim in NI. Check Booklet H.

evidence.note: Building Regulations (Northern Ireland) Technical Booklet H

facts.topic: Regional differences — Northern Ireland

facts.statement: Research on elderly users points to two dimensions that matter most. Rise between 170mm and 190mm feels significantly easier to climb than the private-stair maximum of 220mm. Going of 250mm or more (well above the 220mm minimum) gives a proper foot landing on descent. Push the going wider and the rise lower, and the stair suits ageing joints for years longer.

evidence.note: UK ergonomics research on older-adult stair use

facts.topic: Elderly stair design — what actually helps

facts.statement: Stair falls in older adults' homes are one of the biggest sources of serious injury in the UK — hundreds of deaths and hundreds of thousands of injuries every year, at very significant cost to the NHS. Research also found that in one study, 40% of the staircases in elderly participants' homes didn't meet current government guidelines for pitch, rise and going — even though those participants thought their stairs were fine. Worth mentioning to any client refitting a stair for an ageing relative.
facts.topic: Elderly stair falls — the scale

facts.statement: Research on child stair falls shows a strong protective effect from stair gates that are actually kept closed. Families of children who fell were significantly more likely to either have no gate at all or to have left it open. On any staircase where children under 4 will use the house, fit both a top-of-stairs gate and a bottom gate — the top one prevents the worst falls, the bottom one prevents them climbing unsupervised.

evidence.note: UK child stair-fall multicentre case-control study

facts.topic: Child fall risk — stair gates work

facts.statement: The 100mm sphere test stops a child's head passing through — but it doesn't stop them climbing. Any horizontal element in the balustrade (a horizontal rail or wire) turns the whole thing into a ladder. Best practice for a family home: keep the balustrade vertical spindles only, no horizontal ledges, and consider a solid infill panel on the lower half if very young children are in the house. Regs allow horizontal wires; child safety says avoid them.
facts.topic: Child safe balustrade — no climb design

facts.statement: Any change that affects the character of a Listed Building — including its staircase — needs Listed Building Consent before work starts. That covers replacement, most alteration, and sometimes even significant repair. Doing work without consent is a criminal offence with unlimited fines. Get the consent application in before you touch anything, even if it delays the job.

evidence.note: Historic England · Listed Building Consent Advice Note 16

facts.topic: Historic staircases — Listed Building Consent

facts.statement: Historic England's guidance on staircases is 'minimum intervention.' Repair over replace. If a tread is worn, repair the tread — don't rip out the flight. Individual joints, treads, spindles and balusters can all be repaired in isolation by a skilled joiner. Retaining as much original material as possible is not just aesthetic — it's the legal test that keeps you inside consent and often inside building regs too.

evidence.note: Historic England guidance + IHBC Alterations Guidance Note 2021

facts.topic: Historic staircases — minimum intervention rule

facts.statement: Compatible repair (physically and visually matching), carried out by an experienced craftsperson, is unlikely to affect the special interest of a Listed Building and therefore often doesn't need Listed Building Consent. But the word here is 'unlikely' — never assume. Always check with the local Conservation Officer first. Cost of asking is nil; cost of doing it wrong is prosecution.
facts.topic: Historic repair — when consent may not be needed

facts.statement: External escape stairs on public and commercial buildings are governed by Approved Document B and often BS 5395-3 (industrial stairs). They have to be non-combustible (steel, concrete), have handrails on both sides, and meet minimum widths depending on occupancy load. In a domestic loft conversion, external escape stairs are almost never the answer — the protected internal stairway is. External escapes come in on flats, HMOs and commercial.
facts.topic: Fire escape stair — external

facts.statement: Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) trip into stricter fire regs than a single-family home. The stairs become an escape route serving multiple households, and typically the whole stair needs to be a protected stairway with FD30 doors, and often emergency lighting and mains-wired interlinked alarms throughout. Any client turning a house into an HMO has to plan the stair upgrade at the start, not as an afterthought.

evidence.note: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 + Approved Document B

facts.topic: HMO stair rules

facts.statement: Pressure-fit stair gates are fine at the bottom of a stair for toddlers. At the top of a stair, always use screw-fit — pressure-fit gates can pop out under a running child's weight and turn the safety device into the reason for the fall. When installing at the top, screw into the newel post or an adjoining stud — never into plasterboard alone.
facts.topic: Stair gates — build vs bolt-on

facts.statement: Research on older-adult falls shows the transition point — where a level walking surface meets the first tread — is disproportionately where falls happen. The eye and gait have to switch from level to tread rhythm. Design help: extend the handrail 300mm past the top nosing (already a Doc M rule), keep the top landing well lit, and mark the first descending tread with a contrasting nosing even in a domestic stair.

evidence.note: Frontiers research on stair gait in older adults

facts.topic: Stair transition — level to stair

facts.statement: Old timber staircases fail in predictable ways. Wedges under treads work loose — you'll hear it as squeaks. Housed joints between tread and string open with seasonal movement. Bottom of newel post rots where damp comes up from a solid floor. Handrail scarf joints work loose. All of these are individually repairable, none require replacement of the whole stair. Rebuild the wedges, re-glue the joints, splice the newel base, tighten the handrail — that's a good day's restoration work, not a new stair.

evidence.note: UK joinery restoration practice + Building Conservation Journal

facts.topic: Historic timber staircase — common defects

facts.statement: Sanding an in-situ staircase throws fine dust everywhere and the noise fills the whole house. Before you start: seal doorways with plastic and tape, close every duct in the affected area, cover carpets in the hallway with hardboard runners, and warn the client. On a heated house, run the extraction while sanding and give it another hour after. If refinishing with 2-pack polyurethane, occupants have to be out of the house for the fumes.
facts.topic: Refinishing — protecting the rest of the house

facts.statement: Quick reads on whether a stair quote is honest. Round-number pricing (a suspiciously flat total for a bespoke stair) usually means a guess, not a costed job. No breakdown — timber, manufacture, delivery, fit as separate lines. No lead-time confirmation. No warranty terms. No site visit before quoting. Any of those and the number is fiction. The client will end up paying variations later — or getting a stair that doesn't fit. Honest quotes are itemised and reference the actual measured site. The exact number for any bespoke stair depends on final design, timber species, balustrade type, finish choice, delivery and fit — always confirm with the specific manufacturer you're using.
facts.topic: Getting quotes — signs of a bad quote

facts.statement: The site measure is the single biggest risk on a bespoke stair. Get it wrong and the stair doesn't fit. Every dimension matters: finished floor to finished floor (not subfloor — factor in flooring), joist opening width and length, headroom under the joist above, wall-to-wall at start and finish, and any encroaching services (radiators, sockets, alarm sensors). Take photos of everything. If flooring is going in after, measure both existing and planned finished floor levels.
facts.topic: Ordering — the site measure

facts.statement: If parts arrive before you can fit, treat them like furniture, not building materials. Bring them into the finished house — the same temperature and humidity the fitted stair will live in. Never leave in a garage, van, or open building for more than a day or two. If the client's central heating is on and running at 21°C, the parts need at least 48 hours in that environment to acclimatise before you cut or fit — otherwise they'll shrink after fitting and open joints.
facts.topic: Storing bespoke parts on site

facts.statement: Every bespoke component leaves the workshop wrapped. Standard practice: joinery blanket or bubble wrap with air gaps, plus corner protectors on newel caps and handrail scrolls, plus a rigid outer layer on any polished surface. Never sealed plastic (traps moisture, stains timber, especially on oak and walnut). Label every piece with its position — 'string LH', 'newel 1', 'handrail A-B' — so on-site fitters don't have to work it out.
facts.topic: Wrapping for delivery — practicalities

facts.statement: Timber choice is really two decisions in one. Appearance: colour, grain, and how it takes finish. Performance: hardness (how it stands up to footfall), stability (how much it moves with humidity), and workability (how easily it's machined and finished). Oak scores strongly on both. Pine scores well on workability and price but poorly on hardness — expect visible wear on treads within a few years. Ash is a hidden gem — very hard, stable, light colour, often overlooked.
facts.topic: Choosing timber — appearance vs performance

facts.statement: Modern domestic stair lighting increasingly runs on PIR motion sensors — light comes on as soon as someone approaches, off after a delay. Pair with a low-level dimmer for night use so someone going downstairs at 3am isn't blasted awake. LED strip under nosings, powered by a 24V driver in an accessible location, with the sensor on the top and bottom of the flight. Two-way switching still required for the main light circuit — regs demand a physical switch, not just an automated sensor.
facts.topic: Stair lighting — sensor and dimmer setup

facts.statement: Treads take every step someone ever takes on the stair. On a painted or carpeted stair, MDF or tulipwood does the job at a modest cost. For visible timber treads, oak is the default — hard enough for decades of use, holds finish well, easy to source. Ash if you want a bright modern look. Sapele or American walnut for luxury. Never softwood on a visible tread unless the client accepts wear marks within a few years — softwood dents.
facts.topic: Timber for treads — what to pick

facts.statement: Risers don't see wear. On most stairs they're 12mm plywood or 12mm MDF, painted white to contrast with a hardwood tread. Less expensive, more stable, and the paint job is what the client actually sees. On top-end all-hardwood stairs, solid timber risers matching the tread — but you're paying for it and no one gains anything from the extra timber. Save the budget for balustrade instead.
facts.topic: Timber for risers — the hidden component

facts.statement: The string carries the whole stair. On a standard closed-string stair, redwood pine or hemlock is entirely adequate — the string is hidden or painted. On a cut-string stair where the string edge is visible, match it to the treads (oak string with oak treads). On a curved or floating stair with long unsupported spans, LVL or glulam string is the structural answer — usually clad in a decorative timber for the finished look.
facts.topic: Timber for strings — structural priority

facts.statement: The handrail is the piece your hand touches thousands of times. Priority is feel, not just look. Oak, ash, and beech all machine to a smooth grippable profile and stay comfortable for decades. Walnut and sapele suit high-end feature handrails. Softwood handrails feel wrong under the hand within a few years — dents easily, splinters at the ends. Always solid timber for a handrail, never veneered board.
facts.topic: Timber for handrails — feel matters

facts.statement: Newel posts anchor the stair. Structural priority. Standard newels are 90mm square in the same timber as the handrail — oak with oak handrail, ash with ash. Less expensive new-build stairs use pine newels that are painted white regardless of the rest of the stair (works well with an oak handrail). Turned newels for traditional stairs, square-chamfered for contemporary. Any newel that anchors a stair landing has to be through-bolted, not just glued.
facts.topic: Timber for newel posts — the anchor

facts.statement: You need a lot of balusters. On a typical stair, 40-80 spindles. Multiply the cost per spindle by that number and it decides your timber. Pine spindles painted white — most affordable, works on any painted stair. Oak turned spindles — the default upgrade. Ash for modern square spindles. Metal balusters (twisted iron, plain steel bar) for industrial modern look — check the 100mm sphere rule at design stage because thin metal bars often need extra intermediates. Glass panels replace spindles entirely.
facts.topic: Timber for balusters — practicality vs price

facts.statement: The spandrel panel is the triangular panel that closes off the underside of the stair. On most stairs it's 12mm MDF painted to match the wall. On an open-plan modern stair, veneered plywood matching the treads (oak-faced ply if oak treads) gives a joined-up look. Traditional stairs sometimes use solid tongue-and-groove boards. All three are legal; the choice is aesthetic.
facts.topic: Timber for spandrel panels — under the stair

facts.statement: Standard painted stair combination: tulipwood or hemlock treads and newels for a slight upgrade over softwood, MDF risers, plywood spandrel, and paint the whole thing in a solid Farrow & Ball or Little Greene interior colour. This gives a stable, quiet, dent-resistant painted stair that looks tidy for years. Straight pine works but tends to knot through the paint and needs shellac primer on every visible knot.
facts.topic: Timber for a painted stair — best combination

facts.statement: Standard mid-range stain-finished stair: oak throughout — string, treads, risers, handrail, newels, balusters. Finish with hardwax oil (Osmo Polyx or similar) for the warm depth stain-and-lacquer can't quite match. Alternative: ash throughout with a clear lacquer for a much brighter modern feel at slightly lower cost. Never mix softwood and hardwood on a stain-finished stair — they take stain differently and the difference will show forever.
facts.topic: Timber for a stain-finished stair — best combination

facts.statement: Top-tier bespoke combinations. Walnut handrail with walnut newel caps on an oak stair — the classic dark-on-light luxury look. All-walnut treads, risers, and balustrade — the fully dark stair, expensive and dramatic. Sapele throughout for a rich uniform brown-red. Or an ash-and-walnut contrast, ash-and-wenge, oak-and-black-lacquered-metal. Bespoke isn't just about material — it's about the combination that reads as intentional.
facts.topic: Timber for a luxury bespoke stair

facts.statement: MDF treads are entirely fine on a stair that will be carpeted or fully painted. They're less expensive, stabler, and don't show grain under paint. Where they fail: any visible wear, any moisture exposure, any point-load concentration. MDF edges dent easily, so a chair leg or pushed-across furniture will mark the leading nosing. Also — MDF absorbs water at cut edges, so any stair near a bathroom or in a coastal property should be MR MDF or solid timber, not standard MDF.
facts.topic: MDF treads — when they're fine and when they're not

facts.statement: Visible birch plywood staircases are having a moment in UK contemporary design. The clean pale face and the striped ply-edge line make a strong architectural statement. Common approach: 22mm birch ply treads with the ply edges chamfered, sealed with hardwax oil so the natural colour stays bright. Not for every house — the aesthetic is strongly modern industrial. Where it works, it works brilliantly and often costs less than solid oak.
facts.topic: Birch plywood as a feature material

facts.statement: Oak contains tannic acid. Any ferrous metal fixing — regular steel screws, standard nails, iron cleats — reacts with oak tannin and produces black staining around the fixing head within weeks. On exposed positions (spindle-to-handrail fixings, visible screws through a tread), always use stainless steel or brass. Concealed structural fixings (through-bolts hidden inside a newel) don't matter — but as soon as the fixing is anywhere the eye can reach, non-ferrous only.
facts.topic: Oak tannin + steel fixings

facts.statement: European ash supply has tightened significantly because of ash dieback disease (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus) affecting UK and European populations since the mid-2010s. Availability of long clean boards for staircase strings has dropped and price has risen. American white ash (Fraxinus americana) is not affected and now increasingly imported to fill the gap. Check with your timber merchant on species at the point of ordering — same 'ash' can mean different origins with different supply pictures.
facts.topic: Ash dieback and supply

facts.statement: Beech is very hard and takes finish well, but it's the most unstable common furniture hardwood in the UK — it moves noticeably with seasonal humidity. On a stair, that means gaps at joints in winter, tightness in summer. Fine in a modern well-heated flat with consistent humidity. Not fine in an old cottage with a wood-burner in winter and open windows in summer. If a client is set on beech, warn them upfront.
facts.topic: Beech unstable — where not to use

facts.statement: European oak: more character, more medullary rays, more colour variation, tighter local stock, slightly higher price per cube. American white oak: more uniform, straighter grain, larger board sizes available, slightly less expensive. For a traditional English country home, European oak reads right. For a modern build wanting consistent joinery-grade uniformity, American white oak is the sensible pick. American red oak is a different beast — pinker, coarser, interior-only. Never confuse the three.
facts.topic: American vs European oak — the choice

facts.statement: External timber staircases are one place Accoya has genuinely changed the market. The acetylation process gives Class 1 durability and near-zero movement, so an Accoya external stair holds its geometry for decades in weather that would destroy softwood in 5 years and warp oak in 10. Cost is roughly 3x softwood, similar to oak. The stainless-fixing requirement adds a bit. If the client's ever going to see rain or frost on the stair, this is the timber to price.

evidence.note: UK external stair practice + Accoya guidance

facts.topic: Accoya for exterior stairs

facts.statement: Curved staircases live or die by the string. Solid timber can't curve without laminating, so any curved stair uses glulam — thin timber strips glued around a curved jig, clamped until cure. Standard glulam is spruce; luxury bespoke uses oak or ash glulam so the visible face matches solid components. Accoya glulam for curved external stairs. Any workshop that says they curve solid timber is either laminating (glulam by another name) or over-promising — check the process before signing off.
facts.topic: Glulam for curved strings

facts.statement: Floating stairs — the ones with no visible support structure and treads that appear to hover — need a hidden structural element strong enough to cantilever every tread. LVL (Laminated Veneer Lumber, Kerto is the common brand) is the material of choice. A single LVL string running the length of the stair, hidden inside the wall or behind a cladding, carries the whole load. Domestic LVL comes in strengths up to Kerto Q which handles most floating-stair designs. Structural calculation always required — never guess LVL sizing.
facts.topic: LVL for floating stairs

facts.statement: Genuine mahogany (Swietenia macrophylla) is CITES Appendix II restricted — the entire trade is regulated internationally, new commercial supply is limited, prices are very high, and every board needs paperwork. Realistic modern options: reclaimed mahogany from restoration and demolition (chain-of-custody documented), or Sapele as the modern substitute. Almost every 'mahogany' staircase quoted today by a UK maker is Sapele — the client just doesn't know because the trade name has drifted. Always specify by botanical or trade name to avoid confusion.
facts.topic: Mahogany today — reclaimed only

facts.statement: Wenge is stunning as a feature timber but the sawdust is a known respiratory sensitiser — repeated exposure can trigger allergic reactions and asthma. Always machine with dust extraction and a proper P2/P3 mask, not a paper dust mask. Never dry-sand in a house occupied by anyone with a respiratory condition. If the client wants wenge, tell them the fitter needs to work outside or in a properly extracted workshop — not indoors in front of the client.

evidence.note: UK trade safety knowledge on wenge

facts.topic: Wenge — dust warning

facts.statement: Quick decoder for the letters on sheet material orders. MDF: MR = Moisture Resistant, FR = Fire Retardant, LD = Light Density. Plywood: BB/BB (both faces have small defects), S/BB (one clean face), FSC (certified sustainable source), WBP (Weather and Boil Proof — waterproof glue but not waterproof face). Chipboard: P2 = interior, P3 = interior humid, P5 = load-bearing humid (this is what floor decking usually is). OSB: OSB/3 = load-bearing humid, OSB/4 = heavy load-bearing humid. Ask for the grade by these codes — the yard staff know them.
facts.topic: Sheet material grade abbreviations

facts.statement: For a bespoke stair, sourcing timber isn't a same-day-from-the-yard job. Standard oak boards in commercial lengths — most yards keep stock, order Monday collect Friday. Long clean boards for a curved string (2.4m+ clean) — call three yards, expect one to two weeks. Rare or figured stock (highly figured walnut, quarter-sawn oak, wide boards) — often a specialist merchant with a 2-3 week lead time from Europe. Never quote a bespoke stair with a fixed delivery date until you've confirmed material availability.
facts.topic: Sourcing bespoke timber — the reality

facts.statement: Reclaimed oak from Victorian and Georgian building demolition is a strong option for period stairs where the aged look is wanted from day one. Sources: church restoration timber, mill flooring, old barn beams. Grading is by eye — every board different, more waste (20-30%), higher labour. Reclaimed pitch pine is another common find, good for staircase strings and treads in restoration work. Reclaimed timber usually needs full re-milling, kiln drying to house moisture level, and metal detection before it hits the workshop.
facts.topic: Recycled + reclaimed timber for staircases

facts.statement: A proper 2-pack polyurethane sprayed staircase finish runs to a standard sequence. Sand the timber through 120, 180, 220 grit. Vacuum. Wipe with a tack cloth. Two coats of 2K high-build primer at 100-150 microns wet, sanded flat with 320-400 grit between coats. Two coats of 2K PU topcoat, either matt, satin or gloss, sprayed at 80-120 microns wet each pass. Denib the first topcoat with 400-600 grit before the second. Cure 24-48 hours before use. Miss any of those steps and the finish shows it.
facts.topic: 2K PU spray finish — the full system

facts.statement: For 2K polyurethane spray lacquer on staircases and joinery in the UK, Morrells (based in Stockport) is the market-leader trade brand. Their VLi Polyurethane and 700 Wet-Look Topcoat are the two products spray-shops name most. Comparable rivals: Milesi LGA (Italian), Sayerlack (Italian, stocked by Movac and others), General Finishes Enduro (US, pre-cat waterborne). Pick one system and stick with it — mixing product systems mid-job causes compatibility failures.
facts.topic: Morrells is the UK trade default

facts.statement: Once you mix the 2K catalyst into the base lacquer, the clock starts. Typical pot life is 4-8 hours at 20°C. Any material left in the gun or pot after that will start to gel — will spray poorly, then not at all, then set solid in the gun and ruin it. Rule: mix only what you can spray in one session, and if you're on a big stair split the material into pots you'll finish before pot life expires. Never top up a partly-used pot with fresh mix.
facts.topic: Pot life on a mixed 2K

facts.statement: Waterborne 1K lacquers (Bona Mega EVO, Sikkens BL Unitop) are the go-to when the stair has to be recoated in an occupied house — low odour, low VOC, quick return-to-service. 2K solvent-based PU (Morrells, Milesi, Sayerlack) is the go-to in a proper spray-shop or on unoccupied new-build work — harder film, longer wear, deeper depth of finish. Both are legitimate; the choice is the site, not the product. Don't apply 2K solvent in an occupied house without full extraction and evacuation.
facts.topic: Waterborne vs 2K solvent — pick by situation

facts.statement: Which spray gun for which part of the stair? HVLP turbine gun (Fuji Q4/Q5) for spindles, newel posts, handrail, and small detail — low overspray, precise control. AAA (air-assisted airless, Graco Merkur) for strings, treads, risers, spandrel panels — high throughput, near-HVLP finish. Airless (Graco Ultra) for priming production runs — fast but rough finish, not for topcoats. A spray-shop doing volume runs all three. A one-person shop can do everything with a Fuji Q4 and take longer on the flat panels.
facts.topic: HVLP for detail, AAA for panels

facts.statement: The biggest headache spraying a staircase white is the timber grain showing through even after multiple coats. Standard fix: an acrylic filler / grain sealer on all timber components before the primer goes on. Cheshire's acrylic grain filler, Wood Filler Pro, or a shellac-based sanding sealer all do the job. Apply, sand flat with 240-grit, then straight into the 2K primer. This step alone is what separates a factory-look white staircase from a domestic paint job.
facts.topic: Painting timber white — sealing the grain

facts.statement: A specialist on-site staircase spraying job runs like this. Day 0: site survey, quote, colour matching. Day 1: sheet up the whole area — plastic to the ceiling, plastic on the floor, plastic taped over every door frame, all sockets and switches masked. Sand the stair on-site with vacuum extraction. Vacuum. Tack cloth. Day 2: two coats of 2K primer, sanded between. Day 3: two coats of 2K topcoat. Day 4: cure. Day 5: unwrap, clean, hand over. On a single flight with a balustrade, expect the spray finish to add roughly 30-60% on top of the raw stair fabrication cost, depending on complexity and access — exact number always depends on final design, balustrade type, timber and access constraints, so confirm with the sprayer for the specific project.
facts.topic: On-site staircase spraying — the process
