facts.statement: When a 2K spray finish is being applied on-site (rather than in a spray-shop), the household has to leave for the day of application and for the following 24-48 hours. The isocyanate content of 2K PU is a known respiratory sensitiser — not just an odour issue. Pets out too. Windows on the affected floor closed to trap fumes in the sheeted zone, but the rest of the house ventilated. Only re-occupy once the professional sprayer clears it, not once it stops smelling.
facts.topic: On-site spraying — occupants must vacate

facts.statement: Spraying 2K polyurethane requires full air-fed breathing apparatus (AFB), not just a cartridge respirator. The isocyanates in the catalyst are a known asthma trigger and once sensitised, exposure at any level triggers reactions for life. Alongside the AFB: full spray suit, nitrile gloves, boot covers, eye protection. HSE guidance treats 2K isocyanate spraying as one of the highest-risk operations in a joinery workshop. Never spray 2K in a domestic property without proper AFB kit.
facts.topic: PPE for a spray-shop

facts.statement: On a clear-finish stair (oak tread lacquered clear), the sanding sealer basecoat is what makes the finish look factory-quality. It seals the grain so the topcoat doesn't sink into the wood pores in some places and sit proud in others — which is what creates that patchy uneven look on a badly-finished stair. Two coats of NC sanding sealer, sanded flat, then the topcoat lays down glass-flat. Skip the sanding sealer and no amount of extra topcoat coats will fix it.
facts.topic: Sanding sealer — why it matters on clear finish

facts.statement: The traditional way to close the underside of an open-back staircase is 15mm x 118mm softwood tongue and groove board. Battens fix to the stair carriage at 400-600mm centres, boards nail to the battens with the tongue-and-groove joints running vertically. V-groove joint gives shadow lines that hide any seasonal timber movement. Paint, stain, or clear finish. Warm traditional look, but doesn't provide fire resistance on its own — if the stair is a protected stairway, plasterboard has to go on first with T&G decoratively over it.
facts.topic: T&G board on the stair back — the traditional method

facts.statement: The modern replacement for softwood T&G on a stair back is MDF T&G — 15mm or 18mm pre-primed panels in trade sizes up to 2440mm long. Sharper profile, no knots, no grain to show through paint. Factory-primed twice so needs only two coats of topcoat once fitted. Fixes to battens the same way as softwood T&G. On any painted stair, MDF T&G finishes better than softwood every time. The one downside: MDF is heavier per board — a bit more labour on install.
facts.topic: MDF T&G — the modern alternative

facts.statement: Panelling the wall running up the well side of the stair (the wall the stair passes) is one of the highest-impact finishes in the house — the eye sees it every time someone climbs. Shaker panelling is the safe default: flat rectangular panels formed by 9mm MDF stiles and rails applied directly to the wall. Panel size set to the stair rise and going. Painted the same colour as the wall for subtle, or contrast colour for feature. Runs continuously up the stair with a dado rail at the same height throughout — the dado follows the stair pitch.
facts.topic: Well-side panelling — shaker as the standard

facts.statement: On a Victorian, Georgian or Edwardian property the plain shaker panel can look wrong — too modern for the house. The period-correct alternatives: raised and fielded panels with a beaded edge (Victorian formal), or bolection-moulded panels (Georgian country-house), or plain sheet panelling with applied bead moulding (Edwardian domestic). Cheshire Mouldings and Richard Burbidge both supply the mouldings and panels ready-cut. Colour matches the rest of the house's joinery — usually white satin on modern refurbs, muted heritage colours on more authentic restorations.
facts.topic: Well-side panelling — period-property options

facts.statement: Vertical fluted or slat panelling on the well wall is the contemporary staircase feature of the moment. Available in painted MDF (most affordable), or in real-wood veneered oak, walnut, or ash. Flute widths 40-60mm. Adds strong vertical rhythm to the well and makes the stair feel taller. Popular in hotels, luxury new-builds, and modern renovations. Ships in 2440x1220mm panels — cut to the stair pitch on-site, tricky to install cleanly at the pitch angle. Not for a period home.
facts.topic: Modern fluted panelling — the contemporary look

facts.statement: Standard method for closing the underside of a staircase: batten out the underside with 47x50mm treated timber battens at 400mm centres, screw 12.5mm plasterboard to the battens with drywall screws, tape the joints with scrim tape, then 3.2mm two-coat skim finish over the whole underside. Decorate with mist coat then two topcoats. This is the default across UK domestic staircases — quiet, non-combustible, easy to decorate, and (with fire-line board substituted) fully fire-rated.
facts.topic: Plasterboard the underside — 12.5mm is the default

facts.statement: If the stair is a protected stairway — any loft conversion, any three-storey house, any HMO — the plasterboard on the underside and around the enclosure has to be fire-line grade. Pink 12.5mm fire-line board (Knauf Fireboard, Gyproc Fireline) gives 30 minutes fire resistance. For 60 minutes, use 15mm fire-line. Skim over the pink board finishes it. Two layers of standard 12.5mm plasterboard with staggered joints achieves similar 30-min resistance if fire-line isn't on-site — but the fire-line grade is the specified route.
facts.topic: Protected stairway — fire-line board mandatory

facts.statement: When the plasterboard sits over a substrate that isn't perfectly flat — for example old timber battens on a Victorian stair well, or a stone-and-plaster wall — a coat of bonding coat plaster (8-11mm thick) goes on first to level the surface, then the multi-finish skim goes on top. Bonding coat sets in 2-3 hours, ready to skim within 24 hours. On new plasterboard installed flat, skip the bonding coat and go straight to skim.
facts.topic: Plaster undercoat — bonding coat when needed

facts.statement: Plasterboard, bare wood battens, and old plaster all need sealing with diluted PVA (1 part PVA to 4-5 parts water) before the skim goes on. The PVA seals suction — if you don't PVA, the porous surface sucks moisture out of the plaster too quickly, the plaster grabs, and you can't polish the trowel finish. Apply PVA, let it go tacky (not fully dry), then skim into it. Skipping the PVA is the number-one reason a skim job fails on a new stair enclosure.
facts.topic: PVA sealing before skim

facts.statement: The trimmer joist at the top of a stair well opening — the joist the last tread lands against — gets its front face treated as a visible finish. Standard method: fix a facing board (22mm timber or 18mm MDF) to the trimmer joist face, cut to the joist depth, sitting behind the landing nosing and above the last riser. Painted white on a painted stair, matched to the stair timber on a natural stair. This is what closes the visual gap between the top step and the landing floor — get it wrong and the stair looks unfinished.
facts.topic: Trimmer face — the top-of-well finish

facts.statement: The landing nosing is the piece that runs across the front edge of the landing, capping the trimmer joist and defining the well edge. Standard practice: the landing nosing projects the same distance over the trimmer face as the stair nosings project over their risers — usually 15-25mm — so the eye reads a continuous line up the stair and across the landing. Profile matches the stair nosing (bullnose, pencil-round, ovolo, chamfered). Cut into the landing floorboards, glued and pinned to the trimmer.
facts.topic: Landing nosing — projection and match

facts.statement: Lining the well of a staircase (the vertical space around the opening) is a system, not a single detail. Working outwards from the stair: (1) skirting board where the string meets the wall — matches house skirting. (2) Well-side panelling on the wall running up the stair. (3) Trimmer joist facing where the well opens onto the landing. (4) Landing nosing capping the trimmer edge. (5) Balustrade fixed to the newel and running along the well opening at landing level, guarding the drop. All five have to be visually coordinated for the stair to read as a completed piece.
facts.topic: Well lining — the whole visual system

facts.statement: Where the stair meets the landing, the top newel post typically sits on the landing corner, anchored through-bolted into the trimmer joist below. The handrail from the stair terminates into the newel. From the newel, a horizontal handrail then runs along the landing well edge, supported by landing spindles or a landing balustrade panel. This transition — pitched-rail-to-newel-to-horizontal-rail — is where affordable staircases show. On a good stair, the two rails meet the newel at matched profiles and consistent heights.
facts.topic: Newel to landing — the balustrade transition

facts.statement: Two dominant UK stair-mouldings brands. Cheshire Mouldings — Warrington-based, widest range of pine mouldings and MDF panelling kits, standard trade merchant stock. Richard Burbidge — the premium end, stronger on oak and sapele mouldings and full stair systems. Both cover skirting, architrave, dado rail, panel moulding, and stair-part accessories. Every builders' merchant and specialist stair yard in the UK stocks one or both. If you specify a Cheshire moulding, expect same-day availability; specify Richard Burbidge oak and expect a few days.
facts.topic: Cheshire vs Richard Burbidge — the two UK stair-mould brands

facts.statement: The starting step of a staircase does three jobs at once. First, it's the widest, most-visible step in the house — the eye sees it every time someone walks in. Second, it creates a physical stepping-on point that's wider than the rest of the flight, so it's safer and more comfortable to step onto. Third, it anchors the newel post — the newel sits on the starting step's projection, which gives the whole balustrade structural stability. Get the starting step right and the stair feels grand and settled from the first tread up.
facts.topic: Why starting steps exist

facts.statement: Nine out of ten new UK staircases with a feature starting step use a single bullnose. It's the most popular option because it works everywhere: narrow hallway, wide hallway, wall-hugging stair or free-standing. The curved end projects out on one side, the other end runs into the wall or string. The newel post sits on the projection. It's less expensive than a curtail, less demanding on floor space than a double bullnose, and it flows visually into any handrail termination. The safe default choice.
facts.topic: Single bullnose — the UK default

facts.statement: Whether to specify single or double bullnose is decided by one question: does the stair have a wall on one side? If yes, single bullnose — the curved end faces the room, the straight end runs into the wall. If the stair is fully free-standing with both sides visible (open plan, central staircase in a wide hall), double bullnose — both ends curved, both sides on show. Force a double bullnose into a narrow hallway and it looks cramped; force a single bullnose on a free-standing stair and one side looks unfinished.
facts.topic: Single vs double bullnose — the hallway test

facts.statement: The difference between a bullnose and a curtail is how the tread meets the newel post. On a bullnose, the tread meets the FRONT face of the newel — the newel sits at the back of the projection. On a curtail, the tread WRAPS AROUND the newel — the curved edge of the step follows the base of the newel post so the whole shape flows continuously. Curtails match volute / scroll handrails; bullnoses match straight or turnout handrails. Get this pairing wrong and the stair reads awkwardly.
facts.topic: Bullnose vs curtail — where they meet the newel

facts.statement: A curtail step exists to match a scroll or volute handrail. The curve in the starting step mirrors the spiral of the volute above it, and the two together — flowing from tread edge up through the newel to the volute scroll — create the classic 'grand entrance' look. If a stair has a volute handrail but a plain bullnose step, the effect fails; if it has a curtail step but a straight-terminated handrail, same. Curtails are always specified as a pair with volute handrails, and both are always in the same timber.
facts.topic: Curtail step + volute handrail — the matched pair

facts.statement: A D-end step is not just a bullnose by another name. On a bullnose, the tread projects out and the newel post sits at the back edge of the projection — the balustrade runs from the newel straight up the stair. On a D-end, the tread passes BEYOND the newel and the balustrade returns back into the SIDE of the newel — from above the tread reads as a D shape stuck onto the end of a normal tread. D-ends are common on curved and splayed stairs; bullnoses are common on straight stairs.
facts.topic: D-end vs bullnose — different geometries

facts.statement: An arched bullnose has an ogee or arched profile cut into the front face of the step rather than a plain curve. Gives the starting step a more architectural feature — a fluted or moulded front that catches light and shadow. Georgian country-house staircases used this variant regularly. Higher fabrication cost because the curve is compound: the tread nosing profile, the arched front face, and the timber grain all have to be aligned. Only worth specifying on bespoke work where the rest of the stair carries the same period feel.
facts.topic: Arched bullnose — the Georgian variant

facts.statement: Double starting steps means two feature treads stacked at the foot of the stair — usually a double bullnose or double curtail at the very bottom, then a single bullnose or single curtail above it. The second step is set back by the going, so the eye reads a stepped-back curved shape rising up. Increases the visual grandeur significantly and makes the newel post look taller and more anchored. Two bespoke feature steps cost roughly double a single starting step — worth it on a grand entrance, overkill on a modest hallway.
facts.topic: Double starting steps — the grand entrance

facts.statement: A splayed starting step has an angled end (typically 45°) rather than a curved bullnose. Used when the stair pitches into the hall from a diagonal direction rather than square-on — common in Victorian houses where the original hall geometry isn't rectangular. Less expensive to fabricate than a bullnose because there are no curves cut, but reads as more architectural than a plain square end. Sometimes paired with a bullnose on the other side of the step if only one end faces a wall.
facts.topic: Splayed starting step — angled not curved

facts.statement: On a bullnose starting step, the newel post sits on the projected part of the tread — specifically, at the point where the straight edge of the step meets the curved edge. The newel is through-bolted down through the tread into a solid block below (or into the trimmer joist for a first-floor starting step). Getting the newel position right on the layout is critical — a few millimetres out and the newel doesn't line up with the balustrade above, and the whole spindle spacing looks wrong for the length of the flight.
facts.topic: Newel position on a bullnose

facts.statement: Two ways to fit a bullnose starting step. Whole-step: a complete tread + riser fabricated as one piece with the bullnose curve. More expensive, but structurally solid and the timber grain runs continuously through the curved section. Bullnose riser: just a curved riser sold as a trade part (300mm rise x standard widths in matching timbers), fitted under a standard tread which is extended out to sit on the projection. Less expensive, easier to retrofit onto an existing stair, but the join between the extended tread and the standard tread can show. Whole-step for new bespoke work; riser for retrofit or budget builds.
facts.topic: Bullnose whole-step vs bullnose riser

facts.statement: Scotia is the small concave cove moulding that fits under the front nosing of a starting step (and often every tread on a traditional stair). Gives a decorative shadow line under the nose curve and hides any small gap between the tread and riser. Standard trade profile, mitred and cut on-site to follow the bullnose or curtail curve. Not required by building regs but expected on every proper traditional bullnose fit — a stair without scotia looks unfinished on close inspection. Modern stairs often skip scotia to keep the look clean.
facts.topic: Scotia moulding under the nose

facts.statement: The modern-design counterpoint to the bullnose is a square-edge starting step — a first tread that projects wider than the standard treads (same benefit as a bullnose) but with a sharp 90° corner rather than a curve. Newel sits on the projection the same way. Suits square-profile newels, straight handrail terminations, and contemporary interiors where the traditional bullnose curve would look out of place. Increasingly common on new-builds and modern renovations where the client wants the extra-wide entry benefit without the traditional feature look.
facts.topic: Square-edge starting step — the modern alternative

facts.statement: Before picking a starting step, walk through three questions with the client. One: how wide is the hallway? Narrow (under 900mm free of the stair) — single bullnose only. Wide (over 1200mm) — double bullnose or double curtail on the table. Two: what handrail termination does the stair have? Straight or turnout — bullnose. Scroll or volute — curtail. Three: what era and style is the house? Modern — square-edge or plain bullnose. Traditional / period — curtail, arched bullnose, or double starting steps. Answer those three and the starting step picks itself.
facts.topic: Choosing the starting step — three questions

facts.statement: Rough cost gradient on starting steps, most affordable to most expensive. A bullnose riser retrofit sits at the bottom of the range — the most affordable option because you're adding to an existing standard tread. A single bullnose whole-step is the next step up in cost, roughly 3-5x the retrofit riser. A double bullnose whole-step is around 1.5-2x a single bullnose (both ends curved means more fabrication). Single curtail step is significantly more than double bullnose because the curved timber has to be wrapped around the newel — expect roughly 2x a single bullnose. Double curtail step, the top of the range, sits at roughly 3-4x a single bullnose. Add matching newel post, volute or turnout handrail, and finishing scotia — the starting-step assembly can easily be 15-25% of the total staircase budget on a bespoke build. Exact prices always depend on timber species, joinery style, fit-out complexity and finish — confirm every number with the specific stair maker.
facts.topic: Cost bands on starting steps

facts.statement: The starting step is the most-visible piece of the stair — always specify it in the top-tier visible timber on the project. On an oak stair, oak starting step. On a walnut-and-oak stair, walnut starting step (matched to the handrail). Never save money by putting a less expensive timber on the starting step — everyone who walks in sees it, and mismatch is instantly visible. Trade parts are stocked in pine, oak, ash, sapele, and American black walnut so almost any timber choice on the main stair can be matched on the starting step.
facts.topic: Which timber for the starting step

facts.statement: Fire-line plasterboard on a staircase is only mandatory when the stair is a PROTECTED STAIRWAY. That means: loft conversions (which turn a 2-storey house into 3 storeys), any house that's 3 storeys or more, blocks of flats, HMOs, and workplace or commercial buildings. Standard 2-storey single-family houses have no fire-lining requirement — plain plasterboard, T&G boarding, or plaster-on-lath all comply. Don't over-spec on a job where it isn't needed; don't under-spec on a job where it is.

evidence.note: Approved Document B · Vol 1 practical application

facts.topic: Fire slabs — when they're mandatory

facts.statement: The single decision that flips a staircase from a normal joinery job into a fire-lined protected-stairway job is adding a third storey. In 90% of UK cases that means a loft conversion. The moment you add the third storey, the ENTIRE staircase — ground to top — becomes a protected stairway. Fire-line the underside, fire-line the well walls, upgrade every door off the stair on every level to FD30 self-closing, add mains-linked smoke alarms in the stairwell on every floor. Not just the new loft bit — the whole house. Clients don't expect this and quotes should reflect it upfront.
facts.topic: The trigger: 3rd storey = whole-house upgrade

facts.statement: The standard fire-line board for a UK protected stairway is 12.5mm pink fire-line plasterboard (Knauf Fireboard or Gyproc Fireline). Single layer gives 30 minutes fire resistance, which is what Approved Document B specifies for domestic dwellings up to 3 storeys. Alternative achieving the same rating: two layers of standard 12.5mm plasterboard with joints staggered — more economical on board, more labour on fixing. Fire-line 15mm gives 60 minutes, needed for 4-storey buildings, high-rise flats above the 3rd storey, or fire-fighting stairs.

evidence.note: UK plasterboard trade + Approved Document B

facts.topic: Fire-line board spec — what to order

facts.statement: Under-stair cupboards in a protected stairway need lining even though Doc B allows a small-cupboard door exception for low fire risk. Safe practice: line every under-stair cupboard in a protected stair with fire-line plasterboard as default. If the cupboard houses a boiler, meter, consumer unit, or storage of combustibles (paints, solvents, cleaning products), the door has to be FD30 self-closing. Under-stair boiler cupboards are the single most common fire-lining oversight in loft-conversion sign-offs.

evidence.note: UK loft-conversion practice + Approved Document B

facts.topic: Under-stair cupboard fire-lining

facts.statement: Three surfaces on a staircase need considering for fire lining. UNDERSIDE (the spandrel — the sloped surface under the flight): fire-line plasterboard when it's a protected stairway, standard plasterboard or T&G otherwise. BACK (the vertical wall behind the string): fire-line if that wall is part of the stairwell enclosure separating the stair from a habitable room. SIDES (well walls facing into the stair volume): fire-line if the stair is a protected stairway. On a 2-storey house with no loft conversion, none of these need fire-line grade.
facts.topic: Fire slabs — sides vs back vs underside

facts.statement: Fire-line plasterboard only performs if it's installed properly. Every joint has to be taped with paper tape and jointed with fire-rated jointing compound (not just filler). Every penetration for a socket, switch, downlight, or service pipe has to be fire-sealed with intumescent sealant. Screws at 200mm centres around the perimeter and 300mm centres in the field. Skim finish over the pink board eliminates any tape-and-fill imperfections. Miss any of these details and the 30-minute rating drops significantly under a fire test.
facts.topic: Fire lining install — the details that matter

facts.statement: Minimum staircase headroom is 2000mm clear, measured vertically from the pitch line (the imaginary line joining the front edges of the tread nosings) to any obstruction above. Applies at EVERY point along the flight — not just landings, not just the middle, but every single tread. The one exception is the loft-conversion concession (1900mm centre / 1800mm side). Every other stair in the UK — main house stairs, common stairs in flats, commercial — gets no relaxation. Full 2000mm the whole way.
facts.topic: Headroom — always 2000mm on the pitch line

facts.statement: Nine times out of ten, the point on a staircase where headroom fails is where the flight passes under the trimmer joist at the top of the well opening. The trimmer runs across the width of the stair and its underside is the obstruction the 2000mm is measured to. On older houses with shallow floor zones (say 200mm joists), the trimmer bottom sits low enough that the top few treads can breach 2000mm. Always plot the trimmer bottom against the pitch line on the layout drawing before signing off — it's a lot less expensive to catch it on paper than after the stair's fitted.
facts.topic: Trimmer joist — the headroom pinch point

facts.statement: The loft-conversion headroom concession, from Approved Document K Diagram 1.4: 1900mm at the CENTRE of the stair, dropping to 1800mm at the SIDE where the stair meets the sloping roof. Applies only when the stair is going into a previously non-habitable roof space AND no other practicable stair option exists. If the loft was already habitable, or if a compliant stair with full 2000mm could be fitted somewhere else, the concession is refused. Building control decides — never assume the concession applies.
facts.topic: Headroom loft concession — the exact numbers

facts.statement: Approved Document K defines stair width as the CLEAR WIDTH BETWEEN THE WALLS OR BALUSTRADES. Practical translation: measure at right angles to the direction of travel, from the inside face of anything sticking into the stair volume on the left to the inside face of anything sticking in on the right. That means: if there's a wall one side and a balustrade the other, wall face to balustrade. Both sides walled, wall face to wall face at balustrade height. Both sides open with balustrades, balustrade face to balustrade face. NOT string-to-string, NOT centre-of-wall to centre-of-wall.
facts.topic: Stair width — measured between walls or balustrades

facts.statement: Common mistake on quotes and drawings — measuring stair width string-to-string. The strings are inside the balustrade and wall lines, so string-to-string over-states the compliance width. If a stair has 45mm-thick strings on each side, string-to-string reads 90mm bigger than the actual clear width. Building control measures between the inside faces of walls or balustrades — always. Draw and quote to that same measurement, or the finished stair is narrower than advertised.
facts.topic: String-to-string is NOT the width measurement

facts.statement: Approved Document K sets no absolute minimum width for a private stair in a single-family dwelling. In practice: 800mm is the informal floor for a primary household stair (anything narrower and moving furniture becomes impossible, and standard 900mm door openings won't line up). 600mm is the practical floor for a secondary loft stair. Common bespoke domestic stair widths sit between 850mm and 1000mm. Anything below 800mm on a main stair — expect building control comments even though the reg doesn't set a hard number.

evidence.note: UK domestic stair practice + Approved Document K

facts.topic: Private stair — no Doc K minimum, practical 800mm+

facts.statement: The baseline stair width for commercial and non-domestic buildings is 1200mm clear. Below that, Approved Document B and BS 9999 struggle to sign the escape route. The actual required width scales with occupancy load — every 1000mm of clear width handles roughly 80 people per minute in an escape. So a 100-person office is fine at 1200mm; a 300-person retail floor probably needs 1800mm+. Always calculate against occupancy, not just pick the baseline.
facts.topic: Commercial + non-domestic — 1200mm baseline

facts.statement: Common stairs in blocks of flats and semi-public buildings sit in the middle band: minimum 1000mm clear width (between walls or balustrades). Reduces to 900mm if the stair only serves a single dwelling on the floor. Increases to 1100mm if the stair is also a fire-fighting stair (a stair the fire brigade uses to reach upper floors during a fire). The 1100mm firefighting minimum is fixed regardless of occupancy — it's set by hose reel and equipment carrying, not by escape flow.

evidence.note: Approved Document K + Approved Document B

facts.topic: Semi-public + common flat stair — 1000mm

facts.statement: Any stair wider than 1800mm under Approved Document M — or wider than 2000mm under Doc B escape work — needs a central handrail dividing the width into sections. Each section must not exceed 1000mm typical. The rule catches wide grand-entrance stairs in offices, schools, and public buildings where crowds need something to hold on either side. On a private house, a stair over 1800mm wide is very rare so the rule almost never bites — but if you're specifying a wide feature stair in a large home, plan for it.

evidence.note: Approved Document K + M · central handrail rule

facts.topic: Central handrail on wide stairs

facts.statement: Approved Document M sets a higher stair-width floor for accessibility. Where a stair has to be accessible (public buildings, workplaces, most new-build commercial), the minimum clear width is 1200mm — enough for someone using a walking aid to be helped down by a companion, or for a wheelchair user to be assisted on an evacuation chair. Domestic stairs aren't held to this — Doc M applies to non-dwellings and to accessible-provision homes.
facts.topic: Width for accessibility — Doc M's higher minimum

facts.statement: Practical on-site width check. Take a spirit level or straight edge across the stair at handrail height. Measure from the inside face of the handrail (or wall face if no handrail there) on one side to the inside face of the balustrade or wall on the other. That's the number building control cares about. Not measured at the floor (skirting boards intrude), not at newel-post height (the newel is wider than the balustrade). If the handrail intrudes into the stair volume by more than 100mm from the wall — a common fault — the measurement is taken from the intruding face, and can push you below compliance.
facts.topic: Where to take the width measurement on site

facts.statement: Common misconception — headroom is measured VERTICALLY from the pitch line to the obstruction, not perpendicular to the pitch line. If the stair has a 42° pitch and someone is climbing, they stand vertically upright and their head is vertically above the tread — that's the measurement Doc K uses. Perpendicular-to-pitch is a bigger number and would let more staircases pass, but it's not the compliance measure. Draw the vertical from the nosing straight up to the ceiling/joist above — that distance must be 2000mm at every point.
facts.topic: Headroom is measured VERTICALLY, not perpendicular

facts.statement: UK staircase treads come in three standard trade thicknesses. 22mm — production stairs (carpeted or painted, using laminated timber or MDF). 32mm — mid-range bespoke in solid softwood, natural finish or stained. 40mm — the bespoke premium in oak, ash, walnut or sapele, gives the substantial feel and stands up to decades of footfall. Bespoke workshops will machine to any thickness above these on request, up to 50mm+ for feature stairs and floating designs.
facts.topic: Tread thickness — the three trade defaults

facts.statement: Risers are the vertical faces between treads. Standard trade thicknesses: 9mm plywood or MDF on production stairs (invisible under paint or carpet), 12mm hardwood plywood where a ply-edge look is a feature, 15mm MDF on painted bespoke work for extra rigidity, 22mm solid timber on top-end all-hardwood stairs. Riser fits into a rebate on the underside of the tread above (9mm or 22mm rebate options are the standard trade pre-cuts) and is screw-block braced to the tread below.
facts.topic: Riser thickness — usually the invisible piece

facts.statement: The string carries the weight of the whole stair. Trade minimum: 32mm — anything thinner flexes, and once a string flexes it causes squeaks and eventually joint failure. 38mm is the bespoke sensible upgrade. 48mm is required on cut-string stairs because the cut-outs weaken the string across its section. Housed into the string 12mm to receive treads (or 0.4 times the string thickness, whichever is greater) — that's the pocket the tread sits in, wedged and glued from the back.
facts.topic: String thickness — 32mm minimum, no exceptions

facts.statement: Bespoke workshops can supply treads at any thickness — 25, 32, 40, 45, 50mm+. Reasons to go thicker than 40mm: floating stairs where the tread cantilevers and carries its own weight (50mm+ solid oak or ash), open-riser feature stairs where the tread edge is the visual focus, and any stair where the visual weight of a chunky tread is part of the design. Always specify tread thickness at drawing stage — it changes the going calculation, the housing depth in the string, and the total structural depth of the stair.
facts.topic: Bespoke machined treads — thick means feature

facts.statement: On a cut-string stair the string is machined to the exact profile of every tread and riser — the tread ends visible on the outside of the string. Those cut-outs remove significant material across the string's cross-section, so a 32mm cut string would flex badly. Trade rule: cut strings 48mm minimum. Solid timber only (not laminated) because the profile cuts through the laminations of a plywood string. Waste factor ~15% because the offcuts have no reuse. Cost significantly higher than a closed string but the finished visible tread-end look is why period joinery still specifies it.
facts.topic: Cut string thickness — why 48mm

facts.statement: Two dominant UK trade spindle sizes: 32mm and 41mm square (before turning or profiling). 32mm is the industry standard for domestic stair flights — every builders' merchant and stair yard stocks it. 41mm is the heavier feature spindle for grand entrance stairs, turned traditional balustrades, and stairs where you want wider centres between spindles (fewer 41mm spindles fit before hitting the 100mm sphere rule than 32mm — the timber takes up more of the gap). Both Cheshire Mouldings and Richard Burbidge produce full ranges in both.
facts.topic: Spindle cross-section — 32mm vs 41mm

facts.statement: Standard flight spindle length is 900mm — that's what meets the 900mm minimum handrail height on a domestic stair FLIGHT (measured from pitch line to top of handrail). The spindle sits on the tread nosing (or base rail) at the bottom, passes through 900mm to the underside of the handrail at the top. Bevel-cut at both ends on-site to sit flat on the tread and match the handrail pitch. A 900mm nominal spindle usually leaves 20-40mm of trim after bevelling — plenty for adjustment.
facts.topic: Flight spindle length — 900mm

facts.statement: Standard landing spindle length is 1100mm — that's what meets the 1100mm minimum guarding height on a LANDING for any drop over 600mm (the landing sees more static risk than a flight, so the extra 200mm is required). The landing spindle sits on the landing floor or base rail and passes 1100mm to the underside of the horizontal handrail running along the well edge. Order landing spindles as separate 1100mm items — you can't just recut a 900mm flight spindle to fit, it'll be short.
facts.topic: Landing spindle length — 1100mm

facts.statement: The height difference between flight (900mm) and landing (1100mm) handrails isn't a mistake — it's because the two positions carry different risks. On a flight, the user is actively moving up or down and the 900mm handrail height is measured from the pitch line (tread nosing), so someone standing on a tread has the rail at a comfortable grip height. On a landing, someone can lean on the guarding while standing static — the 200mm extra height stops an adult tipping over the top. Match this at the newel transition: the flight rail arrives at the newel at 900mm from the last nosing, the landing rail exits at 1100mm from the landing floor.

evidence.note: UK stair-design rationale + Approved Document K

facts.topic: Why the flight is 900mm but landing is 1100mm

facts.statement: Metal spindles are typically 12mm round or square bar — MUCH thinner than 32mm or 41mm timber. That thin cross-section means you need many more spindles per metre to meet the 100mm sphere rule, because the timber-vs-metal gap width contributes very differently. Rule of thumb: a 2400mm handrail run needs about 20 timber spindles at 32mm — or about 26 metal spindles at 12mm to comply. Always calculate at design stage before ordering, not after they arrive on site.
facts.topic: Metal spindles — narrower cross-section, more spindles

facts.statement: On cut-string stairs and on all landings, the spindles don't sit directly on the tread edges — they sit on a base rail. The base rail runs horizontal along the flight (on cut strings) or the landing edge, and is grooved to receive the spindle bases. Same timber and matching profile to the handrail above so the balustrade reads as a single continuous piece. Base rail is a stock trade part from both Cheshire Mouldings and Richard Burbidge.
facts.topic: Base rail — when spindles don't sit on treads

facts.statement: Both the handrail and the base rail have a groove running their length to receive the spindle ends. Between the spindles, that groove needs filling with a spindle fillet — a small timber strip cut to match the exact spacing needed. Two fillets per bay (one above, one below the spindle) OR a single fillet on stairs where the spindles pass all the way through. Cut to length on site to set the exact spindle centres. Same timber as the balustrade. Miss the fillets and the groove is left exposed — instantly visible fault.
facts.topic: Spindle fillet — the spacer that hides the groove

facts.statement: The 100mm sphere rule measures the CLEAR GAP between adjacent spindles — not centre-to-centre. If your spindles are 32mm and you set 132mm centres, that's a 100mm clear gap — which is a fail (has to be UNDER 100mm). Design for 99mm clear as your maximum — gives you a mm of tolerance for site measurement variation. On an angled flight, the sphere test applies HORIZONTALLY, so the horizontal projection of the diagonal spindle gap is what matters — a diagonal 100mm gap projects to about 75mm horizontally on a 42° pitch.

evidence.note: Approved Document K + trade calculation practice

facts.topic: 100mm sphere — clear gap not centres

facts.statement: Calculating spindle count for a balustrade run. Step 1: measure between newel posts to get effective length (say 2400mm). Step 2: pick your spindle cross-section (say 32mm). Step 3: solve for the spindle count where the clear gap between adjacent spindles hits 99mm or under. For 2400mm effective with 32mm spindles: 2400 - (99 x gap count) = 32 x spindle count. Approx 20 spindles at 32mm gives 19 gaps of 99mm each — exactly at the limit. For safety go 21 spindles at 32mm which gives 20 gaps of ~94mm. Rule of thumb: one 32mm spindle per 120mm of run.
facts.topic: Spindle spacing — the calculation

facts.statement: A kite winder is the three-tapered-tread arrangement that turns a staircase 90° without a landing. The middle tread of the three is kite-shaped in plan view — that's where the name comes from. All three winders share the same going measured at the pitch line (270mm in from the narrow end). Gives a continuous stepping rhythm through the turn — no landing pause, less floor area used than a quarter-landing turn. The trade standard for turning a domestic staircase 90° when floor area is tight.
facts.topic: Kite winder — what it actually is

facts.statement: Kite winders come in different tread counts. Two-tread winder — very acute taper, hard to walk, often refused by building control on the pitch-line going measurement. Three-tread kite winder — the UK domestic standard for a 90° turn, comfortable to walk, meets regs easily on a well-designed stair. Four-tread winder — most comfortable, more like a curved section than a winder, but takes more floor area (defeats the point of choosing winders over a landing). Three treads is the answer 90% of the time.
facts.topic: Kite winder — three treads is the standard

facts.statement: The narrow end of every winder tread has to be at least 50mm wide. Prevents the taper closing to a point where you can't get a foot on it. On a typical UK 3-tread kite winder in a 900mm-wide stair, the narrow end sits at 50-70mm and the wide end at 200-300mm. Cut too tight and the middle kite tread has almost no walkable centre area — building control fails it and the client trips on it.
facts.topic: Kite winder — narrow end 50mm minimum

facts.statement: When a stair has to turn 90°, two mainstream options. Kite winder — three tapered treads instead of a landing, saves floor area, gives continuous stepping rhythm, less expensive to build. Quarter-landing — a flat square landing at the turn, more floor area, slower to climb, but a much easier place to rest and to move furniture around. Neither is 'preferred' as a general rule — it depends on the constraint. Tight floor plate, tight budget: kite winder. Ageing users, moving big furniture in future, or grander feel: quarter-landing.
facts.topic: Kite winder vs quarter-landing — the choice

facts.statement: Honest answer: no, kite winders are not universally preferred. They're the pragmatic space-saver when floor area is tight. If a house has floor space for a straight run or a quarter-landing turn, most designers and clients pick those over a winder because winders are harder to walk (the tapered treads catch feet if you're not paying attention) and much harder to move furniture around. Where kite winders ARE preferred: terraced houses, narrow Victorian conversions, and any stair where the alternative would be a spiral or a paddle stair. In those situations, the kite winder is the best of the constrained options.
facts.topic: Kite winder — is it the preferred design?

facts.statement: A double winder staircase turns a full 180° using two sets of winders — typically two 3-tread kite winder boxes with straight flights between and around them. Used in tall narrow spaces where a half-turn is needed but a half-landing would take too much floor. Rare in modern new-builds (too fiddly for volume production) but common in period-property conversions. Complex to design and build — every winder still has to meet the pitch-line going rule and the narrow-end 50mm minimum on every tread.
facts.topic: Double winder — when the stair turns 180°

facts.statement: The two dominant UK stair-parts brands for spindles and balusters. Richard Burbidge — deeper stock in oak, sapele, and metal ranges, premium end; produces spindles in Georgian, Colonial, Traditional, Victorian, fluted and stop-chamfer styles. Cheshire Mouldings — widest range of pine and hemlock stock in every UK builders' merchant, competitive pricing, standard trade defaults. Both cover the 32mm and 41mm sizes in 900mm flight and 1100mm landing lengths. If a spindle style is specified from either brand, it's usually same-day or next-day stock at any decent merchant.
facts.topic: Cheshire Mouldings + Richard Burbidge — spindle brands

facts.statement: The string is the diagonal piece that runs the length of a staircase, from bottom to top, carrying the treads and risers. Every stair has two strings — one against the wall (concealed) and one on the balustrade side (visible). The string style you pick sets the visual character of the whole staircase, and it's the single biggest variable in the price. Get the string right and everything else falls into place.
facts.topic: String — what it actually is

facts.statement: Closed string is the standard workhorse of UK staircase joinery. The string is a solid panel running the full length of the flight. Treads and risers are housed into routed slots inside the string — hardwood wedges knock in behind and glue blocks reinforce the joint. The outside face is one clean continuous timber surface from bottom nosing to top nosing — tread ends hidden. Fastest to build, most affordable to price, strongest under foot, quietest to walk on. Fits 90% of UK domestic staircases.
facts.topic: Closed string — the UK default

facts.statement: Cut string is the traditional decorative variant. Instead of housing the treads INSIDE the string, the string is CUT to the exact profile of every tread and riser — a zigzag pattern following the stair — and the treads sit on top of the cut string with the tread ends visible from the outside. The return nosing wraps round the tread end and mitres flush with the string face. Signals prestige because it takes real joinery skill to cut and assemble. Georgian and Victorian country houses standardised on cut string; modern high-end bespoke still specifies it for feature entrance stairs.
facts.topic: Cut string — the traditional feature

facts.statement: Honest cost comparison on a straight domestic staircase. A cut-string stair from a UK maker sits at roughly double a closed-string equivalent — same size, same timber, same everything else, just the string style changed. On an existing quote, upgrading the visible outer string from closed to cut typically adds about 15-25% to the total staircase price (plus VAT). That premium isn't material cost (the timber is similar) — it's labour. Cut string needs 3-4 times more workshop hours because every tread profile is machined into the string and every joint is mitred by hand. Exact numbers depend on final timber species, string dimensions, spindle type and finish — always confirm with the specific stair maker.
facts.topic: The price difference — cut string is roughly double closed

facts.statement: Three real reasons cut string costs more. One: labour — cutting and machining the zigzag profile takes hours per string versus a straight routing pass on a closed string. Two: material waste — the offcuts from the cut profile have no reuse, so waste factor jumps from 5% (closed) to 15% (cut). Three: skilled joinery required — return nosings mitred, riser faces trimmed to fit, spindles fixed directly into the tread top (not into a base rail) — every one of those needs precision at cabinet-maker standard. That's why cut string is a premium product, not a decoration option.
facts.topic: Why cut string costs more

facts.statement: Mitred cut string takes it further. The riser face is mitred so the riser timber comes through to the outside face of the string as a continuous line — no visible joint between riser and string. Tread is cut extra long so the return nosing projects past the string, then mitred flush. The result: a clean flowing line of tread-nosing-riser-tread visible from the side, with no visible joinery. Highest joinery skill on any staircase. Expect to pay 2.5-3x closed-string price. Georgian and grand-house standard.
facts.topic: Mitred cut string — the premium of the premium

facts.statement: Bracketed cut string is the Victorian and Edwardian classic. Cut-string base with decorative brackets fitted under each tread nosing on the outside face of the string. The riser mitres into the bracket. Standard bracket profiles: carved acanthus leaf, plain scroll, geometric fretwork. Almost always paired with scotia cove moulding under each nosing for the full traditional finish. Perfect for period-property restorations. Not for modern minimalist schemes — it reads as heavily traditional the moment it's fitted.
facts.topic: Bracketed cut string — the Victorian decorative variant

facts.statement: Open string is the modern minimalist answer — no visible string on one or both sides of the stair. Treads cantilever from a hidden LVL or steel core, or the balustrade sits directly on the treads with nothing beneath. The floating stair look. Structural engineering calculation required because each tread carries its own load without the string support. If the design is also open-riser, the gap between treads has to meet the 100mm sphere rule for child safety. Almost always paired with a glass or metal balustrade to keep the airy visual. Cost varies widely — a well-engineered floating stair can cost 3-5x a closed string equivalent because of the structural engineering and specialist install.
facts.topic: Open string — the modern floating look

facts.statement: String thicknesses aren't optional guesses. Closed string minimum 32mm softwood, 38mm hardwood or premium bespoke. Cut string minimum 48mm — no exceptions, and solid timber only (laminated will delaminate through the profile cuts). Wall string (concealed side) can safely stay at 32mm on any project because nobody sees it — save the budget for the visible outer string. Anything below the trade minimum flexes under foot, causes squeaks, and eventually opens the tread joints. Once a string flexes there's no fix short of replacing it.
facts.topic: String thickness — trade minimums

facts.statement: String heights (the visible depth from pitch line to bottom edge) come in standard trade sizes. 225mm — the trade standard for a straight domestic staircase in pine or oak. 275mm — a substantial specification for a bespoke stair where the visible string face is a design feature. 300mm+ — grand entrance stairs where the string presence anchors the whole visual. The taller the string, the more substantial the stair reads — worth stepping up from 225 to 275mm on any bespoke visible-string job because the extra 50mm massively changes the finished appearance.
facts.topic: String heights — the visible dimension

facts.statement: Every stair has two strings, but only one is visible. The wall string sits against the wall, hidden by the skirting, plastered up to at the top. The outer string sits on the balustrade side and everyone sees it. Practical rule: always spec the wall string as plain 32mm closed string in pine or MDF, regardless of what the outer string is. On a premium oak cut-string stair, the wall string can still be pine — saves 15-25% of the string cost with zero visible compromise. This is where a good stair maker saves the client money without cutting quality.
facts.topic: Concealed vs visible strings — where to save money

facts.statement: On a cut string, spindles fix directly into the TOP of each tread — they can't sit on a base rail because the string profile falls away between treads. That opens up spindle-design options: any spindle can be used, in any spacing, and the fixing is hidden inside the tread top with a mortise or dowel. On a closed string the spindles usually sit on a base rail (a horizontal timber grooved to receive them) — less expensive, faster, but a slightly less clean visual finish. This is one of the practical reasons cut string reads more premium: the balustrade transitions into the tread with no visible base rail.
facts.topic: Cut string + spindle fixing

facts.statement: Before picking a string style, walk through five questions with the client. One: budget — closed string is the trade-default baseline, cut string sits at roughly double, mitred cut string and open floating stairs sit higher again. Two: era of the house — modern minimalist wants open or plain closed, Victorian wants cut or bracketed cut. Three: how much is the stair on show — hallway stair everyone sees or back-of-house utility stair. Four: what timber and finish — painted stairs suit closed string because the visible face reads as one clean surface, natural-finish oak or walnut suits cut string because the tread grain is on view. Five: will they add a volute or scroll handrail — if yes, cut string with curtail step matches; if no, closed string with straight handrail matches. Answer those five and the string style picks itself. Exact prices always depend on final design, timber species and balustrade specification — always confirm with the manufacturer.
facts.topic: Choosing string style — five questions

facts.statement: Honest breakdown of UK stair-string reality by market tier. Volume housebuilding — 100% closed string, painted or carpeted, pine. Standard bespoke domestic renovation — 90% closed string, timber matched to house, natural or painted finish. Mid-market bespoke — closed string in oak or ash, well finished. Premium bespoke — cut string, or mitred cut string with volute handrail, in oak or walnut or sapele. Ultra-luxury — open floating string with glass balustrade, or curved cut string with bracketed detailing. Each tier is a different order of magnitude on cost from the last, but exact prices always depend on final design, timber species, balustrade type, finish, delivery and fit — knowing where the client sits in tier saves everyone time, and the actual number always comes from the specific manufacturer after full spec is locked.
facts.topic: String style — the domestic vs high-end reality

facts.statement: Two ways to run a handrail up a staircase. Continuous handrail — the rail flows unbroken from bottom to top, over every newel, through volutes and ramps and wreaths. Elegant, expensive, needs all the fittings machined and matched. Post-to-post — the rail runs from newel to newel in straight sections, terminating into each newel with a plain joint. Less expensive, simpler, less flowing. UK domestic default is post-to-post. Bespoke traditional and grand entrance work is where continuous handrail earns its cost. Continuous adds significantly to the joinery labour — always confirm the exact cost impact with the manufacturer after the design is locked.
facts.topic: Continuous vs post-to-post handrail — the choice

facts.statement: The volute handrail and the curtail step are designed to be paired. The spiral scroll at the bottom of the handrail sits directly above the curved edge of the curtail step, and the curve in each mirrors the other. Fit one without the other and the effect is broken — a volute above a plain bullnose reads as unfinished, a curtail step under a straight handrail reads as bare. Always spec them as a matched set at design stage, in the same timber, from the same workshop.
facts.topic: Volute + curtail step — the matched grand entrance

facts.statement: Almost every fitted handrail has an up-easing at the top — a small curved section that transitions the rail from the steep pitch of the flight to horizontal against the top newel post. Without it, the pitched rail meets the newel at 42° and looks wrong. With it, the rail flows smoothly into the newel. It's a small trade fitting, affordable, and easy to overlook on a quote — but every proper handrail install has one. Same at the bottom on continuous handrail systems.
facts.topic: Up-easing — the small fitting nobody sees

facts.statement: Where a stair meets a landing and the handrail turns from pitched (down the flight) to level (across the landing), the two sections join through a ramp — a curved piece that swaps the angle smoothly. Without a ramp the two rails meet at a hard knuckle you can't slide your hand over. Cut on-site to the specific pitch and landing corner, or supplied as a machined trade fitting for common pitches. Continuous-handrail work always uses machined ramps; post-to-post work often terminates into the newel instead and skips the ramp.
facts.topic: Handrail ramp — level to pitched transition

facts.statement: A wreathed handrail is a curved section that follows a curved staircase or wraps around the well opening at a landing. Machined from a solid billet of timber — never laminated — because the curve has to be cut through the timber in three dimensions at once. Wreath making is one of the most demanding pieces of joinery in the trade. High waste factor because the curved shape is cut from a much larger blank. On a curved bespoke stair the wreathed handrail is often the single most expensive component. Always confirm the total cost with the workshop after the design is locked.
facts.topic: Wreath — the joinery pinnacle

facts.statement: Every handrail join on a fitted stair uses a hidden bolt. Traditional rail bolt — threaded rod with a nut, tightened from a pocket cut into the underside of the rail through an access hole. Reliable, well-proven, been used for a century. Zipbolt — modern concealed bolt with a hex drive that's much easier to tighten in tight positions where a spanner won't fit. Both give the same structural join when properly torqued and glued. Zipbolt is now standard on new bespoke work; rail bolts still common on repair and traditional restoration.
facts.topic: Rail bolt vs Zipbolt — the hidden fixing

facts.statement: When a handrail run exceeds the length a single timber piece can supply (over about 3-4m depending on species and stock), the sections are joined with a scarf joint. A long diagonal cut through both handrail ends, glued and bolted (with a rail bolt or Zipbolt) so the join is invisible from above. Requires precise cutting — a badly cut scarf joint shows as a diagonal shadow line and defeats the whole point. Every workshop making bespoke handrails has a scarf-joint jig.
facts.topic: Scarf joint — handrail lengths

facts.statement: When the handrail transitions through a ramp or wreath, the height above the treads or landing must stay within the standard limits — 900mm on the flight (measured from pitch line to top of rail), 1100mm on the landing. Miss this on a wreath and the rail either dips below 900mm at a low point or exceeds practical grip height at a high point. Always plot the rail height at every point on the wreath during design, not just at the ends. Building control checks it.

evidence.note: UK handrail design + Approved Document K

facts.topic: Handrail height on ramps + wreaths

facts.statement: Where a stair has a wall on one side and no newel or balustrade to carry a handrail, a wall-mounted handrail is required if the flight has three or more rises. Mounted on brackets fixed through the plasterboard into the studs or into masonry. Bracket centres typically 900-1200mm. Standoff distance from the wall at least 50mm (Approved Doc M) so the whole hand can wrap around the rail. Common profiles: mopstick (round), pigs ear (D-profile flat against the wall), or matching profile to the main balustrade rail.

evidence.note: UK handrail practice + Approved Document M

facts.topic: Wall-mounted handrail — when it's needed

facts.statement: Two ways to construct a newel post. Solid newel — cut from a single timber billet, can be turned on a lathe for decorative traditional profiles, more expensive because more timber. Box newel — built up from four boards forming a hollow square, less expensive, has to stay square-faced (can't be turned). Structurally both are equally strong once fitted because the strength comes from the through-bolting into the floor, not from the interior mass. Choose solid for turned traditional stairs, box for square modern or painted stairs.
facts.topic: Solid vs box newel — the material choice

facts.statement: The single most important fixing on any staircase is the newel through-bolt. The newel post carries the whole balustrade load and the handrail — if the newel is loose, everything wobbles. Standard fixing: M12 studding or a coach bolt through the newel base into the trimmer joist or a solid timber block bolted under the floor. Never rely on the string alone to hold a newel — the string carries the tread load, not the balustrade side load. Every newel gets a proper through-bolt or it's a fault.
facts.topic: Through-bolt the newel — the fixing that matters

facts.statement: Three ways to join the handrail to the newel post. Mortise and tenon — traditional, strong, needs the newel machined to receive it, best for continuous handrail systems. Dowel joint — less expensive and quicker, two or three dowels between rail end and newel face, common on post-to-post work. Rail bolt or Zipbolt — hidden threaded fixing through a pocket in the rail underside, tightened after glue-up, invisible when finished. Every option is legitimate; pick to match the handrail system and workshop capability.
facts.topic: Newel-to-handrail joint — three options

facts.statement: When a staircase runs against a wall and the handrail needs to terminate against that wall (rather than into a free-standing newel post), the fitting is a half-newel. It's a standard newel split down the middle, mounted flat against the wall through the split back. The visible half projects into the room and looks as though a full newel is half-sunk into the wall. Matched in profile to the full-newel on the balustrade side so the pair reads as one system. Fixed through the wall with counterbored screws into studs or with plugs into masonry.
facts.topic: Half-newel against a wall

facts.statement: On an existing staircase where the newel base is being kept but the shaft is being replaced (or on an upgrade job where a new decorative newel is going on top of an existing plain post), the answer is a pin newel — a newel post with no base, just a pin (tenon or dowel) at the bottom that fits into a socket in the existing base. Saves the time and cost of removing the existing base. Equally as strong as a full newel once glued and mechanically fixed. Every stair-parts supplier stocks pin newels in the same profiles as full newels.
facts.topic: Pin newel — the retrofit shortcut

facts.statement: On a traditional staircase where the landing newel post extends down through the floor and is visible from the room below, a newel drop finishes it. A turned decorative piece hanging under the floor line — acorn, ball, urn, or teardrop profile. Victorian and Georgian standard. Optional but distinctive — turns a plain projecting newel bottom into a feature that anchors the hallway below the stair. Rarely fitted on modern builds because the newel usually stops at the landing floor.
facts.topic: Newel drop — the decorative underhang

facts.statement: The newel cap sits on top of the newel post and finishes it — first thing the eye sees at head height. Standard profiles: ball cap (classic Georgian), flat pyramid (Victorian), round dome (Edwardian), plain flat (modern), acorn or urn (high-end traditional). Fixed with a single dowel or screw through the underside. Get the cap wrong and the whole stair looks slightly off no matter how good the rest is — it's the head-height eye-line detail visitors clock immediately.
facts.topic: Newel cap — the top finish

facts.statement: Standard UK domestic newel post sizes are 90mm square and 100mm square (measured across the shaft, not including any base). 90mm is the volume default — every builders' merchant stocks it in pine and oak. 100mm is for grand or heavier stairs where the extra visual mass looks right — bespoke premium work, wide flights, curtail steps with large volutes. Under 90mm looks weak against a standard handrail; over 100mm looks heavy in a normal domestic hall. Match the newel size to the stair scale.
facts.topic: Newel post sizing — 90mm or 100mm

facts.statement: The straight flight is the simplest staircase shape — all treads in one continuous line from bottom to top, no turns. Most affordable to build, quickest to install, easiest to move furniture up. Takes the most floor length though — a typical 13-tread domestic straight flight eats about 2.8m of floor. Works well in wide open hallways and modern open-plan homes. Rarely fits into narrow terraced houses because there isn't the run length available. UK trade default when there's floor for it.
facts.topic: Stair shape — straight flight

facts.statement: L-shaped stair — two straight flights meeting at a 90° turn, either with a quarter-landing (flat square platform) or with kite winders (three tapered treads). Fits neatly into a corner, takes less floor length than a straight flight, and turns the stair away from the front door in most house layouts. UK domestic default for medium-sized homes because it uses the corner efficiently. Choice between kite winders and quarter-landing at the turn comes down to floor area and whether you'll ever move big furniture up.
facts.topic: Stair shape — L-shape (quarter turn)

facts.statement: U-shaped stair — two parallel flights running opposite directions, connected by a half-landing at the top of the first flight. Also called dogleg, switchback, or half-turn. Ends up facing the opposite direction from the start. Compact in floor plan (roughly a square footprint) and packs a lot of rise into a small area. Common in Victorian terraces and any tall narrow space. Bit slower to climb because of the two-stage journey through the landing, but very good at fitting into a limited floor plate.
facts.topic: Stair shape — U-shape (half turn / dogleg / switchback)

facts.statement: Two variants of the U-shape staircase. Dogleg — the two flights share the same landing wall with no gap between them, no open well in the middle. Compact, affordable, common in Victorian terraces. Open-well U-shape — the two flights are separated by a gap running down the middle between them, with a well opening in the landing. Grander look because the well opens up the vertical space, allows a wreathed handrail to flow round the well edge, and lets light through. Open-well needs more floor area.
facts.topic: Dogleg vs open-well U-shape

facts.statement: Bifurcated stair — starts as one broader flight from the ground floor, meets a wide landing partway up, then splits into two narrower flights heading in opposite directions to different upper floors or wings. The grand-house / hotel / historic estate classic. Requires massive floor area on both levels and works only in properties with enough architectural scale to carry it. Rarely built new in domestic UK — usually seen on renovation projects in country houses or listed buildings.
facts.topic: Stair shape — bifurcated (split) stair

facts.statement: Curved staircase — the flight runs on a continuous curve rather than through square turns, with no landings. Every string, every tread, every handrail section has to be machined to the curve. The most demanding stair to design, manufacture, and install. Takes significant floor area (needs a wide arc). Cost is a large multiple of a straight-flight equivalent. Reserved for high-end bespoke work where the visual statement justifies the joinery. Exact cost always depends on radius, timber, balustrade choice and finish — always confirm the specific number with the manufacturer.
facts.topic: Stair shape — curved / sweeping

facts.statement: Spiral staircase — treads winding around a central column in a continuous rise. Governed by BS 5395-2 rather than Approved Doc K. Categories A through E depending on use (small private, larger private, general public, assembly, escape). Very small footprint compared to any other shape — a spiral can fit into a 1500-2000mm diameter for a Category A private stair. Not comfortable to walk (tapered treads, tight turn) and impossible to move furniture up. Used where floor area is severely limited: loft access, mezzanine access, additional room service. Rarely a primary house stair.
facts.topic: Stair shape — spiral (compact 360° turn)

facts.statement: Helical stair — like a spiral but with a much wider central opening (no central column). The treads follow a helical curve around an open well. Elegant, sweeping, expensive. The visual statement staircase for luxury bespoke work. Governed by BS 5395-2 as spirals are but with different geometry limits because there's no column. Wide enough to be a comfortable primary stair in the right house. Cost is very high — the string is a full wreath, every tread machined to the helix, install requires specialist rigging.
facts.topic: Stair shape — helical (open central well)

facts.statement: Ships ladder or paddle stair — the very steep alternating-tread stair covered under Approved Doc K paragraphs 1.29-1.30. Only legal in a loft conversion where a conventional stair genuinely won't fit, serving one habitable room plus optionally a bathroom or WC. Very small footprint (roughly 1.8m x 0.6m vs 2.8m x 0.9m for a standard stair). Hard to walk, hard to descend, can't move furniture. Not suitable for young children, elderly, anyone unfamiliar. Legal only in the specific loft-conversion situation — never as a main house stair.

evidence.note: Approved Document K + UK space-saver practice

facts.topic: Stair shape — ships ladder / paddle / space saver

facts.statement: Where a loft isn't a habitable conversion but needs occasional access (storage, water tank, general maintenance), a loft ladder is the answer. Aluminium or timber, folding or sliding, mounts to a hatch in the ceiling. Not a staircase in regulatory terms — no Approved Doc K compliance needed. Fire compartmentation still matters: on any three-storey house or loft conversion, the loft hatch has to be an FD30-rated hatch even for storage access, otherwise the protected stairway is breached.

evidence.note: UK loft access practice + Approved Document B

facts.topic: Loft ladder — the pull-down alternative

facts.statement: Picking a stair shape comes down to four constraints. Floor area — straight flight needs the longest run, spiral needs the least. Total rise — spiral packs more rise into a footprint than any other shape. Furniture movement — straight and quarter-landing L-shapes are best; kite winders and spirals are worst. Aesthetic — sweeping curved and open-well U-shape read grand; straight and dogleg read functional. Walk those four with the client and the shape usually picks itself.
facts.topic: Choosing the stair shape — the four constraints

facts.statement: Concrete staircases suit projects where fire performance, durability, and heavy footfall are the priority. Standard on: commercial buildings, blocks of flats, escape stairs, external stairs, industrial premises. Rare in domestic new-build because the weight requires a structure that can carry it (usually excludes standard timber-frame houses). Precast concrete is factory-made and craned in — quick to install, expensive to transport. In-situ cast is poured on-site into formwork — slower but shapes to any geometry.
facts.topic: Non-timber staircase — when concrete makes sense

facts.statement: Three finish options on a concrete tread. Fair face — smooth polished concrete, works for modern interior. Exposed aggregate — the surface stones exposed for grip and industrial texture, standard on external steps. Inset — timber or stone strip set into the top surface of the concrete tread for a warmer visible surface with concrete strength beneath. The inset option is popular in commercial reception areas where a concrete stair feels too cold but structural timber isn't practical.
facts.topic: Concrete tread finishes — smooth vs aggregate vs inset

facts.statement: Steel string carrying timber treads is now the mainstream modern-industrial staircase choice for loft conversions, warehouse conversions, and open-plan renovations. Combines a slim thin-profile string (a 12mm steel plate looks lighter than any 48mm timber string) with the warmth of solid oak or walnut treads underfoot. Fabricated in a metal shop, delivered to the joiner for tread fit and finish. Needs structural engineer sign-off on the steel section — the joiner alone can't spec it.
facts.topic: Steel stringer + timber tread — the modern industrial default

facts.statement: Cantilevered concrete stairs are the most dramatic option — treads projecting from a supporting wall with no visible support beneath. Requires the wall to be structural masonry or reinforced concrete deep enough to carry the cantilever moment. Structural engineer input mandatory at design stage. Common on ultra-high-end residential and commercial architecture where the staircase is a sculptural feature. Almost never retrofittable into existing homes because the wall has to be built to carry it from the beginning.
facts.topic: Cantilevered concrete — sculpture that's also a stair

facts.statement: Structural glass treads (toughened + laminated) fitted to steel or concealed supports create the fully transparent stair. The premium visual statement — expensive, technically demanding, glass must be specified to structural grade under BS 6180 (balustrade) and EN 12600 (impact for treads). Consideration for family homes: treads are visible from below when someone climbs — worth mentioning to any client with young children. Anti-slip surface treatment on the tread face is mandatory by regulation. Cost always depends on structural spec, wall support, and balustrade choice — confirm with the specialist manufacturer.
facts.topic: Glass treads — the transparency premium

facts.statement: The composite staircase — steel structural frame, timber treads, glass balustrade panels, wire or steel handrail — combines the strengths of each material into the most visually refined modern stair. The technical challenge isn't in any single trade; it's coordination. Steel shop, joinery workshop, glazier, and rigger all have to hit the same specification and the same schedule. One project manager holds it together. Cost is very high because of the multi-trade fabrication — always confirm the specific price with the specialist company after design lock.
facts.topic: Composite stair — coordination is the hard part

facts.statement: When to choose non-timber over timber staircase construction. Concrete: fire resistance mandatory (commercial, flats, escape stairs), heavy footfall commercial or industrial. Steel + timber: modern industrial look, loft/warehouse conversion, need thin structural profile. Cantilevered concrete: sculptural feature in a building that can carry it. Glass: transparency is the design driver. In every other domestic and traditional situation, timber is still the right answer — less expensive, easier, warmer, and every joiner in the country can work it.
facts.topic: Non-timber vs timber — the decision

facts.statement: On a closed-string staircase, every tread sits in a housing cut into the string — typically 12mm deep (or 0.4 times the string thickness, whichever is greater). The tread edge is then wedged tight into the back of the housing with a hardwood wedge, glued, and often glue-block braced from below. That housing depth is critical: shallower than 12mm and the tread will work loose within years. Deeper than 15mm on a 32mm string weakens the string. 12-15mm is the sweet spot for a 32mm string, going to 15-18mm on 38mm or 48mm cut strings.
facts.topic: Tread housing depth — the joint that carries the stair

facts.statement: The wedge behind each tread is a small hardwood block cut to a taper (typically 4-6°) that drives tight into the housing behind the tread. Cut on-site to suit each housing. Beech wedge is trade standard (dense hardwood, holds its position). Pine wedge on budget work but softer wedges compress over decades — one reason older pine-wedged stairs squeak. When wedges come loose, drive them tighter from below (if you have access) or inject PU glue and reset — that's the standard squeak fix.
facts.topic: Wedge angle + fit

facts.statement: Glue blocks are small softwood blocks (typically 25-50mm square, 100-150mm long) glued and screwed into the internal corner where each tread meets its riser from behind. Four countersunk screws per block, driven at right angles into the tread and riser. Adds significant stiffness to the tread-riser joint, prevents squeaks, and reinforces the whole stair. Every modern mass-produced staircase uses glue blocks; older traditional stairs may rely only on wedges. When a stair squeaks, the first thing to check from below is whether the glue blocks have come loose — refixing them is a quick effective repair.
facts.topic: Glue blocks — the modern bracing

facts.statement: A squeaking stair has one of three causes. One: loose wedges (traditional housed construction) — access from below, drive tighter or reset with PU glue. Two: loose glue blocks (modern construction) — access from below, screw down or replace. Three: tread flexing against a nail head (nailed treads) — refix with screws, glue the joint. Diagnose by having someone walk up and down while you listen from below. Where the squeak happens tells you which tread and often which joint. If no access from below, the fix is from above by injecting PU foam or thin PU glue into the front joint where tread meets riser.
facts.topic: Squeak diagnosis — from below or from above

facts.statement: A loose newel post is the most serious common stair defect. The newel carries the entire balustrade — if it wobbles, everything above it does too. Causes: the through-bolt has loosened, the timber base has split, or damp has softened the newel base. Check the fixing: if you can access the through-bolt from below (usually in the ceiling below or in the under-stair cupboard), torque it tight. If not accessible, structural screws driven at an angle through the newel base into the adjacent framing can reinforce — but the proper fix is opening up the ceiling to re-fit the through-bolt.
facts.topic: Loose newel post — the structural check

facts.statement: A loose spindle wobbles because the glue at the top (into the handrail groove) or bottom (into the tread or base rail) has failed. The fix: inject PU glue into the loose join, wedge the spindle in position, clamp lightly overnight. If the spindle end has actually broken or split, the spindle has to be replaced — new same-profile spindle cut to length, glued in fresh. Every stair-parts range keeps trade replacement spindles in stock in common profiles. Individual spindle replacement is a 30-minute job for a joiner.
facts.topic: Loose spindle — the glue fix

facts.statement: Wet rot on a staircase starts where damp meets timber and stays for months. Classic locations: the newel base where it meets a solid concrete floor without a damp-proof course, the bottom step against an external wall in an old house, and the string ends where they sit into a wet cellar step below. Wet rot needs 40-60% moisture content in the timber to thrive. The fix: identify and stop the damp source first (damp-proof course, drainage), then splice out the rotted section and replace with treated timber. Never just paint over rot — it spreads.
facts.topic: Wet rot in a staircase — where it starts

facts.statement: Woodworm (the common furniture beetle) attacks old timber staircases, especially softwood risers and unpainted underside timbers. Signs: small round exit holes (1-2mm) with fresh sawdust below, particularly on the underside of the stair where nobody looks. Active infestation vs old damage: fresh dust means it's still active. Treatment: chemical woodworm treatment applied by a specialist, or replacement of severely affected timber. Superficial woodworm on visible surfaces can be treated in-situ; structural infestation of a string or tread requires replacement.
facts.topic: Woodworm in older stairs — signs and treatment

facts.statement: A split running down a string is the most serious stair defect. Once the string is split lengthways, it can no longer carry the treads reliably — the split will open under load and the stair becomes unsafe. Common causes: severe impact, long-term water damage, undersized string (below 32mm), or fitting a heavy stair onto insufficient support at bottom or top. Repair options: strap the split with steel plates through-bolted (temporary fix), splice a new section in (skilled joinery, less expensive than replacement), or replace the whole string (last resort, expensive because it means dismantling the stair). Get a structural opinion before deciding.
facts.topic: Split string — the failure mode that ends a stair

facts.statement: When considering repair vs replace on an existing stair, walk through five checks. One: is the string structurally sound (no splits, no rot)?
