Two: are the treads salvageable (worn is fine, cracked or rotted is not)? Three: does the stair meet current regs (rise/going/headroom) or would a replacement be needed for compliance anyway? Four: does the newel through-bolting still work or has the fixing failed? Five: what's the cosmetic condition — refinishable or beyond it? Score two or more fails and replacement usually beats repair. Score all pass, repair is almost always less expensive and preserves original character.
facts.topic: Repair vs replace — the decision framework

facts.statement: Stair nose protectors are extruded aluminium or brass profiles that clip or screw over the leading edge of each tread. Add anti-slip performance (Pendulum Test Value comfortably over 40), protect the tread nose from wear, and provide the contrasting visual edge Approved Doc K requires on public and common access stairs. Available in stand-alone form (screw fixed to the existing tread nose) or with anodised finish for colour and corrosion resistance. Popular retrofit on schools, offices, and any commercial stair being upgraded for safety without full replacement.
facts.topic: Nose protectors — the retrofit safety upgrade

facts.statement: Rubber inserts fitted into an aluminium nosing profile give the highest anti-slip performance available (Pendulum Test Value well over 40 in wet conditions) and can be replaced when worn without removing the profile itself. Common colours: black, yellow (high-vis), grey. Standard in commercial and public building stairs, external stairs, and any wet-area stair. Available with or without contrasting colour bands to meet Doc K visibility rules simultaneously. Retrofits over existing stairs with pre-drilled screw fixing.
facts.topic: Rubber nosing inserts — the anti-slip upgrade

facts.statement: Frameless glass balustrade panels fix to the stair in one of two ways. Channel fix — a heavy-duty aluminium channel is bolted to the floor or the string, and the glass panels slot in from above. Fully concealed base, cleanest look, easiest to install and align. Standoff fix — cylindrical stainless steel point fixings through the side of the string or trimmer joist hold the glass away from the structure. Shows the fixings as a design feature. Both meet BS 6180:2011 loading. Glass spec is at least 17.52mm toughened laminated when frameless without a top handrail.
facts.topic: Frameless glass balustrade — the fixing choice

facts.statement: Horizontal wire or cable balustrades look modern and industrial but come with a real child-safety issue. Horizontal cables read as a ladder to young children — they can and do climb them. The 100mm sphere rule alone doesn't address this. Best practice in family homes: avoid horizontal cable balustrade below head height, or specify closely-spaced vertical wires instead. If horizontal cable is essential to the design, pair it with a solid infill panel on the bottom third of the balustrade to defeat the ladder effect. Regs don't require this — child safety does.
facts.topic: Wire / cable balustrade — the child safety flag

facts.statement: Where a stair uses kite winders to turn 90°, the skirting board on the wall side has to follow the kite shape — a triangular piece cut to match the winder tread profile. Called kite skirting or kite board. Cut on site from the same skirting stock as the rest of the house. Precision cut needed because every winder is a different shape and the joint between winder skirting and straight skirting has to be tight. Common source of squeaks if fitted loose — always glue and pin.
facts.topic: Kite skirting — the winder-shaped board

facts.statement: Skirting board should run continuously up the wall alongside the staircase, following the pitch of the stair. Cut at the pitch angle at every step where it meets the tread edge, mitred at any corners. Match the house's standard skirting profile so the stair reads as continuous with the rest of the property. On modern builds the pitched skirting is often cut from the same 15-18mm MDF as the rest of the house skirting; on period restorations, matched to the original moulded profile.
facts.topic: Continuous skirting up the well

facts.statement: Two ways to detail the finish where the stair string meets the wall. String upstand — the string has a raised upper edge (an integral upstand) that projects above the tread line acting as its own skirting. Applied skirting — a separate skirting board runs along the wall alongside the string. String upstand is cleaner but only works on cut-string designs where the string extends above the tread. Applied skirting works everywhere else and is what most standard builds use.
facts.topic: String upstand vs applied skirting

facts.statement: Where the skirting board meets the newel post at the bottom or top of the stair, the joint has to be handled properly. Options: cut the skirting into a butt joint against the newel face (simplest, needs the newel positioned flush with the wall line), mitre the skirting round the newel (fiddly but elegant), or run the skirting behind a scribed newel face (traditional, most work). Whatever method is chosen, the joint has to be tight — a gap here is instantly visible at head height.
facts.topic: Skirting-to-newel joint

facts.statement: The site measure is the single most important step before manufacture. Get it wrong and the stair doesn't fit — no polite way to fix that. Record every dimension: finished floor to finished floor (not subfloor — factor in flooring being fitted after), joist opening width AND length, headroom under the joist above at every point along the pitch line, wall-to-wall at start and finish, and any encroaching services (radiators, sockets, alarm sensors, thermostats, coving). Take photos of everything. Two joiners take the measure — one measures, one records — to catch errors on the spot.
facts.topic: Site measure — the make-or-break moment

facts.statement: Before any staircase gets fitted, check the floor is level at both bottom and top landing. Use a long spirit level (at least 1200mm) across the trimmer at the top and across the floor at the bottom. Any dip more than 3-5mm and the stair will fit on the low side and gap on the high side. Shim strategy: pack the low side with hardwood shims under the string end before fixing. Never assume a modern house floor is level — trimmer opening framing regularly wanders by 5-10mm.
facts.topic: Floor level check before install

facts.statement: Same check on the walls where the stair meets — vertical plumb at both ends. Use a spirit level down the full wall height. If the wall is out of plumb by 5mm+ over 2000mm, the stair string will either gap at the top or bottom against the wall, depending on which way the wall leans. Options: pack behind the string with shims, or on major deviations, plane the string back-face to match the wall lean. Better to catch this at measure stage than on install day.
facts.topic: Wall plumb check before install

facts.statement: The trimmer opening in the upper floor joists has to be the size the drawn stair expects. Common site issue: the opening was drawn at 900 x 2400mm and got framed at 890 x 2380mm because someone assumed a bit of tolerance. That 10-20mm shortfall means the stair won't fit and the trimmer has to be re-cut and re-framed — a day's carpentry, plus rescheduling the install. Always measure the actual trimmer opening at site-measure stage and confirm to the workshop drawing office before the stair goes into manufacture.
facts.topic: Trimmer opening size — measure twice

facts.statement: Before install day, walk the stair route and check for services that will be in the way. Radiators at the bottom step position, sockets or switches on the well wall that will end up behind the string, ceiling downlights that will fall inside the trimmer opening, smoke or thermostat sensors on the landing at the top newel position, water pipes in the ceiling below the stair. Any of these have to be diverted or the stair won't fit. Ideally divert 1-2 weeks before install so the electrician / plumber has time and the plaster is dry.
facts.topic: Services check — what's in the way

facts.statement: Before accepting a stair job, walk the physical route the stair components will take from the road to the fitting position. A single closed string can be 3.5m long, 300mm deep — check every doorway width, corner, and low ceiling on the path in. If the string won't fit through a doorway, options: knock-down delivery (the stair supplied in sections and assembled on-site), removing a window temporarily (glazier both ways), or crane hire (external delivery through an upper window). All add cost and time. Better to know at quote stage than on delivery day.
facts.topic: Access route — the physical constraint

facts.statement: Two ways to get a bespoke stair to site. Assembled — the whole flight (strings, treads, risers, newels) built in the workshop, delivered as one unit, lifted into position. Fastest install (single day on a straight flight), best structural integrity, but needs the access route to accept the full assembled size. Knock-down — supplied as loose components (strings, treads, risers, newels, balustrade parts) assembled on-site. Fits anywhere, slower install (2-3 days), needs a skilled joiner on-site to build up. Curved and helical stairs almost always knock-down; straight flights usually assembled.
facts.topic: Assembled vs knock-down delivery

facts.statement: Where the bottom step meets the hallway floor, the transition detail matters. On a hard floor (tile, wood, laminate), the bottom nosing sits directly on the finished floor, ideally with the floor running continuously past the stair rather than butting to it. On a carpeted floor, the carpet either turns up onto the bottom riser (called a nosing wrap) or terminates at a floor bar before the stair, with the bottom step and treads carpeted separately. Coordinate with the flooring contractor at design stage — the level relationship is fixed at the drawn stage.
facts.topic: Bottom step transition to flooring

facts.statement: For carpeted stairs, the standard fixing method uses stair grippers (Smoothedge or dual-fix strips) fitted along the back edge of each tread and the top edge of each riser. Carpet is stretched between the two grippers on each step. Two fitting styles: Waterfall — carpet flows straight over the nosing without being pulled tight round it, faster to fit, less material used. Hollywood — carpet pulled tight around the nosing then pinned or wrapped under, tighter finish, uses more material, more labour. Hollywood is the premium fit; waterfall the volume standard.
facts.topic: Carpet on stairs — gripper strategy

facts.statement: The under-stair space is a common location for consumer units, meters, gas meters, and small boilers. Fine on standard two-storey houses. On a protected stairway (loft conversion, 3-storey, HMO), the under-stair cupboard housing any of these needs to be fully fire-lined with plasterboard, and the door must be FD30 self-closing. Coordinate the electrical and gas contractors so their kit fits the fire-lined enclosure before install. A last-minute realisation that the consumer unit doesn't fit inside the finished cupboard costs a day and a re-build.

evidence.note: UK under-stair coordination + Approved Doc B

facts.topic: Under-stair electrics + boiler

facts.statement: When a new stair is installed into an unfinished house or a fresh loft conversion, the plastering sequence matters. Standard order: stair fitted and rough-set → carpenter installs skirting and architrave around it → plasterer skims all walls and ceilings → decorator paints. Never plaster the walls BEFORE the stair goes in — the stair fit will chip the fresh plaster and everything needs re-doing. If plaster is already on and the stair is a retrofit, protect the walls carefully during fit and expect small make-good touches by the plasterer afterwards.
facts.topic: Plastering around a new stair — the sequence

facts.statement: Cleaning a finished wood staircase is simple if you use the right thing. Damp cloth with a mild pH-neutral cleaner (Method Wood Cleaner, Osmo Wash & Care, or diluted washing-up liquid) works on lacquered and oiled finishes. Never use vinegar on oak — the acid reacts with tannin and etches the finish. Never use ammonia-based cleaners on any lacquered surface — they cloud the finish. Never soak the timber; water sitting on a joint will lift the finish and open the joint. Damp mop, wipe dry.
facts.topic: Cleaning a wood staircase — what to use

facts.statement: Hardwax oil finishes (Osmo Polyx, Fiddes Hard Wax Oil) look brilliant on natural-finish stairs but need periodic maintenance to stay looking that way. Refresh coats: on treads with heavy footfall, once every 12-24 months. On low-traffic areas like handrail, newel, spindles, every 3-5 years. Refresh is easy: clean the surface, light sand with 240-grit if needed, apply a thin coat with a lint-free cloth, wipe off excess. No stripping needed if the finish is intact. Signs it's time: water beading has stopped (finish is worn), colour is dulling in high-wear zones.
facts.topic: Re-oiling schedule — hardwax oil finishes

facts.statement: 2K polyurethane lacquer finishes last 10-15 years on treads with heavy use before they need refreshing. Unlike oil finishes, 2K PU can't be refreshed with a top coat over the old finish — the old lacquer has to be stripped or heavily sanded back first, or the new coat won't bond. Standard refresh procedure: sand back the old finish with 120-180 grit, or use a paint stripper if it won't sand cleanly, prime with 2K primer, then 2K topcoat. Best done by a specialist spray-shop, not DIY. Occupants have to vacate for the isocyanate cure.
facts.topic: Re-lacquering — 2K PU stripping and recoat

facts.statement: A single loose spindle is a homeowner-fixable problem. Grip the spindle at both ends and check where the wobble is (top into the handrail, or bottom into the tread or base rail). Whichever end is loose, inject wood glue or PU glue into the join with a fine nozzle, hold the spindle firm, wedge it in position with tape or shim, let cure overnight. If the spindle is actually broken or the glue join has failed entirely, replacement is a joiner's job — 30-minute call-out. Multiple loose spindles at once suggests a bigger balustrade issue and needs a joiner to look at the whole system.
facts.topic: Fix a loose spindle — DIY the small stuff

facts.statement: Strip and refinish an existing stair when: (1) the finish is worn through to bare timber on the tread nosings and no amount of refresh oil hides it, (2) old finish has yellowed or clouded (common on solvent lacquer from the 80s/90s), (3) the client wants to change colour (stained darker, painted white, etc.), or (4) new tread damage has been repaired and needs colour-matching over the fill. Below those triggers, a periodic refresh coat is usually enough. Full strip and refinish is a specialist job — hire a floor-sander shop or spray-shop.
facts.topic: When to strip and refinish — the trigger points

facts.statement: Two carpet options on a staircase. Full carpet — the whole tread and riser covered, tucked into the corners at the string sides. Softer feel, warmer, quietest under foot, hides worn timber. Runner — a narrower strip of carpet down the centre of the stair, leaving the tread edges visible each side. Traditional look, shows the timber joinery either side (great with cut-string or oak stairs), often uses decorative brass or chrome rods across each nosing. Runners look intentional; full carpet reads as functional. Both are legitimate — pick to match the house.
facts.topic: Stair carpet vs runner — the choice

facts.statement: The traditional way to fix a stair runner is with metal rods that cross each tread at the riser junction. Rods (brass, chrome, or antique bronze finish) sit in cast metal end sockets screwed to the string on each side. Runner passes under each rod and is held in place by the tension. Look: period-property standard. Easy to remove for cleaning or replacement — pull the rods out, take up the runner. More work to fit than modern gripper-fixed carpet, but the finish reads as bespoke and traditional. Popular on Georgian and Victorian restorations.
facts.topic: Rod-fixed stair runners — the traditional detail

facts.statement: External timber staircases live outdoors in UK weather. Softwood pine or spruce lasts about 3-5 years before rot sets in — not fit for purpose. Realistic material options: Accoya (acetylated softwood, 50-year warranty, dimensionally stable, ~3x softwood cost), oak (durable but heavy and moves with moisture, 20-30 years with proper drainage), larch (naturally durable UK-grown option, silvers attractively), or steel-framed with hardwood treads. Every timber external stair also needs stainless or non-ferrous fixings — regular steel corrodes in months.
facts.topic: External timber stair — the material choice

facts.statement: External stairs with a drop over 600mm need guarding — same rule as internal. On a garden step with a drop over 600mm, a proper balustrade or handrail is required by regs, not just aesthetically. External balcony and roof-terrace guarding must be 1100mm minimum from finished floor level (higher than internal because outdoor use has more lean-over risk). Anti-slip surface on the tread is required — Pendulum Test Value wet over 40 for anywhere users may push or turn, over 36 for straight walking.

evidence.note: Approved Document K + external stair practice

facts.topic: External stair guarding + handrails

facts.statement: External stairs in UK climate see ice, frost, and occasional snow. Fitted grit strips or textured anti-slip nosings should be standard on any external stair that will see winter use. Where the client will pay for it, heated nosings (electric mat under an aluminium nosing) prevent ice forming — used on hospital entrance stairs and premium hotel externals. Drainage detail matters too: every tread should shed water away from the stair, not into it (a slight 1° slope on the tread top) and the joints should be sealed against water ingress.
facts.topic: External stair ice + snow safety

facts.statement: When a loft isn't a habitable conversion but needs occasional access (storage, water tank, cold-water storage, general maintenance), a loft ladder is the answer — not a staircase. Aluminium concertina, sliding, or timber folding options. Mounts to a hatch in the ceiling, deploys when needed, folds away when not. Not a staircase in regulatory terms so no Approved Doc K compliance needed. Fire compartmentation still matters though: on any 3-storey house or loft conversion, the loft hatch has to be FD30 fire-rated even if it's only for storage access, otherwise the protected stairway is breached.

evidence.note: UK loft-access practice + Approved Doc B

facts.topic: Loft ladder — the non-conversion option

facts.statement: Every professional stair site measure captures the same standard set of dimensions on a written form (or digital app). Finished floor to finished floor height. Trimmer opening length AND width. Wall-to-wall dimension at start of flight and at end of flight. Landing dimensions at top and bottom. Headroom clearance under the joist above at every point along the pitch line. Any services (radiators, sockets, sensors, coving). Any existing skirting profile to match. Photograph everything from multiple angles. Two joiners on the measure — one dimensioning, one recording — halves the error rate.
facts.topic: Site measure form — what to record

facts.statement: Bespoke stair projects should have a formal design sign-off before manufacture starts. Drawings issued to the client showing all key dimensions, timber species and grades, string style, balustrade type, handrail termination, and starting-step design. Client signs and returns. Once signed, changes cost extra (variation orders). Without formal sign-off, workshops end up building to remembered conversations and disputes are inevitable at delivery. The best workshops send drawings by email with a formal 'please confirm' request; no confirmation = no manufacture start.
facts.topic: Design sign-off — the paper trail

facts.statement: When a client changes their mind mid-project (change from oak to walnut, add a curtail step, spec 41mm spindles instead of 32mm), the change is captured on a variation order — a written note of what's changing, cost impact, and any timeline impact. Signed by both sides before the change goes into manufacture. Protects the client from surprises and the workshop from disputes. Workshops that skip variation orders end up doing free work or losing money on changes; clients who skip them end up with unexpected invoices. Written and signed, always.
facts.topic: Variation order handling

facts.statement: Replacing an entire staircase in an existing house or altering structural elements (moving the trimmer, changing the well opening) triggers Building Regulations. The homeowner or contractor has to submit a Building Notice or Full Plans application to local Building Control before work starts. Straightforward tread or riser replacement, refinishing, or replacing balustrade like-for-like usually doesn't need notification. Loft conversions always need it because of protected stairway rules. Best practice: call the local Building Control before starting anything significant — a 5-minute call saves months of retrospective remedial work.
facts.topic: Building control interaction — when to notify

facts.statement: At the end of a bespoke stair install, the contractor should provide the client with a handover pack. Contents: as-built drawings (the actual dimensions of what was built, not the original design if it changed), warranty terms in writing, care and maintenance guide for the specific finish used, and any Building Control sign-off certificates. Also: the recommended refinishing schedule (when to re-oil, when to have professional lacquer refresh). The handover pack protects the client if they sell the house (evidence of quality install) and protects the contractor if a claim comes back later.
facts.topic: Handover certificate + as-built drawings

facts.statement: Most bespoke UK stair workshops now use CNC routers for the repetitive machining — tread housings cut into the string, mortises for spindle bases, decorative panel profiles. CNC delivers millimetre-precise repeatability across every tread in a flight, which hand-routing can't quite match at that scale. Programmed from the workshop's CAD drawing so the drawn dimensions become the machined dimensions with no interpretation. Speeds up manufacture, tightens joint fit, reduces tread-to-tread variation. Doesn't replace hand-finishing on curved and mitred work — those still need the joiner.
facts.topic: CNC routing on modern staircase manufacture

facts.statement: For period-property stairs where nothing is square or level, 3D laser scanning is now the standard measure tool. Scanner sits on a tripod and captures the entire stairwell as a point cloud in a few minutes. Software builds a millimetre-accurate model of the actual space including every wall lean, floor slope, and joist irregularity. The CAD drawing is generated to match reality, not to assume regularity. Result: bespoke stairs that fit period spaces first time. Standard measurement tape can't achieve the same accuracy on Victorian or Georgian houses where walls lean 15mm+ over 2m.
facts.topic: 3D scan-to-manufacture for period properties

facts.statement: Prefabricated modular stair systems ship as a kit of standard-size components — treads, risers, strings, newels, balustrade — matched to the stair pitch and rise the client's opening actually needs. Volume housebuilder standard: modular kits from a handful of UK trade suppliers cover the vast majority of standard domestic openings. Assembled on site by a joiner in a day. Much less expensive than a bespoke workshop stair. Trade-off: less design freedom, fewer timber options, standard-only detailing. For a straight or L-shape flight in a standard house, often the sensible choice.
facts.topic: Prefab modular stair systems

facts.statement: LED strip fitted along the underside of each tread nosing, powered by a 24V DC driver in the under-stair cupboard, is now standard on modern bespoke stairs. Gives a defined edge to every tread visible in low light without dazzling. Warm-white LED (2700K-3000K) reads warmer against timber; cool-white (4000K+) reads clinical and modern. Never so bright it hides the tread edge — the whole point is to define the edge, not blind the user. Sensor-activated as standard so the stair lights when someone approaches. Integrated at drawing stage — retrofitting LED into an existing stair is fiddly and rarely as clean.
facts.topic: LED strip in nosings — the modern lighting integration

facts.statement: PIR (passive infrared) motion sensors at the top and bottom of the flight trigger the LED nosings when someone approaches. Standard setup: sensor detects motion, LED comes on at daytime brightness for 30-60 seconds, then off. Pair with a photocell so daytime pedestrian traffic doesn't waste power. Add a night mode via a dimmer — after 11pm the sensor triggers the LEDs at 10-20% brightness so someone descending at 3am isn't dazzled. All wired through a small controller (Rako, Loxone, or basic dimmer switch) in the under-stair cupboard.
facts.topic: PIR sensors + dimmer setup

facts.statement: Sensor-driven stair lighting is convenient but Approved Doc P (wiring regs) and Doc M (accessibility) both expect a physical switch — the sensor alone isn't compliant on stairs used as escape routes. Standard install: physical two-way switch at top and bottom of the flight controlling the main circuit, plus the PIR-triggered LED nosings as a secondary always-on aid. In a protected stairway or fire escape route, emergency battery-backed lighting also required — kicks in if mains power fails, keeps the escape route lit long enough for evacuation.

evidence.note: UK stair lighting regs (Doc P + M) + practice

facts.topic: Regulatory switching alongside sensors

facts.statement: Any protected stairway — loft conversion, 3-storey house, HMO, block of flats, commercial — needs emergency lighting on the escape route. Standard spec: mains-powered emergency LED fitting at the head of each flight, with battery backup that gives at least 3 hours of illumination if mains power fails. Tested monthly by the responsible person (landlord, employer). Battery replacement every 4-5 years. Not required on standard 2-storey houses. Coordinated with the electrician at first-fix wiring, not retrofitted after the plasterer has finished.
facts.topic: Emergency lighting on protected stairways

facts.statement: Beyond basic PIR-and-LED lighting, modern smart-home systems can integrate the staircase into whole-house scenes. Voice control (Alexa, Google Home, HomeKit) turns stair lights on and off. Automation rules light the stairs at specific times or when someone comes home. Colour-changing LED nosings for feature scenes (blue for a movie night, warm amber for evening ambience). Cost adds up quickly on top of standard sensor+dimmer setup — worth spec'ing at design stage rather than retrofitting. Confirm the actual price with the AV/smart-home installer after the specific scene design is locked.
facts.topic: Smart-home integration — the modern extras

facts.statement: For ultra-high-end feature stairs, fibre-optic 'starlight' LED effects fit hundreds of pin-point lights into the riser faces — looks like a starry sky when the stair lights come on. Fibre-optic cable runs from a central light engine in the under-stair cupboard, splitting into individual fibres each terminating at a small hole drilled into the riser face. Colour-changing engine gives full RGB control. Popular in luxury nightclub and hotel stairs, occasionally specified for domestic entertainment rooms. Very high install cost — always confirm with the specialist installer after the pattern design is agreed.
facts.topic: Fibre-optic + starlight LED effect

facts.statement: A stair pack is a modular flat-pack staircase kit — strings, treads, risers, newels, balustrade parts — supplied in stock sizes matched to a common opening dimension. Volume-manufactured in high runs, sold through builders' merchants for immediate collection. Assembled on-site by a joiner in a day for a straight flight. Fitting a stair pack costs considerably less than a bespoke workshop stair — appropriate when the opening is a standard size, the client wants pine or standard oak, and there are no design requirements beyond regs compliance.
facts.topic: Stair pack (flat-pack) — what it actually is

facts.statement: Stair packs come in standard configurations but real openings are never exactly standard. Common on-site modifications: shortening the strings to match actual finished floor heights, cutting the trimmer end to match the actual joist opening, trimming the bottom tread to the actual hall width, adjusting the top nosing to sit flush with the finished landing floor. Any of these adds an hour or two to install. If the site opening is more than 20-30mm off the stair-pack standard, a bespoke stair is usually the more sensible choice — the modifications start to eat the price saving.
facts.topic: Stair pack — modifications needed on site

facts.statement: Two questions decide stair pack vs bespoke. One: is the opening standard? A regular new-build opening under 900mm wide with straightforward pitch fits a stair pack; anything unusual needs bespoke. Two: what does the client want? Standard pine or oak in a stock profile — pack. Specific timber, unusual balustrade, cut string, curved run, or premium finish — bespoke. Bespoke cost is considerably more than a pack, but the flexibility is total. Get both quotes when in doubt and let the client decide against the design brief.
facts.topic: Stair pack vs bespoke — the choice

facts.statement: The core workshop tool for staircase manufacture is the tread-housing router — sets the pattern for every housed joint on the strings. Fixed-based router with a template jig cut to the exact housing dimensions (tread width x housing depth). Runs down the string face making identical housings for each tread. On CNC workshops the same job is done by the CNC head. Every stair workshop has either a dedicated router station or a CNC line. Hand-routed housings without a jig are only for repair work or one-off custom sizes.
facts.topic: Router for tread housings — workshop kit

facts.statement: A wedge angle jig is a small workshop template used to cut every tread wedge to exactly the same taper (typically 4-6°). Consistency here matters: uneven wedge angles mean uneven wedge fit, which means the treads sit at slightly different pressures against the strings. Result: some squeak-free, some squeaky, all from the same stair. Every workshop has a wedge jig — usually a bandsaw fence set to the taper angle. A stair that squeaks new is almost always the result of inconsistent wedges.
facts.topic: Wedge angle jig — the small tool that matters

facts.statement: A handrail bolt kit contains the small drill bits, the counterbore for the access hole, the specific nut wrench for the pocket, and the plug cutter for the wooden plug that covers the access hole. Bought as a matched set for the specific rail bolt or Zipbolt system being used. Every stair joiner carries one — trying to fit a hand rail without the right tool means cutting bigger access holes than needed and struggling to reach the nut. Small investment, big time saving.
facts.topic: Handrail bolt tool kit

facts.statement: Fitting an assembled stair into position needs specialist clamps. Stair clamps (long sash clamps or purpose-made stair clamps) hold the string against the wall and the tread ends into the string during glue-up. Pinch bar (a long timber lever with a wedge point) helps lever the stair into final position when it's tight against fixed walls or joists. Every fitting van carries clamps and a pinch bar. Trying to fit an assembled stair with just hands and screws leaves gaps at joints.
facts.topic: Stair clamps + pinch bars

facts.statement: Any professional staircase fitter working in occupied homes should carry public liability insurance to a level appropriate for the work — typical trade minimum is a few million cover, scaling higher for larger commercial jobs. The policy covers accidental damage to the client's property or injury to third parties during the work. Clients should always ask to see the current PL certificate before letting a fitter into their house. Any fitter who can't produce a current certificate isn't worth hiring — one dropped tool on a marble floor costs more than any insurance premium. Exact cover values vary by insurer and job type — always confirm with the specific fitter.
facts.topic: Public liability insurance for fitters

facts.statement: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, any staircase supplied and fitted to a UK consumer has to be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, and as described. If the stair squeaks within days of install, the treads are visibly uneven, or the balustrade wobbles, the consumer has a legal right to have it fixed free of charge. Six-year time limit on making a claim after purchase (five years in Scotland). Normal wear and tear isn't covered — worn treads after 5 years of family use is wear, but a joint opening after a year is a fault.
facts.topic: Consumer Rights Act cover for a fitted stair

facts.statement: Understanding what warranty covers vs what's normal wear helps everyone. Warranty covers: structural defects (loose newel from bad through-bolting), manufacturing faults (cracked tread from a knot in the timber), finish failures within warranty period (lacquer peeling after 6 months). Wear covers: nosings wearing on high-traffic treads, small joint gaps opening from seasonal humidity, general dulling of oil or lacquer over time. Any maker who tries to cover wear under warranty is over-promising; any who refuses to cover a genuine fault under warranty is under-delivering. The line is: was it broken from install day, or has it broken from years of proper use?
facts.topic: Warranty vs wear + tear — the boundary

facts.statement: Practical checklist for choosing a UK stair maker. One: ask to see photos of at least 5 completed jobs similar to yours (not marketing shots — actual customer photos). Two: ask for references from clients who used them 2-3 years ago (recent clients still love them; older clients tell you how it's aged). Three: check they have public liability insurance and Consumer Rights Act awareness. Four: get an itemised quote — timber, manufacture, delivery, fit as separate lines. Five: check their site-measure process (do they visit? photograph? measure everything?). Any red flag means keep looking.
facts.topic: Choosing a staircase maker — the checklist

facts.statement: Standard payment structure on a UK bespoke stair project. 30% deposit on design sign-off (protects the maker's design and material ordering). 40% on manufacture start or delivery (covers materials and workshop labour). 30% on satisfactory install and sign-off (protects the client from paying in full before the work is done). Never pay a deposit larger than 30-40% up front — makers who demand 100% deposit are a warning sign. Protect large deposits with a bank card payment (Section 75 protection) rather than a bank transfer.
facts.topic: Deposit + payment stages — protecting both sides

facts.statement: The word bespoke covers a spectrum in the UK stair industry. True bespoke — every dimension custom to the site, any timber species, any balustrade design, hand-built to order. Modified bespoke — starts from a standard configuration but changes several key elements (timber species, string style, balustrade type). Standard bespoke — a stair pack modified to fit the specific opening dimensions but otherwise a stock design. All three get called bespoke by makers marketing their work. Ask specifically: which elements are being customised, and which are standard components?
facts.topic: What 'bespoke' actually means

facts.statement: Warning signs on any UK staircase quote. Round-number pricing (a suspiciously flat total) usually means guesswork not costing. No breakdown of timber/manufacture/delivery/fit as separate line items. No site visit before quoting (real quotes need real measurements). No warranty terms in writing. Demanding a large upfront deposit (over 40%). Vague timber description ('hardwood' instead of 'European oak Prime grade'). No lead-time confirmation. Any of these and either the number is fiction or the maker is inexperienced. Better to get three quotes and compare like-for-like line items.
facts.topic: Red flags in a stair quote

facts.statement: Every UK builders' merchant runs trade pricing for account customers and retail pricing for cash sales. Trade discounts on stair parts (spindles, newels, handrails, mouldings) typically 15-40% below retail depending on volume. A professional fitter or joinery workshop always buys at trade price, then passes that through in the quote with their own markup. Homeowners buying stair parts direct from a merchant pay retail. Real cost savings come from fitters passing through their trade discounts, not from clients trying to source parts themselves.
facts.topic: Trade vs retail merchant pricing

facts.statement: A broken baluster comes out and a new one goes in — no need to touch the rest of the staircase. Balusters are individual components on almost every UK stair, designed to be replaced one at a time. Most breakages are accidental damage, not manufacturing faults. The two most common causes: moving big furniture past the balustrade (wardrobes, sofas being lifted upstairs), and children climbing or swinging on the balustrade until a single baluster cracks. Good news for anyone facing a broken one — the whole staircase stays where it is.
facts.topic: Broken baluster — yes it can be replaced individually

facts.statement: Standard removal sequence when a baluster's broken. First job: lift out the small timber fillets above and below the baluster with a sharp wood chisel. Fillets are the strips slotted into the groove on the underside of the handrail and the top of the baserail — one either side of every baluster. They're glued and pinned, so patience matters. Rush the chisel and you'll damage the handrail or baserail edge. Once the fillets are out, the baluster usually lifts or slides straight out. On a cut-string stair, also lift the baluster bottom off the dowel driven into the tread top before it comes fully free.
facts.topic: Removing a broken baluster — fillets first

facts.statement: When a baluster breaks, keep every broken piece — even if it's shattered into four or five bits. The original tells the workshop or the woodturner six things nothing else can match. Exact overall length, the turning profile, the timber species, the shoulder positions, the top and bottom cut angles, and the dowel positions if there is one. Any catalogue drawing or phone photograph loses at least one of these to interpretation. The old joiners say it plainly — a broken baluster is still the best drawing you'll ever have.
facts.topic: Keep every broken piece — the best drawing you'll get

facts.statement: Staircase designs change over the decades and manufacturers drop older patterns from stock. If the exact match can't be found in any current trade range, take the original baluster (broken or intact) to a professional woodturner. A skilled turner reproduces old patterns from a sample as a matter of course — trade turners have been keeping old staircases running this way for generations. Cost per bespoke turned baluster is a multiple of a stock spindle, but for one replacement it's the answer. Always confirm the specific cost with the woodturner after showing them the sample.
facts.topic: Discontinued baluster patterns — the woodturner route

facts.statement: Fitting a replacement baluster looks simple until you try to make it work with the rest of the balustrade. The new spindle has to sit squarely in the handrail groove, fit tightly into the baserail groove or tread mortise, be cut at the exact pitch of the flight so it stands vertical, keep consistent spacing to the adjacent spindles (the 100mm sphere rule still applies to the new spacing), and hold structurally through the top and bottom fixings. An experienced carpenter usually manages it; a specialist stair-fitter does it faster and cleaner. Poorly fitted balusters loosen up within months and the visible profile ends up out of line with the rest of the run.
facts.topic: Fitting a replacement baluster properly

facts.statement: Whether a broken baluster can be glued back rather than replaced depends on the damage. Clean single break away from any joint, timber intact on both sides of the break — a good wood adhesive (PVA D3 minimum, PU for extra strength) will hold if the baluster isn't carrying significant structural load. Shattered break, missing pieces, or a break right at the top or bottom joint — always replace. The balustrade is a safety barrier, not just decoration. A repaired baluster with a suspect glue joint is a fall risk waiting to happen if it fails, especially in a home with children or elderly users.
facts.topic: Gluing a broken baluster vs replacing it

facts.statement: Technically you can replace one baluster with a different style — nothing stops you from doing it. In practice, unless you're deliberately creating a decorative feature, one different spindle in a run of matched ones is instantly visible. The eye scans a balustrade as a repeating pattern; anything that breaks the pattern reads as a mistake, not as a design choice. Always match the replacement to the existing profile even if it means paying a woodturner to bespoke-turn it. Skipping the match to save time or cost costs more later in visual pain every time you climb the stair.
facts.topic: Don't mix baluster styles

facts.statement: A broken, cracked, loose or missing baluster reduces the strength of the whole balustrade and creates a gap wide enough that a child's head can pass through. That's not a theoretical risk — it's exactly what the 100mm sphere rule protects against. Any damaged baluster should be repaired or replaced as soon as practical, not left until later. In a home with young children, missing balusters need immediate temporary blocking (a piece of ply cable-tied across the gap) until the proper replacement can be fitted. The wait isn't worth the risk.

evidence.note: UK stair safety guidance + Approved Document K

facts.topic: Broken or missing baluster is a real safety risk

facts.statement: Cost of replacing a single baluster depends on several things at once. Timber species (softwood most affordable, oak next, hardwoods like walnut or sapele on top). Turning complexity (plain square chamfered is most affordable, ornate turned traditional profiles cost more). Whether it's a stock trade profile that can be pulled off the shelf or has to be bespoke-turned to match an old pattern. Whether painting or clear-finishing is included. And labour to fit properly. A simple painted softwood spindle from stock parts is considerably less expensive than a hand-turned hardwood baluster made to match an old original. Exact numbers always depend on final timber, profile, finish and fitter — always confirm with the specific joiner or woodturner before agreeing the work.
facts.topic: Cost of replacing one baluster — what drives the number

facts.statement: A turned baluster is a vertical spindle shaped on a woodturning lathe to create decorative curves, beads, coves, and flowing profiles up its length. Different from a plain square baluster — the timber has been spun and cut into a shaped form. Turned balusters have been used on British staircases for hundreds of years and remain one of the most recognisable features of traditional timber staircases. Structurally they do the same job as a plain spindle; the difference is what they add visually.
facts.topic: Turned baluster — what it is

facts.statement: Traditional turned balusters are made on a woodworking lathe. The timber blank is mounted between two centres (a drive centre at one end, a live centre at the other) and rotated at high speed while the turner cuts material away using specialist chisels and gouges. Controlling the tools against the spinning timber, the turner creates smooth curves, beads, coves, and decorative details. Every stair workshop that turns balusters keeps a lathe and a set of profile jigs. Modern manufacture also uses CNC copy lathes that reproduce identical balusters from a master pattern with millimetre accuracy.
facts.topic: How turned balusters are made — the lathe process

facts.statement: The decorative shapes on a turned baluster aren't random — they come from a classic vocabulary of turning profiles that woodworkers have used for centuries. Beads (small convex half-round rings), coves (concave half-round hollows), ogees (S-shaped curves), fillets (small flat bands separating other shapes), bulbs (large convex swellings), reeds (parallel raised ribs), vees (V-shaped notches), and rings (raised annular bands). These shapes have been used in furniture-making and architecture since Classical times, and combined skilfully they give a balustrade its rhythm and proportion.
facts.topic: Classic turning profiles — the shape vocabulary

facts.statement: Two ways to produce a turned baluster today. Hand turning — a skilled woodturner uses traditional gouges and chisels against the spinning timber. Every baluster is individually shaped so each one is slightly unique. Slower, higher labour cost, preferred for restoration work where original craftsmanship is important. CNC copy turning — a computer-controlled lathe reproduces identical copies from a master pattern. Faster, dimensionally consistent across a whole run, ideal when a stair needs 40-80 matching spindles. Both methods produce excellent results. Choose hand for one-off replacements matching an old original; choose CNC for a new full-set run.
facts.topic: Hand turning vs CNC copy turning

facts.statement: Common question — are turned balusters stronger than square ones? Not really. Strength depends on the timber species, the cross-section dimension at the narrowest point, and how the baluster is fixed at top and bottom. Whether it's turned or square barely matters. A well-fitted 32mm square oak spindle can be just as strong as a turned equivalent. The choice between turned and square is aesthetic — turned reads traditional, square reads modern — not structural.
facts.topic: Turned vs square baluster — strength is not the difference

facts.statement: What separates a well-made turned baluster from a poor one comes down to eight things you can check by eye and hand. Smooth flowing curves with no chatter marks. Crisp detail on beads and vees (edges sharp, not rounded off). Symmetrical turning (every point equidistant from the centre axis). Straight-grain timber (no run-out through the shoulders). No visible machining marks under the finish. Consistent dimensions across the run so every spindle matches the next. Clean shoulders where the turned section meets the plain top and bottom. Accurate top and bottom joint fittings for the handrail groove and the baserail or tread. Best balusters look elegant while staying strong enough for daily household use.
facts.topic: Quality checklist for a turned baluster

facts.statement: If the original newel post is structurally sound but visually dated, decorative newel post covers can be fitted OVER the existing post to give a completely new appearance without removing the structural timber underneath. The cover slips over and fixes to the original with concealed screws or adhesive. Sold in traditional turned, square-panelled, and modern chamfered profiles matched to matching newel caps. If the original post is damaged or structurally unsound, it should be inspected and often replaced rather than covered — never hide a structural problem behind cosmetic timber.
facts.topic: Newel post retrofit covers

facts.statement: One of the most enduringly popular UK staircase looks is painted white balusters combined with a natural-finish hardwood handrail — typically oak, sometimes walnut or sapele. Works because the light-coloured spindles recede visually while the darker rich handrail stands out as a warm horizontal line. Suits everything from modern new-builds to Victorian restorations. Painting the balusters also protects the timber and makes future re-decorating easier — a coat of white satin every few years refreshes the whole balustrade. Widely specified across every price tier from stair pack up to bespoke.
facts.topic: Painted balusters + hardwood handrail — the popular UK combo

facts.statement: Spindle and baluster describe the same component — the vertical piece between the handrail and the tread or baserail. Both terms are used widely in the UK trade and neither is wrong. Homeowners often say spindle; professionals and joinery drawings often say baluster; suppliers use both interchangeably in their catalogues. If somebody asks for a spindle, they mean a baluster. If somebody quotes for a balustrade with 20 balusters, they mean 20 spindles. Same component, different word.
facts.topic: Spindle vs baluster — the same thing

facts.statement: Woodturning is one of the oldest woodworking crafts in the world. Simple pole lathes were in use over 2000 years ago in Roman times and earlier. Decorative turned staircase components became increasingly popular in Britain during the 17th and 18th centuries. Many Georgian, Victorian, and Edwardian homes still carry their original hand-turned balusters today — some over 200 years old and still doing their job. That longevity is part of why turned balusters remain in demand: they age well, they can be repaired or reproduced, and they connect a new stair to a long tradition of craftsmanship.
facts.topic: Historical context — turned balusters through the centuries

facts.statement: A skilled woodturner can often identify the period of a staircase just by looking at the turning profile of one baluster. Baluster designs have moved through architectural fashions the same way clothing has — Jacobean bulbous columns in the 1600s, slender Georgian classical proportions in the 1700s, ornate Victorian variety in the 1800s, plainer Edwardian and Arts and Crafts in the early 1900s. The profile itself is the clue. That's why keeping a broken baluster matters twice over: it lets a matching replacement be turned, and it preserves a piece of the house's story that can be dated and understood on sight.
facts.topic: A woodturner can date a stair from the baluster profile

facts.statement: Balusters have evolved over hundreds of years and every shape tells a story. Some were designed to suit the architecture of the period, some reflected the skills of local craftsmen or the machinery available at the time, and some reflected the status of the home — grand houses got elaborate carved and turned balusters, cottages got plain square ones. A simple square baluster creates a clean modern appearance; turned balusters with beads and curves add character and tradition. Today homeowners choose by what they like the look of, but historically the choice often reflected something bigger about the house.
facts.topic: Baluster shapes through history

facts.statement: Surprisingly the hardest part of turning a baluster isn't the turning itself. It's making every one exactly the same. If one baluster is a few millimetres different from the next, the eye picks it up straight away once they're installed in a row. Professional workshops use gauges, templates and copy lathes to keep every spindle identical across a run of 40-80. Consistency across the set matters more than any single virtuoso spindle — that's what separates a factory-quality balustrade from a variable-looking one.
facts.topic: Hardest part of making a turned baluster — consistency

facts.statement: Timber naturally holds a lot of moisture when the tree is felled. Before it can be used for stairs it has to be dried down to a workable moisture content — typically 8-12% for interior joinery in a heated UK house. Kiln drying does that in controlled conditions over days to weeks, much faster than air drying and to a consistent target. Using timber that's too wet leads to gaps, cracks, twisting and squeaks once the stair is installed inside a heated home and the timber continues shrinking. Every professional workshop specifies kiln-dried stock — always confirm the moisture content spec with the supplier.
facts.topic: Kiln-dried timber — why staircase makers use it

facts.statement: Grain is the natural direction of the wood fibres running through the timber. A baluster or tread with straight grain is stronger and more stable than one with wild, twisted or interlocked grain. Grain direction also affects machining (cutting against the grain tears the fibres), sanding (the surface finishes cleaner with the grain), staining (end grain absorbs more, side grain less), and even how light reflects off the finished timber. Experienced joiners inspect every board before machining — the grain determines the final quality of the whole staircase.
facts.topic: Grain direction matters

facts.statement: Weight differences between staircase timbers come from density. Rough scale (all values air-dry): pine and tulipwood around 450-500 kg/m³ — light. Walnut and cherry around 620-660 kg/m³. Oak and ash around 680-720 kg/m³ — noticeably heavier. Beech around 720 kg/m³ — extremely hard and compact. A solid oak stair weighs roughly one and a half times a pine equivalent of the same dimensions. Heavier timber often feels more solid underfoot, but weight alone doesn't determine quality — good design, correct moisture content and proper installation matter equally.
facts.topic: Timber weight by species

facts.statement: Timber is a natural material and it will always respond to changes in temperature and humidity — even the finest stair ever built will expand and contract slightly throughout its life. The goal of good staircase making is not to eliminate movement, it's to CONTROL it. Kiln-drying to the right moisture content, allowing expansion at the ends of long components, choosing dimensionally stable species where movement matters most, and accepting seasonal gaps as normal rather than as faults. Any workshop or fitter who promises zero movement is over-promising.
facts.topic: Timber movement — control it, don't try to stop it

facts.statement: Many staircases are supplied unfinished because every home is different. Some homeowners want natural oak clear-lacquered, some want painted white, some want a dark stain, some want hardwax oil. Leaving the stair unfinished at delivery lets the homeowner apply the finish that suits the rest of the interior — matched to existing joinery, flooring or wall colour. Finish choice usually gets locked at design stage, but the actual application often happens after fit-out so the timber isn't damaged during the building work still going on around it.
facts.topic: Why staircases are supplied unfinished

facts.statement: A feature staircase is one designed to be a main visual attraction of the home rather than just connecting two floors. Common elements: curved handrails, glass balustrades, oversized newel posts, decorative volutes, hardwood construction, floating treads, integrated statement lighting. A feature stair is often the first thing visitors notice on walking in — worth spending more on because it does design work for the whole hall or entrance space, not just carrying people between floors. Not every house needs one; where the architecture supports it, one changes the whole ground floor.
facts.topic: Feature staircase — what qualifies

facts.statement: Before dispatch, professional workshops mark every component of a bespoke stair — each tread, riser, string section, newel, and handrail section is numbered so it can be assembled on site exactly as it was machined. Reduces mistakes during installation, ensures every joint fits the way it was fitted in the workshop dry-run, and lets the fitter work through a big kit of parts without guessing. Think of it as a giant timber jigsaw puzzle where every piece has its own position and orientation. No numbering = install-day confusion.
facts.topic: Why manufacturers number every part

facts.statement: Dry fitting is assembling the whole staircase in the workshop WITHOUT glue before the final glued assembly. Lets the workshop check joint accuracy, overall dimensions, alignment of strings and treads, handrail fit, and baluster spacing — all before commitment. Any adjustments made at this stage are quick and easy; the same adjustments after glue-up are far harder. Experienced workshops treat dry fitting as one of the most important quality-control stages — a stair that assembles cleanly dry will assemble cleanly wet.
facts.topic: Dry fitting — the workshop QC stage

facts.statement: Handcrafted staircases involve far more manual work than standard production stairs. Curved strings, shaped handrails, bespoke newel posts, custom joinery, wreaths — all require skilled hand work rather than automated machinery. Result: significantly more workshop hours per stair, which is what drives handcrafted cost above standard. Not just about the finished look; it's about the labour hours that go in. Handcrafted stairs are often unique pieces that can't be ordered from a catalogue. Exact cost impact always depends on complexity — confirm with the workshop after design lock.
facts.topic: Handcrafted vs automated production — labour is the difference

facts.statement: A well-designed and properly maintained timber staircase lasts for many decades — often well over 100 years. Many historic UK homes still use their original staircases, proving quality timber and good craftsmanship stand up to time. Most repairs over the years involve replacing worn components (balusters, handrails, individual treads) rather than the whole staircase. That's the case for spending well at build stage: a good stair built once outlasts three affordable replacements and preserves the character of the house through generations.
facts.topic: A well-made staircase can outlive its house

facts.statement: A common assumption: all timber staircases eventually squeak. Not true. A stair built with kiln-dried timber, proper wedging, glue blocks correctly fitted, and adequate string thickness can stay quiet for decades. When squeaks do develop later, they're often from seasonal timber movement rather than build fault — two pieces of timber moving against each other after years of normal use. A squeak isn't automatically a sign of poor workmanship; some stairs squeak within months of install (build fault), some develop occasional squeaks in year 10 (natural movement).
facts.topic: Not every staircase squeaks

facts.statement: Some homeowners notice their staircase only squeaks in winter. There's a physical reason. In winter, central heating dries the indoor air, timber shrinks, and tiny gaps develop between joints that were previously tight — allowing components to move against each other and squeak. In summer the humidity rises again, timber absorbs moisture and expands, and the gaps close up. The squeak disappears naturally. This is why some stairs sound perfect in July and creaky in January — the timber is doing exactly what timber does. Not a fault, just physics.
facts.topic: Winter squeaks + summer silence

facts.statement: New staircases sometimes develop small surface cracks in the first year or two — often called seasoning checks. Usually caused by natural timber movement rather than poor workmanship. As the timber continues to adapt to the moisture level in the actual home (which is often drier than the workshop), the surface may develop fine cracks around knots or along the grain. Most are cosmetic and don't affect structural strength. Large cracks, cracks widening over time, or cracks through structural joints should always be inspected by the manufacturer — those aren't seasoning, they're something else.
facts.topic: Seasoning checks — small cracks are normal

facts.statement: Small allowances between components on a new stair aren't measurement errors — they're deliberate. Timber expands and contracts throughout the year, and a stair fitted absolutely tight with no allowance for movement will actually develop more problems than one with a millimetre or two of expansion room. Where you'll see it: string ends against walls, handrail scarf joints, big landing panels. Good staircase making is about controlling timber movement, not preventing it. A gap you can slide a business card into is often exactly what a component needs to work properly for the next 50 years.
facts.topic: Expansion gaps by design

facts.statement: Dragging heavy furniture across timber treads causes deep scratches, dents, broken nosings, loose balusters and damaged handrails. All expensive to repair, some of it irreversible. Professional removal companies lift furniture clear of the staircase whenever possible; homeowners moving big items themselves should always protect the treads with blankets, thick cardboard, or specialist protective coverings. Never drag directly on the timber. A single wardrobe pulled across a set of oak treads can end up costing more in refinishing than the removal-man saved.
facts.topic: Dragging furniture damages staircases

facts.statement: A finished staircase is one of the most vulnerable items inside a new home. Install it too early and it gets damaged by plastering, brick dust, paint splashes, heavy foot traffic from every other trade, dropped tools, building materials stored on treads, and moisture from wet trades. Builders therefore install the finished staircase late in the build — once plastering is done and the property is drying out. Sometimes a temporary rough stair goes in first for access during the build, then gets swapped for the finished piece near completion.
facts.topic: Why stairs go in near the end of a build

facts.statement: Natural sunlight contains ultraviolet (UV) rays that gradually change the colour of exposed timber. Oak often becomes slightly warmer and richer in colour with UV exposure. Walnut typically LIGHTENS over time rather than darkens. Areas covered by rugs, runners or furniture receive less UV and age at a different rate — lift a rug off a stair after 10 years and you'll see the shadow. This colour change is natural and one of the reasons timber develops character as it ages. If uniform colour matters to the client, plan the rug/runner placement at day one — the differential ageing will always show.
facts.topic: Sunlight ages timber — the differential

facts.statement: Most people naturally walk the same route up and down their own staircase every day. Over thousands of trips, certain treads take much more foot traffic than others. The first step, the last step, and the middle-of-the-tread walking line usually wear the fastest. Perfectly normal and one of the reasons stair runners became popular — they protect the highest-wear line down the centre while leaving the tread edges visible each side. If wear on the walking line becomes an issue, refinishing the exposed nosings or adding a runner is usually the fix, not replacement.
facts.topic: Some treads wear faster — the walking line

facts.statement: Most staircase problems are repairable — loose handrails, broken balusters, worn treads, squeaks, loose wedges, damaged newel caps, surface scratches, general wear. Individual components come out and go back in without disturbing the whole stair. Full replacement is usually only necessary if there's major structural damage (split string, rot through the newel base), the stair fails current regulations after other work triggered a compliance check, or the client wants a complete redesign. Nine repair jobs out of ten cost a fraction of a replacement — always get a repair quote before assuming a stair needs replacing.
facts.topic: What can be repaired vs when to replace

facts.statement: Hardwood trees grow much more slowly than softwood — an oak takes 60-120 years to reach staircase-sized boards versus 25-40 years for a spruce or pine. The timber is denser, harder to machine (blunts blades faster, needs more feed pressure), and often takes longer to prepare and finish. All of that increases workshop hours per component. Result: hardwood staircases sit at a considerable multiple of softwood equivalents on cost — but they also produce a stair that resists everyday wear far better and lasts significantly longer. Confirm the actual cost impact with the workshop after specifying the exact species.
facts.topic: Why hardwood costs more than softwood

facts.statement: The single most important measurement in staircase design is finished-floor-to-finished-floor height — from the top of the finished ground floor to the top of the finished upper floor. Everything else on the stair is calculated from this one dimension: total rise, individual step rise, going, pitch, number of treads. Get this wrong at measure stage and every rise in the finished stair is wrong. Professional workshops confirm this dimension at least twice before production starts, and specifically flag any planned floor finishes (carpet, tile, timber) so the FINISHED level is what gets used, not the subfloor.
facts.topic: Finished-floor-to-finished-floor — THE measurement

facts.statement: Modern CNC machinery produces excellent accuracy on repetitive parts, but hand tools are still essential on every bespoke stair. A sharp chisel, a block plane, or a rasp lets the joiner make tiny adjustments no machine can — trimming a housing that ended up 0.5mm too tight, easing a spindle end into a slightly out-of-square groove, fitting a scarf joint that has to look invisible. Many perfectly-fitting staircases owe their final quality to a few careful strokes with a hand tool at the very end of the install. The machinery gets you 98% of the way; the hand tools do the last 2%.
facts.topic: Hand tools still essential

facts.statement: Bespoke workshops can start preparing materials and machining standard components before the house reaches staircase stage — timber acclimatising, standard sections cut, jigs set up. But most workshops confirm final site measurements before COMPLETING manufacture, because openings drift during construction and building drawings rarely match the eventual reality. Standard sequence: order at design stage, workshop starts prep work, site measure at first-fix stage (walls up, ceilings on, floor levels defined), manufacture completes, install towards the end of second fix. Don't ask a workshop to build a stair from architectural drawings alone — the measure has to be real.
facts.topic: Making the stair before the house is finished

facts.statement: Large staircases can be difficult to transport through doorways, hallways, and narrow properties. Manufacturing them in sections — the flight in one piece, the landing in another, the balustrade separate — allows easier delivery and install while still achieving a seamless finished look once assembled on site. Joints are cut so they're almost invisible once the balustrade and handrail run over them. On big curved stairs and grand entrance staircases, sectional delivery is the norm rather than the exception. Discussed at design stage — the workshop knows what fits through the client's front door before committing to an assembled build.
facts.topic: Sectional manufacture — why big stairs come in pieces

facts.statement: Two staircases might look almost identical and be built with completely different jointing methods, timber species, or fixing systems underneath. An experienced staircase maker spends more time inspecting a stair than performing the actual repair — because the wrong diagnosis leads to the wrong fix, and the underlying problem comes back. Check from below (glue blocks, wedges), check the newel through-bolt, check the string for splits, listen while walking every tread, watch how the balustrade moves under lateral push. Only then quote the fix. The old workshop saying: measure twice, cut once — but inspect three times before blaming the staircase.
facts.topic: Why experienced makers inspect before advising

facts.statement: A quality staircase often goes unnoticed. The steps feel solid, the handrail feels comfortable under the hand, the joints are tight, the balusters line up perfectly, there are no unexpected creaks or movements. Visitors rarely comment on a staircase that works perfectly — they only notice one that doesn't (a wobble, a squeak, a loose spindle). For a staircase maker, the goal is a stair that people walk on for years without ever thinking about it. That anonymity is often the greatest compliment the trade offers.
facts.topic: The sign of a well-made staircase — it goes unnoticed

facts.statement: Many experienced staircase makers can walk up a staircase and identify — just from the sound and feel under their feet — whether it's built with softwood, hardwood, MDF treads, whether the wedges have loosened, or whether movement is developing in a joint. Years of experience train the senses as much as the eyes. A hollow-sounding tread under weight often means the glue blocks have come loose; a slight lateral flex means the string might be undersized; a hard bright ring versus a soft muffled thud says hardwood versus softwood. That kind of walk-and-feel diagnosis is knowledge nothing on paper can capture.
facts.topic: Nex Workshop Fact — walk-and-feel diagnosis

facts.statement: Every staircase reflects the choices made during its creation — the timber that was selected, the craftsman who built it, the home it was designed for, the family who use it every day. Unlike most building components, a staircase becomes part of everyday life. Children learn to climb on it, families decorate the newel post at Christmas, generations use the same steps for decades. That's why the old saying holds: you don't just build a staircase — you build part of someone's home for life.
facts.topic: Every staircase tells a story

facts.statement: The best staircase makers aren't remembered because they built the fanciest staircase. They're remembered because 30 years later the staircase is still solid, still safe, and still looks beautiful. Good craftsmanship isn't judged on the day it's fitted — it's judged by how well it stands the test of time. A stair delivered perfectly to the client on day one but squeaking within a year is a failure; a stair that looks slightly less spectacular on day one but is still tight, level and quiet at year 30 is a success. Time is the honest reviewer.
facts.topic: Nex Craftsman's Note — the 30-year test

facts.statement: The baserail is the horizontal timber rail that sits below the balusters on any stair where the spindles don't fix straight into the tread. Three jobs at once: it keeps the balusters evenly spaced and structurally anchored, it creates a neat finishing detail along the line of the flight or landing, and it takes the horizontal component of the load from the whole balustrade back to the newels. Standard on landings, on all closed-string stair balustrade lines, and on any run where the spindles don't sit on tread edges. Cut-string stairs skip the flight baserail because the spindles fix directly into the tread top instead.
facts.topic: Baserail — what it actually does

facts.statement: Most UK timber staircase systems supply the handrail and baserail as a matched pair — same timber species, same profile at the mating face, same groove width and depth to receive the spindle ends. The two rails are designed to work together as a system. Ordering a handrail from one profile and a baserail from another usually means the spindle ends won't seat properly at one end or the other. Always spec both together, from the same supplier or the same workshop, in the same timber. Trade catalogues explicitly list them as matched sets for exactly this reason.
facts.topic: Baserail + handrail — matched pair

facts.statement: Handrail fillets are narrow timber strips fitted into the groove of the handrail (and matching baserail) BETWEEN each pair of balusters. Two per bay on stairs where the spindles pass into grooves on both ends. Job: they lock the balusters into position by filling the groove tightly, hide the groove where no spindle sits, and set the exact spindle-to-spindle spacing that meets the 100mm sphere rule. Cut to length on site to give whatever centres the balustrade design needs. When a broken baluster needs replacing, removing the fillets on either side is normally the first step of the job.
facts.topic: Handrail fillet — the piece between every spindle

facts.statement: If you look at a fitted balustrade and see the groove of the handrail or baserail visible between spindles, the fillets are either missing or badly fitted. A properly finished balustrade has NO visible groove — the fillets fill it end-to-end. Immediate visual quality check on any stair install. Missing fillets also let spindles move slightly (they're no longer wedged in position), which quickly leads to loose spindles and eventually rattle when someone leans on the handrail. Any decent joiner fits fillets as standard; missing fillets on a new job is a snag to raise immediately.
facts.topic: Fillets missing — the immediate tell

facts.statement: If you walk into a stately home built between roughly 1600 and 1680 and see fat oak balusters that bulge out in the middle like tiny wooden vases stacked one on top of the other, that's Jacobean. Big oversized newel posts often carved with heraldic beasts or coats of arms. Dog-leg layouts almost exclusively. Solid oak throughout because that's what was around. The mood: heavy, ceremonial, built to last centuries — and centuries later it still is.
facts.topic: Jacobean staircase — the bulbous 1600s look

facts.statement: Late 1600s the twist baluster showed up on English staircases — one continuous spiral cut into the whole spindle, made possible by new lathe techniques imported from the continent. Walnut started appearing alongside oak. Gates at the bottom of the flight were common (baby-proofing is not a modern invention). The whole thing got a bit lighter, a bit more elegant, a bit less 'medieval fortress'.
facts.topic: William & Mary — the twist arrives

facts.statement: Early 1700s the balusters slimmed down noticeably. Mahogany started arriving from the Caribbean colonies and instantly became the timber to have. Proportions got Palladian — designed by ratio, not eye. Three balusters per tread became the polite standard on any serious house. This is when the British staircase transitioned from 'structural feature' to 'display of taste'.
facts.topic: Queen Anne + early Georgian — elegance kicks in

facts.statement: Mid-to-late 1700s: cut-string construction with decorative brackets under every tread nosing, mahogany handrails, slender square-plan balusters set three per tread, elaborate carved volutes at the starting step. The Georgian staircase is arguably the most refined design the trade has ever produced — everything since has either copied it or reacted against it. Restoration work on Georgian houses is a specialism in its own right.
facts.topic: High Georgian — cut string peaks

facts.statement: Early 1800s the ironmasters got in on staircases. Ornate cast-iron balustrade panels replaced timber spindles in fashionable London townhouses. S-scrolls, anthemion leaves, geometric patterns — all mass-producible from moulds, all less expensive than timber turning at the volumes required. The Regency staircase is the first industrial-age stair, even if it still looks handmade.
facts.topic: Regency — ironwork enters

facts.statement: The Victorian era (1837-1901) is where every staircase style you've ever seen turns up somewhere in the country. Cast iron scrollwork, heavily turned timber balusters, gothic revival pointed newels, bracketed cut strings in every conceivable timber, tile risers on grander examples. Mass production meant every terrace got a stair, and every terrace's stair reflected the local builder's taste. If you're working on a Victorian house restoration, the answer to 'what's period-correct?' is nearly always 'a bit of everything, actually.'
facts.topic: Victorian — every possible variation, all at once

facts.statement: By the early 1900s people had had quite enough of Victorian excess. Edwardian staircases went cleaner: plainer square balusters, less ornate newels, honest visible joinery. The Arts and Crafts movement pushed this further — celebrate the timber, celebrate the maker, no fake ornament. Oak came back into fashion. Many early 20th century houses still have the original stair and it still looks perfectly modern — that's how well the reaction worked.
facts.topic: Edwardian + Arts and Crafts — the reaction

facts.statement: 1920s-30s: staircases went geometric. Chrome and stainless steel balustrades, cast glass, angular newels, stepped chevron risers, black and white marble on grander projects. Not many Art Deco stairs survive intact in UK houses — most got ripped out in the 1970s along with everything else Deco — but the surviving examples in old cinemas and hotels are increasingly protected. If a client mentions restoring an Art Deco original, refer to a listed-building specialist. It's a rare skill.
facts.topic: Art Deco stairs — geometry takes over

facts.statement: 1950s-60s: the modernists killed the balustrade infill. Open-riser stairs, single central steel spine, hardwood treads floating with no visible support, minimal or wire balustrade, big open well letting light through. Half the stair-design vocabulary used in modern homes today comes from mid-century modern experiments. The look reads as contemporary even 70 years later — genuinely timeless design.
facts.topic: Mid-century modern — the floating stair invented

facts.statement: Right now: frameless glass balustrades, single-plate steel strings, solid oak or walnut treads at 40mm+, LED nosings sensor-activated, and — interestingly — a quiet return of the curved wreathed handrail on grand houses that want the modern kit with the traditional flow. Contemporary UK staircases pick the best bits from every previous era and combine them. The trend line: less material, more precision.
facts.topic: Contemporary — glass, steel, and the return of the wreath

facts.statement: Traditional Japanese staircases (kaidan) run steeper and narrower than anything UK regs would allow — often 55-60° pitch, no handrail, treads sometimes doubling as drawer fronts (kaidan tansu). Built entirely from clear-grained cedar or cypress, joined without metal fixings using traditional Japanese joinery. Not something you'd fit in Britain (Approved Doc K would refuse it before the design left the drawing) but a useful reminder that stair conventions are cultural, not universal.
facts.topic: Japanese kaidan — the compact wooden staircase

facts.statement: Scandinavian staircase design took modernism and ran with it. Blonde birch or ash treads on white-painted steel or timber stringers, open risers, thin metal cable or vertical steel bar balustrades, matt-white walls. The whole look reads as light, airy, and about as far from a Georgian stair as it's possible to get while staying practical. UK homeowners increasingly ask for 'a Scandi stair' — this is what they mean.
facts.topic: Scandinavian stairs — minimal timber

facts.statement: Two mainstream American traditions worth knowing.
