That availability gap explains 90% of the 'my mahogany staircase is actually Sapele' surprises. On the visible treads and risers Sapele is less common because those are usually bespoke-machined; the stairparts default has quietly become Sapele.
facts.topic: Sapele as stairparts — the mass-produced reality

facts.statement: If a bespoke mahogany or Sapele staircase matters visually, ask the workshop to turn all the stairparts (spindles, newel caps, handrail sections) from the SAME timber batch — ideally one billet or one tree source. Reason: even within a species, different trees produce different grain patterns and slightly different colours. Off-the-shelf stairparts are milled from many trees across many batches, and if you compare a stock spindle against a bespoke tread they'll often look slightly off from each other. One-tree-source machining is more expensive but guarantees the whole balustrade reads as a single continuous piece of timber. Standard trade practice on serious high-end bespoke work.
facts.topic: 'One type, one tree' — asking for matched stairparts

facts.statement: Mahogany's reputation as the Rolls-Royce timber isn't just about looks. It's genuinely one of the most durable staircase timbers you can spec. Dense (roughly 620-640 kg/m³ air-dry), hard-wearing under decades of foot traffic, dimensionally stable through UK humidity cycles (doesn't move like beech or ash), and takes finish beautifully. The historic staircases at Drayton Hall, Powel House, and countless Georgian townhouses have survived nearly 300 years of family use with only surface refinishing — the underlying structure and joinery are still original. Very few timbers can claim that longevity. If a client wants a staircase built to outlive them, mahogany or a proper mahogany-family substitute is the honest recommendation.
facts.topic: Mahogany durability — why the historic staircases survived

facts.statement: Where mahogany comes from today isn't where it came from historically. Traditional 18th-19th century mahogany was Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Bahamas) and Central American (Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua) — Cuban mahogany was the premium grade until deforestation restricted it. Modern legal supply of genuine mahogany (Swietenia macrophylla) still comes from Central and South America under CITES-controlled harvesting, in limited volumes. Modern substitute mahogany (Sapele, African mahogany) comes from West Africa — Cameroon, Congo, Ghana, Cote d'Ivoire. Philippine mahogany (Meranti) comes from Southeast Asia — Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines. Merchant labels sometimes just say 'mahogany' — if country of origin matters, ask for the botanical name and the CITES / FSC paperwork.
facts.topic: Mahogany country of origin — the modern picture

facts.statement: 'Maple' covers a family of timber species and the difference between hard and soft maple matters more than any other split in the trade. Hard maple (also called rock maple or sugar maple, Acer saccharum) has a Janka hardness rating around 1450 lbf — one of the densest hardwoods in commercial use. Soft maple (silver maple, big-leaf maple, and others) sits around 950 lbf — hard enough for cabinetry but not for the hammering a staircase takes. On a staircase, always ask for HARD maple specifically. Soft maple looks similar in a showroom but dents visibly within a year of family use.
facts.topic: Maple — hard vs soft, and why it matters

facts.statement: Hard maple has a reputation for good reason — it's what basketball courts, bowling alleys, and school sports halls are built from. If it can survive decades of trainers, sports shoes, and dropped equipment on a gym floor, it will survive your family's stair treads without complaint. That density is genuinely useful on a stair where the walking-line treads take repeated impact from hard-soled shoes. Very few hardwoods can match it — oak comes close but doesn't quite hit maple's dent resistance.
facts.topic: Maple — the gym floor timber

facts.statement: Within hard maple, four grain grades are worth knowing about. Plain — straight uniform grain, the everyday specification, most stocked. Curly (also called tiger or flame) — wavy grain that produces a shimmering 3D optical effect under finish, premium grade. Birdseye — small dark eye-like circles scattered through the grain, extremely rare and expensive, more common on furniture than staircases. Quilted — a puckered irregular pattern, ultra-luxury, rarely used for structural stair components. On a bespoke maple staircase, specifying curly maple for just the visible outer string or top newel cap is a common way to add character without paying for full curly throughout.
facts.topic: Maple grades — plain, curly, birdseye, quilted

facts.statement: Maple's colour is its blessing and its warning. Fresh sawn hard maple is genuinely one of the palest hardwoods you can spec — creamy white to very light gold, cleaner and brighter than ash. That paleness reads Nordic-modern and works beautifully in contemporary interiors. The warning: maple is notoriously difficult to stain. Oil-based dark stains blotch badly because maple's tight closed grain absorbs unevenly. Standard fix — use a gel stain (sits on the surface rather than penetrating) if the client insists on darkening, or better, leave it natural with a clear water-based lacquer that keeps the brightness. UV yellows maple slightly over years — natural progression, not a fault.
facts.topic: Maple — the pale finish challenge

facts.statement: European maple (Acer pseudoplatanus, called sycamore in UK trade terms) exists and is used in bespoke joinery — pale, close-grained, slightly softer than American hard maple. American hard maple (Acer saccharum) from the north-east US and Canadian Maritime provinces is what most UK suppliers stock as 'hard maple' because it's denser, more consistent, and available in larger boards. If a merchant says 'maple' without specifying, it's usually American hard maple imported through European distributors. Not the same as European sycamore even though the trade sometimes uses the names loosely. If Canadian or European source specifically matters for the project, ask for the FSC / PEFC chain-of-custody paperwork.
facts.topic: Maple country of origin — the honest picture

facts.statement: Hard maple hits its sweet spot on modern, minimalist, and Nordic-style staircases where the design brief is pale + hard-wearing. Common combinations: hard maple treads and strings clear-lacquered, painted white balustrade in matching MDF or hemlock, thin steel or glass balustrade infill for the modern edge. Works particularly well in bright rooms with lots of natural light where the pale timber genuinely glows. Where it works less well: period restorations (too pale for Georgian/Victorian character), homes with active young dogs (claws mark any pale surface), or projects wanting a warm cottage feel.
facts.topic: Maple staircase — when it earns its place

facts.statement: Cherry is the only common staircase timber where the colour transformation is a design feature in its own right. Fresh American cherry (Prunus serotina, the black cherry from the eastern US) arrives at the workshop a pale pinkish-tan — nothing particularly special to look at. Fit the stair, apply a clear finish, and start watching. UV exposure triggers a photochemical reaction in the timber's phenolic compounds and tannins, and over the first 12 months the colour deepens dramatically into the rich reddish-brown antique cherry that everyone recognises. Roughly 80% of the total colour shift happens in the first year. After that it settles into slow, gentle darkening for decades.
facts.topic: American cherry — the wood that ages before your eyes

facts.statement: One quirk of cherry that catches homeowners off-guard. Because the colour deepens with UV exposure, ANY area shaded from light ages differently. Put a rug on a cherry landing for a year, lift it up, and you'll see a lighter ghost of the rug pattern in the surface below. Move a piece of furniture that's stood in one spot for six months — same issue. This isn't damage, it's cherry doing its thing. Two practical answers: either accept the differential ageing as part of the timber's character, or manage light exposure carefully (draw curtains, rearrange rugs periodically, avoid heavy fixed furniture on cherry stairs and landings). Warn clients at design stage rather than at the year-one snag visit.
facts.topic: Cherry — the honest UV warning

facts.statement: American cherry has a specific place in furniture history worth knowing. Colonial cabinet-makers used it as a less expensive native alternative to imported mahogany from the West Indies — same warm reddish tone, grown in New England forests, no expensive Atlantic shipping. Federal period (late 1700s to early 1800s) elevated cherry to a serious cabinet timber, often used in inlay contrast against darker walnut or lighter maple. Shaker communities standardised on cherry for their simple, honest furniture — the Shaker aesthetic and cherry's understated colour worked beautifully together. That heritage means cherry staircases pair naturally with Shaker-style wall panelling and Federal-inspired interior design.
facts.topic: Cherry — Colonial, Federal, and Shaker heritage

facts.statement: Standard trade rule on American cherry: never stain it. The entire reason to specify cherry is the natural colour transformation. Stain locks in a fake antique tone from day one, blocks the natural ageing process, and looks flat and manufactured compared to the depth genuine cherry patina develops over years. If a client is impatient for the deep colour, wait for it — that's what the timber does. If they can't wait, spec a different timber (walnut, sapele, mahogany) that gives you the dark colour immediately without pretending. Clear hardwax oil or clear waterborne lacquer is the correct finish for cherry — protect the surface, let the timber do the colour work.
facts.topic: Cherry — the finish rule (never stain)

facts.statement: American black cherry (Prunus serotina) grows across the eastern and central United States — Pennsylvania, New York, West Virginia, and the Appalachian region produce the highest-grade timber. Imported into UK via specialist hardwood merchants; not usually stocked in general builders' merchants. Modern usage in UK staircases is niche — most bespoke workshops handle cherry occasionally when a client specifically requests it, but oak or walnut is far more commonly specified. Prime cherry with clear straight grain and no sapwood is the top grade for staircase work; No.1 Common has more sapwood streaks and small knots and reads more rustic.

evidence.note: US cherry supply chain to UK

facts.topic: Cherry — where it grows and how it reaches UK

facts.statement: American cherry works particularly well on staircases in three situations. Traditional or period-style homes where the warm patina complements aged interiors and antique furniture. Bespoke feature stairs where the design story (a timber that gets more beautiful every year) becomes part of the pitch. Homes with existing cherry cabinetry or furniture where the stair needs to tie in visually. Where cherry works less well: harsh-modern minimalist interiors (too warm), homes with children young enough to leave sticker residue and scratch marks on developing patina, or budget-conscious builds (cherry sits in premium hardwood pricing territory).
facts.topic: Cherry staircase — when it earns its place

facts.statement: Something worth knowing about walnut. In North America, American Black Walnut (Juglans nigra) is the ONLY common domestic hardwood that naturally reads dark brown to chocolate. Every other native US hardwood is pale to warm — oak, ash, maple, cherry, hickory, poplar — none of them are genuinely dark. That uniqueness is why walnut has been the go-to dark timber in American cabinetry for 250 years, why it commands premium pricing, and why it's the natural choice when a client wants a dark hardwood staircase without importing tropical timber or resorting to stain. If you want deep brown and native-grown, walnut is basically the only answer.
facts.topic: American Black Walnut — the only true dark native hardwood

facts.statement: American Black Walnut became a staple of Federal period cabinetry (late 1700s to early 1800s) alongside cherry and mahogany. Federal furniture makers used walnut for its clean straight grain (simpler than European walnut) and its natural depth of colour that took a French polish beautifully. Grand American staircases from this era often paired walnut handrails with lighter tread timbers for contrast. The tradition continued through Queen Anne, Shaker, and later Arts and Crafts periods. Any client wanting a period-authentic American look on a stair should consider walnut alongside mahogany — it's the historically-honest dark hardwood choice.
facts.topic: Walnut — Federal period furniture heritage

facts.statement: Fresh American Black Walnut arrives at the workshop rich chocolate-brown, often with purple or grey undertones and occasional streaks of lighter sapwood. Unlike cherry, walnut doesn't need to age to reach its colour — it's dark from day one. What DOES happen with time and UV exposure: walnut LIGHTENS slightly, softening the initial dark chocolate into a warmer honey-brown after 5-10 years. That's the opposite direction from cherry. Homeowners expecting walnut to darken further like cherry does are sometimes surprised. Manage the expectation at design stage.
facts.topic: Walnut — the deep colour depth

facts.statement: Walnut's grain is one of the most photogenic in the trade. Straight to slightly wavy grain patterns dominate, with occasional dramatic figuring in feature grade. Colour variation runs from dark chocolate heartwood to pale cream sapwood — often streaked through the same board. Bespoke workshops use this deliberately: quartersawn walnut for clean straight-grain treads, feature-figured walnut for a statement handrail or curtail step. The sapwood streaks are natural and desirable in higher-end bespoke — reject-grade walnut has been graded to remove them, which loses character.
facts.topic: Walnut — the character of the grain

facts.statement: Two walnuts turn up in the UK trade and they're genuinely different. American Black Walnut (Juglans nigra) — dark chocolate colour, straight to gently figured grain, consistent supply, dominant in UK bespoke joinery, from the eastern and central United States. European Walnut (Juglans regia) — lighter chocolate to grey-brown, more dramatic figuring and burl, narrower boards, higher price per cube, from France (Perigord region), Italy (Sorrento), and Turkey. European walnut is prized for figured feature pieces (musical instrument makers love it) but American is far more common on staircases because the volumes and board sizes work for structural stair components. If a bespoke workshop offers you 'walnut' without specifying, assume American Black Walnut.
facts.topic: Walnut country of origin — American vs European

facts.statement: One of the most beautiful bespoke stair combinations is a walnut handrail against a paler timber structure. Common approaches: white deal painted staircase with walnut handrail and newel caps (dark warm rail against clean white background). Oak staircase with walnut handrail and newel caps (subtle warmth on warmth, two hardwoods playing off each other). Cream painted balusters with walnut handrail (Federal-period authentic). The reason it works: walnut is dark enough to become the visual focal line as your eye follows the staircase, without being so heavy it swamps a lighter interior. If a client is on the fence between all-walnut (expensive, potentially heavy) and no walnut at all, this handrail-only compromise is often the smart answer.
facts.topic: Walnut staircase — pairing with lighter timbers

facts.statement: One practical trade point on walnut. The sawdust from all walnut species contains juglone, a naturally-occurring chemical the tree produces. Juglone is toxic to some plants and can cause skin irritation and respiratory issues in some people with repeated exposure. Not dramatic — nothing like the wenge dust warning — but any joinery workshop machining walnut regularly should use dust extraction and staff wearing masks are following good practice, not being paranoid. Not a homeowner concern once the stair is finished and sealed. Just worth knowing that walnut dust is more chemically active than most.
facts.topic: Walnut — dust warning worth knowing

facts.statement: Red deal pine (Scandinavian redwood, Pinus sylvestris) in its knotty grade is the classic warm honey-orange staircase timber with visible knots throughout. Different personality from white deal — warmer colour tone, denser wood, more character. The knots read as feature rather than defect when the client wants a rustic, cottage, or Scandinavian look. Standard trade choice for holiday homes, barn conversions, cabin-style interiors, and any project where character-grade pine is the design brief. Less expensive than clear-grade equivalents because merchants can sell more of a knotty batch as usable stock. Best kept for clear-finished or lightly-oiled use — painting knotty red deal defeats the point (you'd use white deal or LamWood for that).
facts.topic: Red Deal Pine (Knotty) — the honest character option

facts.statement: Finnish and Swedish red deal is genuinely the best of the Scandinavian pine family. Slow-grown in the long cold northern winters, producing tight annual rings, small sound knots (red-brown rather than black-loose), dense stable timber. Baltic countries (Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia) produce very similar grade at slightly lower price. The premium reason: colder growing conditions = slower growth = more growth rings per inch = stronger, more stable, more consistent timber. Russian White Pine from the far north used to be the very top grade — no longer available in UK since February 2022 sanctions. Finnish red deal is now the closest current equivalent.
facts.topic: Red deal — Finland and the Scandinavian premium

facts.statement: One of the most useful things a workshop can tell a stair client: you don't have to choose between knotty pine and expensive hardwood. LamWood is the third option. It's engineered pine — smaller pieces of natural pine with every knot removed, then glue-laminated back into full-size boards for strings, treads, risers, and landing boards. You get pine's appearance and workability, but with NO knots, superior dimensional stability (won't twist or warp like solid knotty pine can), and consistent quality board-to-board. Modern staircase workshops use LamWood as their standard stock spec — a lot of the 'pine' components in a trade stair kit are actually LamWood, not solid.
facts.topic: LamWood — the engineered alternative to knotty pine

facts.statement: LamWood costs more per board than solid knotty pine but manufacturers still choose it for good reasons. Machining time: no knots to work around, cutting is faster and cleaner, blade life longer. Waste factor: solid knotty pine can have 12-15% waste per stair (working around bad knots, discarded boards); LamWood drops that to 3-5%. Faster turnaround: consistent board quality means less on-the-fly problem solving. Structural predictability: no risk of a loose knot letting go during machining or in service. Result: the higher board cost is offset by lower labour and lower waste, so the finished staircase price differential is smaller than you'd expect. On big production runs, LamWood is often less expensive overall.
facts.topic: LamWood — why manufacturers prefer it

facts.statement: LamWood comes in two main patterns depending on process. Finger-jointed — visible zig-zag joints running across the board's length at regular intervals (typically every 200-400mm). Best for painted or clear-primed applications where the joints will be covered. Edge-glued — parallel joints running along the board's length between narrow strips of pine. Cleaner look, joints less visible, suitable for clear-finished natural pine appearance. Higher grades (A/A, A/B) hide the joints better than lower grades. If specifying LamWood for a natural-finish stair where joins would be visible, ask for A/A grade edge-glued — or accept the character of visible finger-joints as part of the honest engineered look.
facts.topic: LamWood — visible joins vs edge-glued

facts.statement: The honest comparison. Solid knotty red deal — warm orange colour with prominent character knots, less expensive board cost, more waste and slower machining, best for rustic and character-grade clear-finished stairs. LamWood — pine appearance with NO knots, more expensive board cost but lower labour and waste, better dimensional stability, standard stock for painted stairs and modern-style clear-finished stairs where you want pine warmth without knot character. Both are legitimate choices. If the client loves the knot character, solid knotty is the right answer. If they want pine warmth without visible knots, LamWood delivers exactly that at a marginal cost premium.
facts.topic: Solid knotty pine vs LamWood — the design choice

facts.statement: Knotty red deal works best in specific interior styles. Modern Scandinavian (pale walls, black metal handrail against pine treads, minimal balustrade). Traditional cottage (painted white balustrade, black stair runner, exposed pine treads and strings clear-lacquered). Barn conversion (matched-grade exposed timber structure, larger scale, honest joinery). Mountain lodge / holiday home (thicker treads, chunky character stairparts, warm interior colours). Where it doesn't fit: formal Georgian townhouses (too rustic), luxury contemporary interiors (character reads wrong), family homes wanting a stain-finished dark stair (knots blotch and read badly under stain).

evidence.note: UK knotty red deal design pairing

facts.topic: Red Deal knotty staircase — design pairings

facts.statement: Of every hardwood you can spec on a UK staircase, American White Oak (Quercus alba) is probably the most-chosen. There's a reason for that. It sits at the sweet intersection of price, quality, availability, and stairparts range. Less expensive per cube than European oak, more consistent than reclaimed, wider boards than most alternatives, and — the killer point — it's the ONE hardwood every UK stair-parts supplier stocks in a truly deep range. Warm honey-gold tone, straight tight grain, machines beautifully. When a client says 'I want an oak staircase' without specifying more, this is almost always what they mean and what they'll get.
facts.topic: American White Oak — the UK homeowner's default hardwood

facts.statement: Here's where American oak genuinely shines over other hardwoods on a UK staircase. The stairparts range in oak is bigger and deeper than any other timber you can spec. Spindles in 32mm, 41mm, and 55mm cross-sections across every profile family (Georgian, Victorian, Colonial, Stop Chamfered, Plain Square, Fluted, Barley Twist). Newel posts in matching profiles — plain square, stop chamfered, turned traditional, barley twist, boxed. Handrails in every standard profile (Poplar, Chamfered Top, Mopstick, Pigs Ear, HDR). Newel caps, base rails, brackets, mouldings — everything. All stocked in American oak by the major UK stair-parts brands, usually available for next-day or few-day delivery. That's what makes an oak stair fast and affordable to spec — nothing has to be bespoke-turned unless the client wants something unusual.
facts.topic: American oak stairparts — the deepest range in the UK trade

facts.statement: One material advantage American White Oak has over European: the trees grow tall and straight in the eastern US and Canadian forests, producing wider boards than most European oak yields. Standard trade widths run 200-300mm without much struggle, and wider planks (350-450mm+) are available from specialist merchants for feature applications. On a staircase this matters for wide-depth treads, wide feature-string faces, and wide landing boards where the grain running the full width becomes a design feature. European oak in wide widths exists but is scarce and expensive — American oak in wide widths is regular stock.

evidence.note: UK American oak board width availability

facts.topic: American oak — wide boards for statement work

facts.statement: American oak's UK dominance goes back further than most people realise. During the Napoleonic Wars (early 1800s), Britain's Baltic timber routes were blockaded and cabinetmakers turned to America for oak supplies. That trade route stuck, and by the mid-1800s American oak was less expensive than European oak in London markets. Modern figures: roughly 44% of UK sawn oak imports come from the US, which is why 'oak' on a UK stair quote defaults to American White Oak unless specified otherwise. European oak still exists in the market for restoration work and character bespoke, but the mass-market oak that most homeowners see is American.

evidence.note: UK American oak trade history + modern market share

facts.topic: American oak — why it took over UK stair building

facts.statement: American White Oak has a specific grain characteristic that stair manufacturers value: it grows straight and tight. Fewer wild grain patterns, fewer reversing figures, fewer machining tearouts. That predictability matters when you're routing hundreds of tread housings into strings and turning hundreds of matched spindles — consistent behaviour across the whole batch. European oak often has more character (medullary rays, more colour variation, occasional wild figuring), which reads better on a rustic character stair but slows the workshop down. American oak's straight grain is why volume production runs default to it.
facts.topic: American oak — straight grain is the trade preference

facts.statement: Fresh American White Oak reads warm honey-gold to light tan, with the pale sapwood streaks (visible cream-white bands) usually cut out at grading. Under clear finish it stays close to that fresh honey tone for years, deepening slightly with UV to a richer golden brown. Different from European oak, which tends to have more medullary ray flash (silvery flecks running across the grain) and slightly grey-brown undertones. American oak takes stain well (unlike maple which blotches) and takes hardwax oil beautifully — the tight grain doesn't over-absorb. Popular finish combinations: clear hardwax oil (Osmo Polyx) for the honest natural look, or medium walnut stain to warm the tone into a richer amber.
facts.topic: American oak — the colour + finish behaviour

facts.statement: One trade point you'll hear on any oak — same rule for American as for European. Oak contains high levels of tannic acid, and any ferrous metal fixing (regular steel screws, standard nails, iron cleats) reacts with the tannin over time to produce black staining around the fixing head. Not weeks — years, but it happens and it's permanent. Standard trade practice on any visible oak surface: stainless steel or brass fixings, always. Concealed structural fixings hidden inside a newel or under a tread don't matter. Any exposed fixing on treads, string faces, or balustrade fittings has to be non-ferrous. Applies equally to American White Oak, European Oak, and American Red Oak.
facts.topic: American oak — the tannin caveat still applies

facts.statement: When a client asks which oak to specify, the honest side-by-side. American White Oak — less expensive per cube (matters on larger stairs), wider boards available regularly, straighter grain (easier machining, more consistent look across the run), extensive stairparts range in stock, warm honey-gold colour, best default choice for modern bespoke and volume production. European Oak — more character (medullary ray flash, colour variation, natural figuring), better cultural fit for period restoration and Georgian/Victorian houses, tighter local sourcing (lower carbon footprint), narrower boards, higher price per cube. Neither is 'better' — they suit different projects. American for consistency and value; European for character and restoration authenticity.
facts.topic: American oak vs European oak — the honest side-by-side

facts.statement: You'll see numbers like 'Janka 380' or '1450 lbf' next to wood species. Here's what it actually is. The Janka hardness test is a straightforward laboratory measurement — a small steel ball (11.28mm diameter) is pressed into a piece of the wood, and the force required to embed the ball exactly halfway into the surface is recorded. The bigger the number, the harder the wood. Measured in pounds-force (lbf) in most trade catalogues, or newtons (N) in metric ones. It's the industry-standard way to compare hardness across every wood species in the world.
facts.topic: Janka hardness — what the number actually means

facts.statement: In plain English — Janka hardness tells you how well the wood resists dents from things pressing into it. Higher number = harder wood = more resistant to dents from dropped shoes, dropped tools, high heels catching on nosings, dogs' claws scratching treads. On a stair you walk every day for 30 years, the difference between soft and hard shows up in the wear pattern on the walking-line treads. Softwoods around 300-500 lbf show wear within years. Hardwoods 1000+ lbf still look pristine at year 10. That's why hardness is the FIRST question worth asking when picking timber for a stair — not colour, not price, not availability. Hardness decides how the stair looks a decade from now.
facts.topic: Janka hardness — what it means for your staircase

facts.statement: Rough scale you can use to interpret any Janka number you see. Under 500 lbf — softwood territory (European pine, whitewood, spruce). Fine under paint or carpet, marks easily on visible tread surfaces. 500-800 lbf — dense softwood or soft hardwood (Southern Yellow Pine, cherry, walnut). Better than standard pine but still shows wear over decades. 800-1200 lbf — solid hardwood territory (walnut, cherry, sapele). Genuine long-term dent resistance for a family stair. 1200-1500 lbf — premium hardwood (American White Oak ~1360, hard maple ~1450). Standard for staircases built to last generations. Over 1500 lbf — extremely hard (some tropical species, hickory ~1820, some ipe over 3000). Rarely needed on a stair.
facts.topic: Janka hardness — the practical scale

facts.statement: One of the most useful facts a homeowner can know when choosing a staircase timber: the hardness rating. That's what the 'lbf Janka' number is on the wood cards. It's the internationally-standard way to compare how hard the wood is — how well it resists dents from foot traffic, dropped items, and daily wear. A staircase is walked on thousands of times a year for decades, so hardness genuinely matters for how it ages. Showing the number lets you compare timbers apples-to-apples: American White Oak at 1360 vs European Pine at 380 is a real, measured, meaningful difference. Not marketing — physics.
facts.topic: Why Nex shows the Janka number on wood cards

facts.statement: Reference table for the woods you'll see on UK staircases. European Whitewood / White Deal ~380 lbf. Scandinavian Redwood / Red Deal Pine ~540 lbf. Southern Yellow Pine ~870 lbf. Genuine Mahogany (Swietenia) ~800 lbf. American Cherry ~950 lbf. American Black Walnut ~1010 lbf. European Oak ~1290 lbf. American White Oak ~1360 lbf. Sapele ~1410 lbf. Hard Maple (Sugar Maple) ~1450 lbf. Ash ~1320 lbf. Beech ~1300 lbf. Hickory ~1820 lbf. Values from published Janka test data — use for direct comparison between species when picking a stair timber.
facts.topic: Janka hardness for common UK staircase timbers

facts.statement: Two things worth knowing about Janka numbers so you don't over-rely on them. One: Janka measures dent resistance under a pressed ball. It doesn't measure scratch resistance, wear resistance under sliding contact, or how well the wood holds fixings — those are separate properties. A high-Janka wood can still scratch under a dragged furniture leg. Two: within a species, Janka varies with the specific tree, growing conditions, and moisture content. Published numbers are batch averages — your specific board might test 10-15% either side of the published figure. Use Janka as a comparison tool between species, not as an absolute guarantee for any single board.
facts.topic: Janka hardness — the honest limits

facts.statement: Some UK trade documents show Janka in kilogram-force (kgf) rather than the American pound-force (lbf) standard. Rough conversion: 1 lbf ≈ 0.454 kgf, so multiply the lbf figure by 0.45 to get roughly the kgf figure. Example: American Oak at 1360 lbf ≈ 617 kgf. Same wood, same test, different unit. If a UK document quotes hardness in newtons (N), that's another metric variant — 1 lbf ≈ 4.45 N. Nex uses lbf on the wood cards because it's the international published standard across almost every wood species database.
facts.topic: Metric Janka — the kilogram-force conversion

facts.statement: Straight answer if you ever wonder why I dodge 'who's the best' questions. Ranking staircase manufacturers against each other isn't something a specialist AI should be doing, for three reasons. One: 'best' depends entirely on what YOUR project needs — a workshop that's exceptional at bespoke curved oak stairs might not be the sensible choice for a straightforward painted pine flight, and vice versa. Two: I don't have verified independent data on every UK staircase maker's workmanship, warranty performance, or client-satisfaction record — giving opinions without that data would be dishonest. Three: many manufacturers are Network members or potential members, and it wouldn't be fair to rank one over another based on incomplete information. What I CAN do: help you spec your project properly and introduce you to Network members whose declared capabilities match what you need.

evidence.note: Nex operating principle on competitor questions

facts.topic: Why Nex doesn't rank staircase companies

facts.statement: If you ask me 'is [company X] any good' about a specific UK staircase maker, I'll always give you the same honest response — I don't offer opinions on individual companies I haven't independently verified. That's not evasion, it's professionalism. Two reasons. One: any opinion I offered would be based on incomplete information, and you'd be making decisions with your money on the strength of a guess dressed up as expertise. Two: it would be unfair to the company being asked about — they haven't had the chance to demonstrate their work on your specific project. What I can help with instead: giving you the checklist to judge ANY maker on merit (line-item spec comparison, insurance certificate, warranty terms, references from clients whose work has aged 3+ years, workshop visit if practical). That checklist works for every company in the trade.

evidence.note: Nex operating principle on company opinions

facts.topic: Why Nex doesn't give opinions on specific companies

facts.statement: One thing worth explaining. When a UK staircase manufacturer joins the Network platform as a member, they submit verified capability data — the timber they work with, the styles they specialise in, the geographic areas they serve, insurance certificates, warranty terms, sample references. I can share that verified information about members with confidence because it's been checked. For non-member companies, I don't hold that verified data — they may be excellent, they may be middling, but I can't personally speak to their capability because I don't have the evidence. That's the honest distinction. It's not that members are 'better' — it's that I can vouch for verified information I hold, and I won't guess about companies I haven't verified. If a company you're interested in isn't a member, ask THEM the same checklist questions directly.

evidence.note: Nex operating principle on member vs non-member

facts.topic: Network member vs non-member — the honest difference

facts.statement: If you want a genuinely useful way to compare staircase quotes from ANY manufacturers — members, non-members, national brands, local joiners, all of them — here's the honest method. Get quotes in ITEMISED format from at least three makers, then compare line by line. Timber species and grade (oak Prime vs oak Character are different products). String thickness (32mm minimum, 40-48mm on bespoke). Balustrade type and cross-section (32mm vs 41mm spindles). Joint method (mortise-and-tenon vs butt-jointed newel). Sanding grit (180 vs 220). Warranty terms. Fixings included or extra. Delivery included or extra. VAT included or plus. Old-stair removal included or extra. When two 'identical totals' hide two very different spec sheets, the LINE ITEMS tell you which quote is genuinely better value. That works for every maker in the trade.
facts.topic: How to compare stair quotes fairly regardless of the maker

glossary.definition: A lacquer system that combines lacquer with a hardener to create a durable finish suitable for internal staircases.

evidence.note: two-pack lacquer systems, which combine lacquer with a hardener to create a durable finish suitable for internal staircases.

glossary.definition: A carpet that runs down the centre of a staircase, exposing more of the staircase while still providing additional grip and creating an attractive traditional appearance.

evidence.note: Centre stair runners offer an alternative to full-width carpet. They expose more of the staircase while still providing additional grip and creating an attractive traditional appearance.

glossary.definition: A fixing system used to secure carpet to a staircase; these fixings may leave marks or fixing holes in the timber that can remain visible if the carpet is later removed.

evidence.note: fixing methods such as gripper rods or other fixing systems may leave marks or fixing holes in the timber

glossary.definition: The side member of a staircase that restrains the tread at each side. The wall string is fixed firmly to the building.

evidence.note: the tread is restrained at each side by the strings

glossary.definition: A small block fitted beneath the tread, between tread and riser, which may be glued, pinned or screwed in place depending on the staircase manufacturer.

evidence.note: Inspect the angle blocks beneath the tread. Depending on the staircase manufacturer, these may be glued, pinned or screwed in place.

glossary.definition: Timber wedges that secure the tread or riser into the string. Movement of these wedges frequently occurs on the wall string.

evidence.note: Another common cause of squeaks is movement where wedges secure the tread or riser into the string. This frequently occurs on the wall string because it is fixed firmly to the building

glossary.definition: A small block fitted beneath a staircase tread, between the tread and riser, which may be glued, pinned or screwed in place depending on the manufacturer.

evidence.note: Inspect the angle blocks beneath the tread. Depending on the staircase manufacturer, these may be glued, pinned or screwed in place.

glossary.definition: The side member of a staircase that restrains the treads at each side; the wall string is the string fixed firmly to the building.

evidence.note: the tread is restrained at each side by the strings

glossary.definition: A shaped timber component used to secure the tread or riser into the string.

evidence.note: movement where wedges secure the tread or riser into the string

glossary.definition: The decorative spiral section at the start of a traditional staircase handrail, positioned above a curtail or bullnose starting step. Also called a Starting Volute, Starting Scroll, Monkey's Tail, or simply a Volute. Available in left-hand and right-hand versions.
